stories.Headline: Samsung executive predicts users will direct AI agents through conversation
stories.Summary:
JB Park, President and CEO of Samsung Southwest Asia, wrote an opinion piece arguing that conversation is the real future of artificial intelligence. In the piece, whose views he said were his own, Park wrote that adoption of AI will not happen overnight. He also said that "agents will replace everything else," though the piece stated that agents will not replace everything else. Park predicted that users will tell AI agents what they want and that the agents will then carry out tasks for them. He traced the history of computing from ENIAC, built in the 1940s for the US military and requiring specialised programmers, to the command line, which made computing more accessible.

He also cited Xerox PARC's Alto, which added a mouse and icons in the 1970s, and touchscreens, which brought computing to people's palms. Citing ITU figures, the piece said six billion people used the internet in 2025, up from two billion in 2010, and that 82% of people aged 10 and over have mobile phones. It also cited WHO figures that 1.3 billion people live with disabilities, and said natural language interfaces can serve them. According to the piece, AI breaks plain-language goals into tasks, and India's digital growth has come mostly through mobile phones, including the Digital India BHASHINI initiative, an AI-driven multilingual translation platform.

The piece noted that AI may miss context and produce wrong answers, and that privacy must be part of its design. It cited reports of AI agents acting beyond their instructions, and said experts call for human approval for consequential actions and for agents to be easy to stop. Guardrails are needed to earn public trust, and companies should work with regulatory bodies, with transparency, accountability, safety, security and privacy given priority, according to the piece. Park also said the touch interface did not kill the keyboard and mouse, and that he expects icons and menus to remain with a smart layer on top.

stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping job roles and increasing the demand for cloud and AI talent, according to rediff.com. Tech roles have seen a 7 per cent year-on-year decrease, and hiring for entry-level positions has softened. Large tech firms are experiencing a mass migration of AI talent, with more than 100 core senior positions transferring, as reported by eu.36kr.com. Top annual salaries have reached 20 million RMB.

Tencent's Hunyuan team gained infra expert Zhang Chi and Xiao Xuefeng, who previously led the ByteDance Seed visual AI platform team. Feng Jiashi, the former head of the ByteDance Seed large model visual basic research team, joined the multimodal team at the Tencent AGI Research Center. Nearly 70 technical staff members departed the ByteDance Seed foundational model team. Other moves include Baidu Group Vice President Wu Tian joining Sany Group and Wenxin foundational large model post-training lead Liu Jing moving to Zhongguancun University.

Several executives have left major firms to start their own companies. Former Feishu Products Vice President Qi Junyuan founded Cijian Wuxian, and former Jianying commercialization head Chen Mian founded Yanyu Technology. Lin Junyang, who was the technical lead for the Alibaba Tongyi Qianwen large model, founded Pragmatik Labs. Additionally, Alibaba Cloud Computing Platform Chief Architect Lin Wei launched a startup plan in August 2026.

Recent departures include Hunyuan chief research scientist Pang Tianyu and former Tencent Hunyuan Multimodal Model Department head Bo Liefeng, both of whom left their posts in November 2026. Talent is now flowing into video generation, embodied intelligence, and world models.

SHRM Chief Knowledge Officer Alexander Alonso stated, "governance, not AI itself, determines whether technology ends up empowering or constraining people." SHRM CEO for APAC & MENA Achal Khanna said, "AI is part of the story, but it is not the whole story." Rediff.com reports that one-third of workers in the US use AI tools that are prohibited. stories.Summary:
The Philippines and South Korea are seeking stronger cooperation on artificial intelligence to help micro, small and medium enterprises access new technologies, expand their markets and compete regionally. The push came at the 2026 ROK-Philippines-ASEAN AI+ Connectivity Forum, held in Makati City on Thursday, 26 November 2026. After the Philippines' ASEAN chairship, the forum took place, organized by the Stratbase Institute in partnership with the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in the Philippines.

Prof. Victor Andres Manhit, founder and CEO of the Stratbase Group, said "Digital transformation must be inclusive for it to be meaningful." He called for tools, training and financing for MSMEs, and urged that regional commitments be turned into cross-border trade opportunities. Lee Dong-gi, South Korean Ambassador to the Philippines, said AI cooperation should strengthen local capabilities and create opportunities across ASEAN.

DICT Secretary Jay de Claro cited the ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on AI-Powered MSME Growth, which was adopted during the Philippines' 2026 ASEAN chairship. He also cited Executive Order 131, which adopts the Philippine AI Governance Framework and establishes the National Artificial Intelligence Council. "AI must not become an advantage reserved only for large companies. It must also become an opportunity for our smallest businesses," de Claro said.

Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Leo Herrera-Lim and PCCI President George Barcelon discussed regional digital cooperation at the forum.

stories.Headline: Israel's government fast-tracks data centre permits to build a national AI hub, Netanyahu says
stories.Summary:
Israel's government is fast-tracking data centre construction and cutting red tape to build an AI hub, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said. The national AI plan was announced in June. "We will turn Israel into a global AI superpower," Netanyahu said. In a September interview with Israeli media, he said: "Within five years, we will be the third AI power."

US semiconductor company Nvidia acquired Israeli networking company Mellanox in April 2020 for nearly $7bn. Nvidia's networking revenue was more than $21bn in the third quarter of 2026, about 18 percent of its quarterly revenue. Nvidia Israel has 6,000 employees across seven R&D centres, and a planned campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa is to have up to 10,000 employees.

Ofek Data Center, planned as the largest Israeli facility, is due for completion in the second half of 2029 north of Ashdod port. US digital infrastructure firm Serverfarm and the Israel Infrastructure Fund (IIF) are behind it. Its initial cost is $1.5bn, with $5bn in planned future upgrades. It is to launch with 130MW of capacity and expand to 200MW. Israel currently has 67 data centres, according to research group Data Center Map.

AI data centres were classed as national infrastructure in February, and last month the Israeli Electrical Authority imposed a cap of 200MW on new data centres. "Fast-tracking permits is a governance decision," said Rajiv Dalal, an independent AI governance researcher. "Securing the electricity to run what gets built is a governability question." Eli Cohen, Minister of Energy and Infrastructure, backs nuclear energy for servers. The offshore gas fields Tamar, Leviathan and Karish are in use, and a fourth, Katlan, is expected online in 2027. A gas-fired station of 850MW is planned for Ofek.

"They are the territorial anchor of AI power," said Mark Esposito, a Harvard Berkman Klein scholar. "In the coming years, it will become clear which countries will succeed," said Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate. "Stable local inferencing is going to become an important support," said Mark Muro, a Brookings senior fellow. Roughly 51 percent of the world's data centres are in the US, and the European Commission estimates a data localisation premium of 30 percent or more in the EU. "For politically and security-sensitive applications, you don't want foreign powers to listen in," said Bertin Martens, a Bruegel senior fellow. "Maybe we will be less prone to criticising something," said Simone Vannuccini, a professor at University Cote d'Azur.

Aivres is another Nvidia "elite" partner that previously operated under the name Inspur. The U.S. government blacklisted Inspur firms in March 2023, claiming their servers were used by the Chinese military. Aivres exported Blackwell chips to Southeast Asia, with some going to providers for ByteDance and Alibaba. CBS News reported these exports totaled $3 billion, while Anadolu Ajansı, a Turkish state news agency, reported that exports between April 2024 and February 2026 totaled $5.6 billion.

Research for the CBS investigation was provided by C4ADS, a Washington security nonprofit. While 2CRSi is also an Nvidia elite partner, a $300 million chip smuggling case involved California businessman Greg Lui. Additionally, Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, runs a Singapore company called Megaspeed. U.S. officials have not accused RiCloud AI of any wrongdoing.

stories.Summary:
State Sen. Michelle Hinchey, D-Kingston, has introduced bill S.10741 in the state Senate, according to observertoday.com and post-journal.com. The bill was introduced in November 2026. It would add a section to the state Judiciary Law. The measure would bar judges from relying on fabricated legal authority.

Under the bill, knowing or reckless use of artificial intelligence would be deemed misconduct. AI use alone would not count as misconduct. Good-faith interpretation errors would be exempt, as would immaterial clerical errors and immaterial errors that are quickly corrected. The Commission on Judicial Conduct would weigh factors including the number of fabricated authorities and the effect on the case's disposition.

The factors would also include verification procedures and training, along with repetition and prompt correction. Hinchey said, "New York should not wait for comparable judicial failures to cause harm in this state." She said, "This bill will establish a clear rule of judicial accountability before such misconduct causes substantial harm in New York." She said, "Courts across the country are beginning to confront this reality of AI-generated legal citations."

The Unified Court System released an AI interim policy in October 2025. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, spoke on the Senate floor that month. Grassley found AI errors by staff of two federal judges and urged formal AI guidance measures. The bill awaits Senate consideration.

More than 60% of judges have used an AI tool, and 22.4% used AI weekly or daily. Thirty percent used AI for legal research, and 15.5% used it for document review. Daniel Linna, director of Northwestern Pritzker Law, said, "Even though some judges have been wary, there are plenty who think AI creates opportunities for improving access to the courts."

V.S. Subrahmanian is director of the Northwestern Security & AI Lab. Of the judges surveyed, 45.5% said no AI training was provided. In chambers, 25.9% permit AI, and 7.4% permit and encourage it. Twenty percent formally prohibit AI use, and 17.6% discourage it without prohibiting it. Another 24.1% have no official AI policy.

stories.Headline: Cellular Intelligence Announces Nature Machine Intelligence Publication Establishing a New Scaling Law for Biological AI
stories.Summary:
Cellular Intelligence, a clinical-stage AI biotechnology company based in Boston, announced on 26 November 2026 that Nature Machine Intelligence has published a study titled "A measurement noise scaling law for cellular representation learning." The paper establishes a new scaling law for biological AI, according to the company. It sets measurement noise as a quantifiable scaling dimension alongside dataset and model size. The study analysed more than 2,000 AI model configurations across gene expression, microscopy imaging and protein sequence data. It found a consistent logarithmic relationship between measurement noise and AI performance, with measurement quality predicting performance.

According to the findings, larger datasets and more powerful models alone may not suffice. Many technologies capture under half of RNA molecules per cell, the study notes. Protein sequence models proved resilient to typical sequencing error rates, while single-cell transcriptomic models were constrained by measurement sensitivity. The transformer-based Geneformer model was more resilient to measurement noise, and the scVI variational autoencoder captured more biological information.

The study also introduces tools to estimate sequencing depth. Dr. Allon Klein, scientific co-founder of Cellular Intelligence and a professor of systems biology at Harvard Medical School, co-led the study. "Scaling laws changed how AI investments are made by making performance predictable," Klein said. Micha Breakstone, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Cellular Intelligence, said: "Drug discovery has long relied on trial and error because we lack the ability to reliably predict how cells respond to therapeutic interventions."

Gokul Gowri, Ph.D., a Tayebati Postdoctoral Fellow at MIT, co-led the study, and Dan Raviv, Director of Computational Biology and Machine Learning at Cellular Intelligence, is a co-author. The paper is available at nature.com/articles/s42256-026-01332-7. Cellular Intelligence operates in Boston and Denmark and holds global rights to STEM-PD, a Phase 2-ready cell therapy for Parkinson's disease with FDA Fast Track designation. Media contact Kimberly Ha of KKH Advisors can be reached at 917-291-5744.

stories.Headline: Columbia leads NHLBI precision medicine data center for AI-driven disorder research
stories.Summary:
Columbia University Irving Medical Center has been selected for a central role in the NHLBI Super Intelligence Initiative, formerly the Artificial Intelligence Initiative, the medical center announced on November 17, 2026. The initiative aims to speed the discovery of treatments for heart, lung, blood and sleep disorders. It combines large-scale biomedical data with artificial intelligence and seeks new targets for potential therapies.

Elizabeth Oelsner, an associate professor of medicine at the Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, and R. Graham Barr, the Hamilton Southworth Professor of Medicine and Epidemiology, lead Columbia's team. The team will establish a Precision Medicine Epidemiology Center, which will serve as the initiative's data coordinating center. More than 20 co-investigators from Columbia and its partners are involved. The center will advise on the design and data collection protocols and provide guidance for new AI-enabled studies.

The work builds on Columbia's experience in building cohorts and in cross-cohort collaboration and data harmonization, according to the medical center. Its deep learning work harmonized more than 125,000 lung and cardiac CT scans. Columbia's team will serve on the initiative's Scientific Leadership Committee, alongside researchers from Stanford University and Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

stories.Headline: Congress takes up AI copyright as the TRAIN Act and courts shape training rules
stories.Summary:
When the new Congressional session begins in the new year, AI will remain a top priority for federal lawmakers, and the copyright rules for AI remain unclear. Copyright laws predate generative AI, and whether training on copyrighted works is fair use is unsettled. Human authorship is essential to copyright, a 2023 federal court ruling held, and the D.C. Circuit upheld that ruling in 2025.

The TRAIN Act, the Transparency and Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence Networks Act, would let copyright holders access AI training records. Senator Peter Welch, Democrat of Vermont, Senator Marsha Blackburn, Republican of Tennessee, Senator Adam Schiff, Democrat of California, and Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, sponsored the Senate version, introduced in 2025. Representative Madeleine Dean, Democrat of Pennsylvania, and Representative Nathaniel Moran, Republican of Texas, sponsored the House version, introduced in January. The bill is endorsed by SAG-AFTRA, the Recording Academy and the Authors Guild. Other bills, the COPIED Media Act, S. 1396, the AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act, S. 2367, and the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, a discussion draft, would impose civil liability for training on copyrighted material.

At a 2025 Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on generative AI copyright, Maxwell Pritt, an attorney and panelist, said Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic were "running the largest domestic piracy of intellectual property in our nation's history." David Baldacci, an author, said AI generating storylines that ripped off his work felt like someone had "stolen" everything he'd created. Representative Dean said: "There is no path for creators to know if their work has been used, without their permission and without compensation, to train AI models."

The White House released a national AI legislative framework in March. "Similarly, Congress should not take any actions that would impact the judiciary's resolution of whether training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use," it added. The framework backs voluntary licensing or a collective rights system and protecting voice and likeness from unauthorized use. In September, the Department of Justice filed a brief supporting OpenAI, arguing that training large language models on copyrighted texts is lawful.

The Congressional Research Service released a Generative AI and Copyright Law report last week, finding that existing law applied to AI and that there was no AI-specific statute. Congress can pass clarifying legislation or let courts shape the law. Policymakers could require AI firms to license copyrighted works, though licensing at scale could prove difficult. Options include voluntary licensing, collective rights management, compulsory licensing and creator opt-out systems. Newsweek sought comment from the White House, lawmakers and advocacy groups.

stories.Headline: Illinois Supreme Court appoints 18 members to new AI committee chaired by Jeffrey Goffinet
stories.Summary:
The Illinois Supreme Court announced Tuesday that it has appointed 18 members to a new standing committee on artificial intelligence. The committee will examine the ways in which AI may be applied within the judicial system in a safe and effective manner. Its work includes evaluating risks to data privacy, confidentiality and cybersecurity, as well as compliance with court records rules. The committee will also develop safeguards and ethical standards to protect sensitive information and maintain public confidence. It will examine how AI might streamline court processes and administration, and recommend training, oversight and governance measures.

The Administrative Office of the Illinois Courts will provide administrative support. Members are appointed by the Supreme Court and serve three-year terms. Retired Judge Jeffrey A. Goffinet will chair the committee, having previously co-chaired the Illinois Supreme Court AI Task Force. Third Judicial Circuit Judge Sara D. Smith of Madison County will serve as vice chairperson.

The committee is tasked with preserving “accuracy, fairness, and judicial independence,” and will submit regular reports and recommendations. Members with terms expiring December 31, 2027 include Joel B. Bruckman, a partner at Smith Gambrell & Russell, Cook County Circuit Judge Megan E. Goldish, Nineteenth Judicial Circuit Associate Judge George T. Pappas, Oliver Roberts, a part-time law instructor at Washington University in St. Louis School of Law and co-director of the WashU Law AI Collaborative, First District Appellate Court Justice Rena Van Tine, and Judge Smith. Among those with terms expiring December 31, 2028 are Judge Goffinet, First District Appellate Court Justice Thaddeus L. Wilson, Dev Thain, Program Manager and Head of Academic Partnerships at Spellbook, Ashish S. Prasad, a lecturer at University of Chicago Law School and vice president and general counsel of HaystackID, Matthew Prochaska, Clerk of the Circuit Court of Kendall County, and Eleventh Circuit Judge Sarah R. Duffy. Included among those with terms expiring December 31, 2029 are Mark Palmer, chief counsel of the Illinois Supreme Court Commission on Professionalism, Cook County Circuit Judge Nichole C. Patton, Samuel Oh, chief executive officer at Concorda, Jennifer A. Mao-Jones, president of the University of Pennsylvania JD/MBA Alumni Association, Twelfth Judicial Circuit Judge John Connor, and Fifth District Appellate Court Justice Judy L. Cates.

stories.Headline: Undisclosed AI use affects at least 25 court cases in England and Wales in 2026
stories.Summary:
At least 25 court cases in England and Wales were affected in 2026 by undisclosed use of artificial intelligence, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism whose findings were shared with The Guardian. Judges complained about AI-generated material including witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, The Guardian reporters Robert Booth and Mark Wilding wrote on 26 November 2026. The cases included a High Court tax dispute marred by AI hallucinations, a police officer who used AI to write a witness statement, and a barrister who argued from an AI-invented ruling.

In one case, a police officer uploaded an interview transcript to Microsoft Copilot and asked for "the most impactful victim personal statement possible" and "the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS", according to Startup Fortune. The Court of Appeal dismissed Derbyshire man Jerome Gibson's challenge to his 44-month sentence in R v Jerome Gibson on 22 September, and said "that no police officer should ever prepare a witness statement of any kind in this way". The officer was removed from frontline duty. In a High Court dispute between two Nigerian oil companies valued at $21m and £16m, a judge warned of "the dangers of relying on the product of AI without verification".

Brett Dixon, president of the Law Society, said: "You go from three pages from a lawyer … using human judgment to a rambling 60 pages from a commercial AI". Lord Sales, a supreme court judge, said the court was "increasingly concerned" about AI and that "The greater long-term danger is that human beings gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong". ICC Judge Mark Mullen wrote that AI "has the potential to be wholly unreliable" in a case where a junior solicitor relied on chatbot research that invented a quote from a fictitious statute. Brian Flanagan, associate professor at Maynooth University, said: "We have seen how vulnerable the court system is to the introduction of AI".

Many of the cases involved litigants representing themselves, while legal professionals also used AI to speed research. The Civil Justice Council, in a final report dated 29 October, recommended that witnesses declare AI "has not generated or influenced its substantive content", proposals not yet in force. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We're aware of the growing use of AI in our courts" and cited additional judges, legal officers and case management systems. Matthew Lee, a barrister at Doughty Street Chambers, said he was "really struggling to get a feel for how serious the problem is in the county court and magistrates' courts", and the count of 25 is likely low because most UK judgments are never published.

stories.Headline: Illinois requires large AI developers to assess risks and report incidents within 72 hours
stories.Summary:
Illinois will enact a set of new laws in 2027 covering e-bikes, event tickets, school emergency response, artificial intelligence, health care and insurance, abc7chicago.com reported. The micromobility law regulates toy vehicles and motor-driven bicycles. It raises the top speed for low-speed gas bicycles to 28 miles per hour and bars devices capable of more than 28 miles per hour from sidewalks, bike lanes, paths and roadways. E-bikes above 750 watts and 28 miles per hour would need a license, registration, title and insurance, and retailers could not market such devices as low-speed e-bikes.

The law also sets safety rules and passenger limits for operators under 18. The minimum age is 15 for operating a class 1 or class 2 low-speed e-bike, while a person must be 16 or older to operate a low-speed gas bicycle. A fair ticket access law takes effect Jan. 1 and bans bots, multiple accounts and deceptive resale practices, with event facilities required to report violations to the attorney general. A ban on speculative ticket sales is already in effect.

Alyssa's Law strengthens school emergency response by requiring districts and private schools to consider a mobile panic alert system by the 2028-2029 school year. The systems notify first responders and integrate with 911. The law is named for Alyssa Alhadeff, who was killed in the 2018 Parkland school shooting. A Blue Envelope Program law also takes effect Jan. 1, establishing a statewide program for people with autism spectrum disorder. The Illinois secretary of state designs and provides the envelopes, which hold vehicle documents, emergency contacts and communication preferences, and the program is voluntary for drivers.

House Bill 4255 adds species including cougars, jaguars, leopards, lions, tigers, bears and elephants to the traveling act animal offense. Senate Bill 315 sets AI safety and transparency standards, requiring large frontier AI developers to assess catastrophic risks, report critical safety incidents and undergo audits, with whistleblower protections for employees. Incidents must be reported within 72 hours, or 24 hours if there is imminent risk, to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and the attorney general, and IEMA is to establish a public reporting mechanism with the attorney general. Annual independent audits are required, with redacted reports published.

A dental coverage reimbursement law takes effect Jan. 1, barring insurers from requiring card or electronic payment only and from using payment preference as a credentialing factor. Diaper packaging must list ingredients in descending order, with ingredients at 1% or less exempt. House Bill 4698 requires notice of possible separate billing at offices, clinics and group practices, but not individual providers. Facilities must refer residents only to licensed home service providers and display Department of Public Health educational materials, with a $1,000 civil penalty for violating the referral requirements.

House Bill 4859 clarifies that share tables meet the food-sharing plan requirement; share tables hold unopened food for others at no cost. House Bill 4273 limits homeowners insurance premium increases, requiring 60 days' notice for increases over 10% and barring premiums that are excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory. House Bill 4788 requires CPR training on breasted and non-breasted manikins beginning in the 2029-2030 school year. Senate Bill 3314 requires an annual faculty teaching load report from the Illinois Board of Higher Education covering credit hours by institution, tenure, degree and certification.

House Bill 4397 updates school psychologist credentialing and scope, aligning it with National Association of School Psychologists standards. Senate Bill 2762 expands coverage for seizure detection devices, prohibiting prior authorization and cost-sharing for covered devices and extending coverage to state employee, local government, school and Medicaid plans. Senate Bill 3037 updates the Illinois Energy Efficient Building Act, incorporating ANSI/IES lighting standards into the Stretch Energy Code.

Separately, fintech.global reported that the EU AI Act is the first regulation focused entirely on AI. It cited a Goldman Sachs survey of 434 chief investment and financial officers finding that 62% of firms already use AI, up from 48% in 2025, and an EIOPA report that 40% of firms use generative AI in customer service and 32% in claims management. stories.Headline: Lenders pause billions in ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent data centre loans after US chip curbs
stories.Summary:
Lenders have paused billions of dollars in data centre loans tied to ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, according to Bloomberg, following legal and export control risks raised by new US chip curbs. Banks are delaying or dropping deals, including financing for Bridge Data Centres, Digital Halo and Aolani, and are reviewing their exposure through loan sales and risk transfers. More than US$49 billion in data centre lending has been made since 2023, and projects are not expected to stop.

Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres is seeking a US$6.6 billion loan, equivalent to S$8.51 billion, for Malaysian facilities used by ByteDance. A US$372 million loan is sought for the Digital Halo data centre in Malaysia, backed by Partners Group, and one bank passed on the fully underwritten deal. Multiple banks are reassessing a US$480 million loan for Singapore-based Aolani, which is linked to Alibaba. Bain referred questions to BDC, which declined to comment, and ByteDance did not respond to a request for comment. Digital Halo, Aolani and Alibaba did not respond to questions, and Partners Group declined to comment.

Last week the US announced a licence requirement for advanced AI chip purchases, and data centres leasing compute to Chinese firms in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil need a separate licence, with a 90-day window to obtain one. More than twelve bankers said teams were awaiting answers, and the curbs would at least delay potential deals. A sweeping review of data centre clients has been launched by Singapore's major banks, and Citigroup, Standard Chartered and these banks are reducing AI and data centre debt exposure through secondary loan sales and significant risk transfers, with some doing so. A UOB representative declined to comment, citing deal confidentiality, while an SRT deal of around US$1 billion is being sought by United Overseas Bank to offload data centre and infrastructure loan risks.

Private lenders are growing more cautious: at least one fund declined a US$300 million loan to GMI Cloud, an Nvidia cloud partner, for a Thai data centre, and GMI Cloud and Tencent did not answer comment requests. DayOne Data Centers, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, has put a US public listing on hold, and a BlackRock-led consortium is considering lowering its offer for an Asia Pacific data centre portfolio. Ben Kostrzewa, an international trade lawyer at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, said: "It could be a good pause, to take stock and to review these projects, given how frothy the market has been for a while." He added: "It won't stop all these data centers being built, it won't stop the market, but it will slow it all down."

stories.Headline: Peter Gabriel releases album o\i exploring AI and what it means to be human
stories.Summary:
Peter Gabriel, the 76-year-old singer and multi-instrumentalist and former Genesis frontman, has released a new album that reflects on what it means to be human and responds to artificial intelligence, the Macau Daily Times reported. The album is titled "o\i," according to that outlet, while the Bucks County Beacon gives the title as "o/i." It carries 13 tracks, most of them over five minutes, with "One by One (Bright-Side Mix)" running nearly 10 minutes. Among the songs are the upbeat "Who Are We Talking To?", "Been Undone," "Sacrament," "What Lies Ahead" and "Looking for the Happy."

One song from the album was released with each full moon in 2026. The record is a companion piece to Gabriel's 2023 album "i/o." Its lyrics take up nature and mortality, with Christian imagery used occasionally, and its sound draws on world music. The Bucks County Beacon described the non-traditional release as creative by some accounts and hokey by others, and said it subverts the attention economy.

Both outlets described a tension between lighthearted tracks and an urgent message, and said the album has been praised for engaging with current reality. Gabriel, a seven-time Grammy winner who has been inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame twice, has said he fears AI will replace human-created art. The Bucks County Beacon quoted him describing "this fierce intelligence, that challenges the very thing that makes us, us." The Macau Daily Times credited its report to Krysta Fauria of the Associated Press.

stories.Headline: OakBridge hosts India Law AI Tech Summit and awards in New Delhi on November 28
stories.Summary:
OakBridge is hosting the India Law AI Tech Summit (ILATS) and its awards ceremony on November 28 at the Shangri-La Eros in New Delhi, according to Bar and Bench. Dr DY Chandrachud, former Chief Justice of India, and Justice Sanjay Karol, former Supreme Court judge, are attending as Chief Guests. Chandrachud will deliver the inaugural session address, and Karol will give the valedictory address. The awards ceremony follows the valedictory address, and the summit ends with a vote of thanks at 5 PM.

Chandrachud's address is titled "AI for All: AI Governance and Trust, the Case for Judicial Access and an Empowered India." Dr Shardul S Shroff, Executive Chairman of Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas & Co., will speak on "The Law Firm of Tomorrow: Technology, Talent and Transformation." Dr Lalit Bhasin, President of the Society of Indian Law Firms (SILF), will address "Expanding Role of AI Legal-Tech - A catalyst for Law & Justice Transformation." Dr Shailesh Haribhakti, Board Chairperson and Director for leading Indian companies, will speak on "The AI-Native Boardroom: From Hindsight to Foresight," and L Badri Narayanan, Executive Partner at Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan, on "From AI Pilots to Enterprise Scale: The Legal Architecture for Trustworthy AI."

Panel discussions follow the addresses. Brian Tang, Founding Executive Director of LITE Lab HKU and Co-Chair of ALITA, moderates the first panel on "Innovating for World Class AI-Infused Legal Service Delivery." Prof (Dr) Mini Srivastava, Assistant Professor at Amity University, moderates the second, "The Great Legal Services Reset: What GCs Expect, What Law Firms Must Change and Where Technology Fits In." Anghrija Chakraborty, Leader for Governance, Risk & Compliance and Data Privacy & AI Governance, moderates the third, "The Privilege Gap: DPDP, Confidentiality and Cross-Border Data," and Ashima Ohri moderates the fourth, "Accelerating AI Adoption for Governance and Excellence."

Panelists include Komal Gupta, Chief Innovation Officer at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas; Sara Narassimadevera, Assistant General Counsel for Asia Pacific at McKinsey & Company; Kanan Dhru, General Partner at Ritam Ventures; and Rohit Shukla, Chief Digital Officer at Khaitan & Co. Others are Ravi Singhania, Managing Partner at Singhania & Partners; Sanjeev Kumar Sharma, Senior Partner and National Head of Litigation & Dispute Resolution at White & Brief; and Lakshika Joshi of Harvard Business Publishing. The lineup also includes Chitra Nair of Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, Vatsal Gaur, Founder and CEO of LextronAI, Sachin Kalra, Deputy General Counsel and Head Regulatory at HT Media Ltd., and Dr A Venkatesan, General Manager at GAIL (India) Limited. Niti Mittal, General Counsel at Coforge; Dr Shruti Bedi, Professor and Director at UILS, Panjab University; Khushboo Khandelwal, Senior Vice President and Head of Legal, Secretarial & Compliance at Bajaj Capital Ltd; Ira Dhasmana, VP and Legal Head at Sinch Cloud Communication Services India Pvt Ltd; Rajiv Malik, Legal Leader at LG Electronics; and Parvesh Kheterpal, General Counsel at AMPYR Energy are also listed.

According to Bar and Bench, among General Counsel and legal leaders, leadership and impact in technology adoption, compliance and governance are recognised by the awards.

stories.Headline: Trump reinstates Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, signaling US AI regulation is a non-starter
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang denied that President Donald Trump played any role in his return as Nvidia’s chief executive, calling the claim “completely untrue” at a town hall on the 24th. Reports had said Trump called a board meeting, and that his administration assured the board there was no national security threat. Huang said “the board carried out the duties.” Trump, however, said he persuaded the board, adding, “I think my involvement was very important.”

Trump gained $15 million from Nvidia shares after the stock surged 30 percent. He traded Nvidia shares 44 times between January and September, with buys of $6 million and $17 million and sells of $4 million and $12 million. His holdings were worth between $6 million and $71 million on September 23. Democratic Senator Ron Wyden said, “Huang’s return shows that our national security is for sale.”

Huang apologised to staff on Tuesday and said he was in therapy. He resigned on 12 November over extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy. The Nvidia board initially said there would be no reinstatement, but later called Huang “the right person to lead Nvidia.” Huang said, “I made some terrible mistakes,” and that breaking the code of conduct was “not acceptable.” He dismissed the claim of Trump pressure.

Trump said, “I spoke to them,” and, “And I convinced them.” Nvidia shares rose 30 percent on Tuesday but fell 6 percent at the close. Fawad Razaqzada, an analyst at Forex.com, said, “The optimism faded quickly.” Ken Mahoney, president of Mahoney Asset Management, called it a “one-day wonder.” Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, said, “There’s no precedent for any of this.”

Trump, who is 80, invited himself onto the board call and assured the board there would be no justice department action. The justice department is headed by Trump’s former personal lawyer. Trump intervened to halt an AI stock plunge after top tech investors told him the economy depended on Huang. The move breaks with the U.S. free enterprise tradition; in 2009 the White House secured the departure of GM’s head, and former President Barack Obama did not boast about it.

Trump held 370,000 Nvidia shares as of September 30. AI shares have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid bubble fears since ChatGPT’s 2022 launch. Mahoney said, “sellers have absolute control of the market here.” Nvidia processors are key for AI models, and Nvidia became a central bank for AI startups. Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said, “Jensen out of Nvidia basically was the equivalent,” and, “He is the AI bank.”

The board is still overseeing an internal investigation into Chinese espionage, and the justice department is investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore company that allegedly routed Nvidia processors to China. Megaspeed executive Alice Huang stepped down in 2025. The SEC has opened an inquiry into Nvidia accounting. U.S. Attorney-General Todd Blanche said, “Nvidia is a good corporate citizen.” Huang is set to appear at a closed-door House hearing on December 1 and a livestreamed Senate hearing on December 3. Ives said, “Jensen is like the pilot on the aeroplane.” Politicians from both parties are angry, and Democrats take control of Congress in January.

stories.Headline: US Treasury proposes broad ban on American AI investments in China
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Treasury Department has proposed a new rule under the COINS Act that would strictly limit American investments in foreign entities developing artificial intelligence, which the proposal calls super intelligence. This rule would replace current tiered regulations and technical thresholds with a broad ban on any investment in companies creating these systems, regardless of their intended use. Additionally, the proposal expands restrictions on quantum technology to include the development of related software and algorithms.

The rule targets companies linked to countries of concern, specifically those influenced by China. It introduces a new control test to identify these entities and includes a list of Chinese military companies. Penalties for violations could reach $250,000 or twice the value of the transaction. Meanwhile, the administration is considering a separate requirement for U.S. firms to disclose if they use Chinese AI models. Interested parties must submit their comments on the proposed rule by December 7, 2026.

stories.Headline: Bank of England flags rising financial risks as AI-linked borrowing grows
stories.Summary:
The Bank of England said risks to the global financial system have grown further in recent months, as global borrowing costs rose and the Middle East conflict continued. In its half-yearly Financial Stability Report, the central bank said AI hyperscalers are on track to issue more than US$300 billion of bonds this year, according to businesstimes.com.sg. Yahoo Finance put the figure at more than $305 billion of debt for building AI data centres. The Bank said valuations remain "stretched" on some measures and depend on tech firms delivering AI profits.

The Bank flagged complex borrowing structures for AI and data centres as a worry. It said the sector's debt issuance exceeded most governments' annual borrowing, including Britain's. The Bank said that stress in one area was increasingly likely to propagate to another because of "the very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing - in a form that is increasingly complex, circular and opaque". Share prices on major indices are down around 4 to 6 per cent over the past three months, though spillovers to other markets have been limited so far.

Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation at the Bank of England, said: "It's a very live part of our supervision." The resilience of AI sentiment is a top Bank priority, Yahoo Finance reported. Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, declined to comment on Nvidia turmoil and US governance, saying: "I think the UK has made good choices in that respect." The Bank flagged risks from frontier AI models and from long-term quantum computer encryption. It said: "The immediate financial stability priority is an orderly transition to quantum-resistant cryptography." Bailey urged international testing of AI models, including with China, saying: "AI does not stop at the borders, and so we need to tackle these questions together."

The Bank set an end-2031 deadline for quantum-resistant cryptography on high-priority systems and end-2035 for all remaining systems, saying systemically important firms should move earlier. It urged firms to avoid relying on a single critical software provider, citing Microsoft and Google cloud outages. The Bank expects inflation near 5 per cent in 2027. It said that over the next three years, 6.5 million British households are likely to face higher monthly mortgage payments, with a median £100 increase, less than in 2023 and 2024. Around a million households that last refinanced before the 2022 rate rises face a median £200 increase next year, Yahoo Finance reported. The Bank judged household finances resilient, with debt and servicing costs below pre-crisis levels, and announced on Thursday that it plans lower capital requirements for more domestically focused British lenders.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns open-source AI could let attackers target banks and hospitals
stories.Summary:
Mehdi Hasan, a journalist, reacted on X on Wednesday, November 25, to comments Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder, made about artificial intelligence. Gates warned that AI could be used to attack banks, hospitals and power grids. He made the remarks during an appearance at Financial Times Live. Hasan posted his reaction on X. Gates said that "hospitals, the electric network, banks, all depend on a very complex set of software."

He pointed to the "offensive capability of AI models to find flaws," and singled out "particularly the open source where you take out all of the monitoring and safeguards." He called for AI regulation in the United States and worldwide. He also praised AI while noting that it could cause job losses. Hasan wrote on X that "What's so frustrating is that why are all these people all saying this now, all at the end of 2026." He added that "they didn't realize or know this beforehand or could have warned."

Gates said AI could also be used to build defensive software, which he estimated would take about five years. In an episode of the Decoder Podcast released October 22, he said, "My big concern is this 20-year transition period," referring to a 20-year period of AI disruption. He said AI performs white-collar jobs more cheaply, faster and more accurately, while some tasks stay with humans, such as art, childcare and sports. He said work gives people purpose, and he asserted the need for AI regulations.

stories.Headline: CharacterAI auctions 21 million users' private chats after bankruptcy filing
stories.Summary:
CharacterAI, a US AI chatbot company, has put its platform and user chat records up for auction after filing for bankruptcy protection in October. The sale covers the private conversations of more than 21 million accounts, ranging from mental health discussions to sexual content. Court approval of the auction was reported on the 25th, with the sale handled through the US Bankruptcy Court in Delaware. The auction, set for the 1st of next month, has a minimum bid of $10 million, and a bidder affiliated with Octave Advisors is involved.

Risk scores and trained AI models are also part of the sale. The company once had over 20 million monthly users, including more than 2.1 million minor accounts. An exception in its terms allowed the transfer of assets in a sale. A privacy monitor was appointed by the court, and the sale was asked to be blocked by the attorneys general of about 40 states.

South Korean users face similar risks, according to the report. Korean law allows such a transfer without consent, requiring only advance notice and an option to refuse, and Korea has no bankruptcy privacy review system. Domestic chatbots such as Zeta by Scatter Lab and Crack by Wrtn Technologies keep chats until they are deleted. Choi Byung-ho, a Korea University professor, said, "Personal data should be viewed as a kind of 'rental (lending)' concept, and withdrawal should be possible at any time."

stories.Headline: Netflix builds Quasar to assess API change impact before releases
stories.Summary:
Netflix, the streaming company, has developed an internal tool called Quasar that identifies repositories using library API symbols and assesses the downstream impact before releases, according to techgig.com. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons and reports affected repositories, dependency versions and call sites. It was built to address the limits of compatibility tools, dependency graphs and text searches. Quasar uses the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, which indexes symbol definitions and references. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, and the data is stored in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queried through Amazon Athena.

The tool compares API definitions between commits in pull request analysis and finds added, removed and modified symbols. In a Netflix example involving the removal of a deprecated method, 137 repositories were affected across three library versions. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes and incomplete coverage are among the blind spots, and an API being unused is not proven by the absence of indexed references. Antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, said "observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths." Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team, "acknowledged these blind spots and described ongoing work to complement static evidence with runtime analysis."

The signals inform removal decisions but do not guarantee safe deletion. Quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation. SCIP supports Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes, with Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Findings are exposed through REST, GraphQL and an MCP server to developers and coding agents. Netflix plans to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, with agents identifying public API changes before pull requests.

stories.Headline: New York attorney general Letitia James forms ASSET unit to enforce AI safety laws
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on November 17, 2026 that she has created the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency (ASSET) Unit within the Office of the Attorney General. The unit sits in the Economic Justice Division and works with the Bureau of Internet and Technology. It leads enforcement of the RAISE Act and other AI safety laws, develops policy proposals and provides technical expertise for investigations. Data privacy, digital scams, cybersecurity and online safety are among its priorities, and the office encourages whistleblower complaints from AI employees.

Public disclosure of safety measures and prompt reporting of safety incidents are required of frontier AI model developers under the RAISE Act, which takes effect January 1, 2027 and regulates them. A ban on unsafe chatbot features for children under bill S.9051B/A.10379C begins in June 2027. The office also pointed to General Business Law Article 47 on chatbot suicide detection, the SHIELD Act's requirement for reasonable data security practices, the Synthetic Performer Disclosure Act effective June 2026 and Penal Law § 245.15 on intimate images, alongside its broad civil enforcement authority.

Crowell & Moring LLP said: "AI-enforcement exposure extends beyond AI developers to AI deployers and users." The office advised companies to map applicable AI obligations, strengthen safety and incident-response controls and align public AI claims with their practices.

stories.Headline: Character.AI names Smirks and Pangs as stalking horse bidder for user data auction
stories.Summary:
Character.AI, a failed chatbot startup, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October and announced a plan to sell the company and its assets. On November 13, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC was incorporated in Delaware, and on November 14, Character.AI named it as the stalking horse bidder, the initial bidder that opens an auction. The bid covers the consumer app and user data, with Smirks and Pangs offering $10 million for the data. Character.AI sought to keep the bidder's backers secret, and other bidders have not yet been disclosed.

Last week, 42 state attorneys general moved to block the sale, citing the privacy of children's sensitive data. According to the attorneys general, many of the platform's millions of users were underage, including more than 21 million American accounts, of which 2.1 million belonged to minors. Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida, died by suicide in 2024, a death tied to his relationship with an AI character. This week, a judge approved the bid to open the auction, conditioned on revealing the operators, and the auction is slated for December 1.

Octave Advisors, a New York-based investment firm, was revealed as the prospective buyer's backer. Phil Weiser, the Colorado Attorney General, said: "Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder." He added: "A company's financial troubles do not give it the right to disregard its responsibility to protect consumers, especially children." Disney made a separate stalking horse bid of $20 million to license intellectual property, and said it would hire most of the workforce.

stories.Headline: Law scholars argue that banning generative AI in India could violate free speech rights
stories.Summary:
Sanya Darakhshan Kishwar, an assistant professor at Jindal Global Law School, O.P. Jindal Global University, and Taskin Akhtar, a student at National University of Study and Research in Law, Ranchi, argued against a blanket ban on generative AI in a blog post published on 27 November 2026. The post says such a ban could violate free speech rights under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution. It defines hallucination as large language models stating falsehoods confidently, such as an invented fact, quotation or case citation.

The authors argue that harm depends on the tool and the human user, noting that AI results carry a disclaimer that the AI can make mistakes and that users are responsible for verifying results. They point out that India previously banned several Chinese apps, including TikTok and WeChat, which had legally allowed alternatives. Possible bans, they write, range from all free AI tools to a single AI tool, and a blanket ban would mean no exceptions and no comparable alternative.

The post cites the restrictions listed in Article 19(2) of the Indian Constitution, including sovereignty, security, public order and morality, and says falsity or the prospect of being misled is not among them. It also refers to the four questions of the proportionality test.

stories.Headline: Anthropic debuts on public market at $83 per share with near $2 trillion valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of Claude language models, made its public market debut on November 19, 2026, at $83 per share, reaching a market capitalisation of near $2 trillion. By Monday, November 23, 2026, the stock was trading at $84.37. The company, backed by Google and Amazon, had raised $141.1 billion in private funding.

The Hindu In Focus Podcast examined the IPO's impact on AI governance, on global AI users and on the significance for rivals like OpenAI. John Xavier, Technology Editor at The Hindu, said the episode "cuts through the noise and breaks down what news readers need to know about the Anthropic IPO breakout." The article was published on November 25, 2026.

stories.Headline: Morgan Stanley and MUFG prepare a $4.5 billion loan for CoreWeave to fund Meta GPUs in Georgia
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group are preparing to market a $4.5 billion loan for CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV), according to Bloomberg, which reported the plan on Wednesday. The money would finance GPUs for Meta Platforms at a data center in Dalton, Georgia. Marketing could begin as soon as next week. CoreWeave would draw the proceeds from an escrow account, and the chips would serve as collateral. The loan is to be repaid in installments over its life, and it is expected to receive investment-grade ratings because of the Meta contract.

A preliminary yield of 7% to 7.5% is being discussed, though pricing and timing could still change. By comparison, CoreWeave's 9% bonds due 2031 yielded about 18% on Wednesday. On Nov. 10, executives told analysts the company would avoid unsecured debt at prevailing yields and finance its spending with customer-tied loans. At the end of September, total debt at CoreWeave stood at $47.5 billion, including $17.6 billion under delayed-draw term loans. It draws on the facilities as it builds infrastructure and repays principal as contracts generate cash.

In March, Morgan Stanley and MUFG arranged an $8.5 billion facility, and the company has investment-grade ratings from Moody's and Morningstar DBRS. This year, CoreWeave plans $37 billion to $39 billion in capital spending. About 175 megawatts are leased at the Core Scientific Dalton site, with billing for about 75 MW there, according to a Nov. 5 Core Scientific statement, and the CoreWeave buildout is expected to be completed in early 2027. About 590 MW is leased to CoreWeave across five sites.

stories.Headline: Comcast's Elizabeth Chernow Presses for Published Rules on Who Gets Early Access to AI
stories.Summary:
Elizabeth Chernow, associate vice president of public policy at Comcast, will speak on a Dec. 1 panel titled "What Do We Have to Fear? AI and Catastrophic Risk." The panel is scheduled for 9:50 a.m. at an event called Broadband and AI in the Next Congress in Washington. Chernow has been at Comcast since 2010 and serves as secretary of the Communications Sector Coordinating Council. Caroline Zier of OpenAI will also join the panel, which Cat Zakrzewski, a White House reporter at The Washington Post, will moderate.

Chernow co-authored two papers on early access to frontier AI models. The first, "Responsible Advanced Access for Frontier AI Models," was posted May 12 through Aspen Digital. The second, "The IGI Framework for Responsible Early Access to Frontier AI Models," was posted Sept. 17 and calls for published rules on early access. It would have NIST, the federal standards agency, draft cyber-skill criteria, and it names Gold Eagle, the White House AI vulnerability clearinghouse, as the central venue. Executive Order 14409 allows up to 30 days with a model, down from 90 days in an earlier draft.

The second paper warns that "entire segments of critical infrastructure may be left vulnerable" and argues that "critical infrastructure operators should not have to rely on vendor claims alone." It also addresses "collecting, deduplicating, and disseminating these findings."

Rachel Appleton represents Reflection AI, which builds open-weight models and put its Laser agent behind vetted access on Nov. 17, Axios reported. Open questions include whether the 30-day window under Executive Order 14409 is enough for operators, whether eligibility rules should be set in statute, who pays to fix AI-found flaws at smaller networks, and whether Chernow backs federal-only AI cybersecurity rules.

stories.Headline: US and EU law make publishing nonconsensual sexual deepfakes a crime
stories.Summary:
Using AI tools is legal for individuals in the US, UK and EU, and no country was found to ban AI use outright, according to felloai.com. The law judges AI output and how it is subsequently used. The article examines 15 AI uses against the law across those jurisdictions and offers general information, not legal advice.

In the US, publishing a sexual deepfake is a federal crime under the TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed on 19 May 2025, carrying up to 2 years in prison for an adult victim and up to 3 years for a minor victim. The law covers knowingly publishing an intimate digital forgery without consent, and platforms must remove images within 48 hours.

Minnesota bans nudify websites and apps from 1 August 2026, with a civil penalty of up to $500,000 per use sought by the state attorney general. According to the European Parliament, companies offering and using nudifier AI systems are bound by the EU ban on them from 2 December 2026, while private non-professional users fall outside the deployer definition.

In February 2024 the Federal Communications Commission confirmed that AI voices count as an artificial voice under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so AI-voice robocalls need prior express consent. Impersonating a person to deceive or defraud is illegal, and fraud law applies whether the imitation is a mimic or a model. On 14 August 2024 the Federal Trade Commission's final rule banned reviews from nonexistent people, naming AI-generated fake reviews as an example, with civil penalties for violators.

In 2024 the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Delphia and Global Predictions over false claims about their use of AI, and the investment advisers paid $400,000 in total penalties. A January 2025 US Copyright Office report said copyright "does not extend to purely AI-generated material," and prompts alone are insufficient for authorship, while AI-assisted human work keeps protection. Selling AI art is legal but hard to protect, and Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing requires disclosure of AI content.

Spotify allows vocal impersonation only with the artist's authorisation, and YouTube requires disclosure of realistic AI content. Removing a watermark is illegal in some US cases under Section 1202 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which forbids removing copyright management information to hide infringement. Using AI for homework, essays or work is not a crime, though it is a rule question for a school, college or employer; AI application essays count as fraud under Common App policy and break school honour codes, though neither the school nor the application breach is a crime. Resume and cover letter use is legal, though false claims can cost the job, and chat, research, coding help, AI art and images, selling AI books with disclosure, AI music on Spotify or YouTube with limits, and trading bots for one's own account are all legal, with securities law applying to claims rather than the tool. A face swap of a friend with consent is legal, and voice clone legality depends on use, with consent, fraud law and platform rules deciding. The three levels are legal, against the rules and illegal, with penalties of a fine, a lawsuit or prison, and most crimes are old fraud, harassment and copyright laws, as few new laws were written for deepfakes.

stories.Headline: Mateo AI Studio presents an AI-generated interactive period drama at Seoul festival
stories.Summary:
Mateo AI Studio, a Seoul-based AI-native content studio, presented its generative AI production work at the AI Content Festival 2026 at COEX in Seoul, according to a company announcement dated Nov. 27. The studio's "Wiin Theater" (Great Figures Theater) is an interactive period drama made with support from the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA). It runs three episodes, with subjects including the painter Kim Hong-do, Crown Prince Sohyeon and the Joseon official Choe Bu. All of its footage was generated by AI, and viewers choose outcomes at key turning points.

The studio also made "Raphael," which it calls the first fully generative-AI feature film. A combat android who meets the last priest of humanity is followed in the two-hour-18-minute sci-fi action drama, and at the 2026 Marché du Film and at an official Kling AI session in Cannes, key scenes were shown. It was released exclusively at Lotte Cinema on Nov. 25.

CEO Jung Myun-young spoke on Nov. 12 at a conference session titled "New Standards for Investment in the AI Era," which gathered investors and funded founders. In a pre-Series A round in 2026, 2 billion won ($1.4 million) was raised by the studio from investor Smart Study Ventures.

Running its own AI pipeline from pre-production to post-production, the studio builds original film, drama and animation intellectual property, and "Mateo" and "Witness", its 2024 AI short films, won top prizes at Korean and foreign festivals, with the shorts sold to streaming services. The studio is pursuing overseas distribution.

stories.Headline: Reflection AI lobbyist Rachel Appleton urges Congress to require transparency from advanced AI developers
stories.Summary:
Rachel Appleton, government relations lead for the Americas at Reflection AI, will speak on a panel at 9:50 a.m. Dec. 1 at the National Press Club in Washington. The event is titled "Broadband and AI in the Next Congress," and her panel is called "What Do We Have to Fear? AI and Catastrophic Risk." Cat Zakrzewski, a White House reporter for The Washington Post, will moderate. Appleton has urged Congress to require transparency from advanced AI developers, a push aimed at national security risks.

Reflection AI releases model settings for download and modification, and the company argues that open access helps researchers scrutinize safety. Open-weight models publish numerical settings that can be downloaded, run and modified, while closed-weight developers keep settings private and offer service access instead. Reflection's model Beam has published weights, and the company sells services around its models. Its safety framework says open weights allow outside inspection.

Among Reflection's lobbyists, as listed in a federal lobbying disclosure, is Appleton, with topics including AI governance and open models; she is a former federal affairs lead at Anthropic, the maker of the Claude model family, and has also worked with the Senate Judiciary Committee, the Justice Department and Instacart, the grocery delivery company. A 2025 Washingtonian profile of Appleton said transparency legislation protects against "national security risks." At the 2024 South by Southwest conference, she described the EU AI Act's open-source carve-out as "a fairly narrow exception in the end," remarks AI Business reported. She welcomed bipartisan congressional attention to AI, and her remarks explained EU law rather than Reflection policy.

In May, Reflection announced an agreement with the Energy Department for the Genesis Mission, a federal AI-for-science effort, offering an open AI platform to national lab scientists. Users can strip model safeguards after release. A Nov. 5 report by Reflection described Beam tests on weapons, cyberattacks and loss of control, with outside evaluators helping test the model. Reflection rated the added risk "limited" in four assessed categories, a rating it said did not mean the model posed no danger. Open release is Reflection's default, though its framework allows withholding models with irreversible severe risks. Its cybersecurity-testing tool Laser is limited to vetted organizations in early access. Open questions include whether Appleton will pitch open models as a national asset, how California's shutdown duty affects released weights, and whether vetted access extends to open models.

stories.Headline: Bank of Korea governor Shin Hyun-song questions semiconductor stock valuations
stories.Summary:
Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song questioned the valuation of semiconductor stocks at a press conference on Nov. 26, 2026, at the Bank of Korea in Jung-gu, Seoul. He said it was hard to account for the figures involved. “It is difficult to explain the fact that semiconductor companies’ operating profits for this year are 700 trillion won,” he said. He also put the market capitalization of semiconductor stocks at under 2,000 trillion won, against expected national income of 3,000 trillion won this year.

Shin suggested that share prices had fallen too far relative to fundamentals, according to BusinessKorea. He noted that semiconductor prices had risen twofold compared with last year and warned that a sharp correction in chip prices could add to uncertainty. “We have figured out at least the earnings for next year in advance,” he said, citing sales proceeds and long-term contracts.

Samsung Electronics had a market capitalization of about 1,004 trillion won on Nov. 26 and SK hynix about 745 trillion won, for a combined 1,749 trillion won. That is a 58% fall from their combined peak of about 4,174 trillion won on June 25. “This shows how much the stock market is swayed by investor sentiment,” Shin said. “Corporate growth and the stock market share the same roots.”

Shin linked stagnation in the stock market to slower consumption, and the central bank cut its private consumption growth forecast to 1.8% from 2.1%. The report was edited by Park Seon-young of BusinessKorea.

stories.Headline: Zerbib questions who pays for Nvidia software updates in Nokia AI radio strategy
stories.Summary:
An industry voice, Zerbib, has questioned the economics of Nokia's AI radio strategy, asking who carries the running costs and who takes the profits, according to comments made to Light Reading. Zerbib warned that Nvidia software update fees could erode savings for carriers, and said recurring software charges belong in any savings calculation. Zerbib also said a technical edge differs from economic gain, and sees possible cannibalization of Nokia's revenue. Adoption alone would not show incremental business, Zerbib said, and did not rule out the collaboration.

The questions come alongside a series of Nokia announcements. On 16 November, Nokia and ASUS announced a multi-year agreement licensing Nokia video technology for ASUS devices, which settles a patent dispute tied to it, with financial terms kept confidential and Nokia as the licensor. On 17 November, Nokia announced worldwide availability of its Fiber on the Go broadband solution, which includes flexible payment options, and said more than 600,000 connections are in service in South Africa. Also on 17 November, a disclosure showed Nvidia cut its Nokia stake by 56% in the third quarter of 2026, a sale concerning Nvidia's shareholder position only, while Nokia shares were down 2.9% at EUR 6.52 on Tradegate amid a broader AI stock slide on Wall Street, where inflation and tariff worries weighed on US equities, according to the Associated Press.

On the same day as the ASUS deal, the AI Gigafactory Northern consortium was founded with Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda, and the partners intend to bid for AI infrastructure in the Nordic and Baltic region.

stories.Headline: UK regulators hold pre-launch talks with Meta over Muse personal AI agent
stories.Summary:
Meta launched Muse, which can send emails, book travel and do Christmas shopping: a personal AI agent. The UK launch of Muse drew a co-ordinated response from regulators. The Competition and Markets Authority and the Information Commissioner's Office confirmed they held pre-launch talks with Meta about its duty to comply with UK laws. The regulators signalled scrutiny for all companies deploying personal AI agents.

Meta amended its terms and conditions to make them fairer. The CMA described its position as a watching brief and avoided mandatory or prescriptive guidance for personal AI agents. It said it expects clear, consistent and transparent presentation of agents, the right information at the right time for consumers, and real control over agents, and that compliance responsibility lies with the companies deploying them.

The ICO published a statement and a blog on the Muse launch, focusing on data protection law obligations. It told Meta that users must understand and control how their data is used. A voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme that lets the ICO review Muse in practice and user feedback was committed to by Meta. The ICO urged privacy by design and by default and said it will act against organisations that ignore privacy risks. It concluded its call for evidence on agentic AI and committed to publish guidance in spring 2027.

The CMA and ICO are members of the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum, which also includes Ofcom and the Financial Conduct Authority. The forum sent a letter to UK government ministers on personal AI agents saying the law applies in full and will be enforced, and that businesses may face scrutiny from multiple regulators at once. A proposed Digital Fairness Act was announced on 11 November 2026, with the European Commission advocating an interventionist approach in the European Economic Area. The draft proposals would require traders deploying AI agents in e-commerce to give consumers control over automated systems, offer three modes selected on first use, disclose conflicts of interest, provide pre-contractual information and transmit consumer contact details, and would bar traders from compelling use of automated systems. The UK's agile approach follows a government steer not to block innovation. The article was published on 27 November 2026 and written by Richard Collie, Lorna Cropper and Tessa Lloyd.

stories.Headline: India’s public schools face harm from both inaction and rushed AI adoption, CyberPeace policy intern Kartik Nandal warns
stories.Summary:
India's public schools face a policy bind in which both doing nothing on artificial intelligence and adopting it hastily would harm students, according to Kartik Nandal, an intern in policy and advocacy at CyberPeace. Private schools already use generative AI, while government schools lack basic connectivity. Four failure areas overlap in classrooms, Nandal wrote: the digital divide, learning shortfalls, data oversight and gender disparity. India has 24.72 crore students and 14.67 lakh schools, with a pupil-teacher ratio of 24 to 1, according to UDISE+ 2025-26. The secondary dropout rate is 9.5%, and 67.4% of schools have internet, though rural government schools lack hardware and connectivity.

A 2024 ASER survey found that 54.2% of rural Class 8 pupils could not do basic Class 4 division. Economists Lant Pritchett and Amanda Beatty hold that advanced teaching technology fails without the basics, and rushed AI risks cognitive offloading, meaning reliance on technology over one's own thinking. MIT learning scientist Justin Reich coined the term EdTech Matthew Effect for how new classroom tools widen achievement gaps. In a study at a US high school, students did 48% better on practice papers with a GPT-4 bot but 17% worse on closed-book results after the bot was removed.

Among 14- to 16-year-olds, 36% of boys and 27% of girls own a smartphone, ASER 2024 found, and families restrict girls' screen time more than boys', leaving girls dependent on supervised school access. Section 9 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which covers parental consent and bans on tracking, is scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027, after an 18-month transition window following notification of the DPDP Rules. Until then those protections are inactive, and penalties of up to ₹200 crore can be imposed by the Data Protection Board. EdTech vendors are locking schools into their ecosystems before enforcement, and schools prefer free licenses to cut costs, while free trials surrender typing, response-delay and error data.

In December 2022 the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights convened a meeting with Byju Raveendran, CEO of BYJU'S, over allegations about child data and aggressive sales methods aimed at parents. BYJU'S stated it "had never purchased student data." Free EdTech apps record test results, viewing history and parents' phone numbers, and sales staff target worried households for premium subscriptions, while generative AI turns classroom prompts into training material. Policymakers must address infrastructure, learning, girls' access and data protection together, CyberPeace said.

stories.Headline: INCOMPAS CEO Chip Pickering urges Congress and the FCC to streamline permits for data centers, fiber and transmission
stories.Summary:
Chip Pickering, CEO of INCOMPAS, is calling on Congress and the FCC to remove barriers to building AI infrastructure. Pickering, a former Mississippi congressman who served six House terms, cited lengthy energy project reviews and local fiber network permits as obstacles. He is scheduled to speak on a panel at 11:15 a.m. on Dec. 1 at the National Press Club in Washington. The panel is titled "Permitting Reform and the AI Race," part of the event "Broadband and AI in the Next Congress," for which INCOMPAS is a Silver sponsor.

Pickering said the permitting timeline should reflect that priority when a data center that is genuinely part of American AI infrastructure is served by a fiber route or transmission line. He also said, "That means streamlining permitting so that data centers, fiber networks, and transmission infrastructure can be deployed without years of regulatory delay." INCOMPAS seeks clearer local permit timelines and reasonable local permit fees, according to the group.

The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on Nov. 19 by a vote of 62 to 33. It also directs FERC to protect electricity customers in relation to large computational loads and data centers. INCOMPAS backed the permitting effort, and Pickering said it would provide "more energy capacity and a modern electric grid to support continued economic growth."

Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., objects to the package, citing environmental protections and public participation. Markey is scheduled to speak at the Dec. 1 event. Brian Ford, NTCA vice president for federal regulatory affairs, is also listed, and Christopher Cole, Law360 senior telecom reporter, moderates. Questions at the event are expected on permits, grid costs and a state AI law pause.

Pickering helped shape the Telecommunications Act of 1996 and worked for Sen. Trent Lott, R-Miss. He has led INCOMPAS since 2014. He also worked with Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., to recruit large data center projects to Mississippi, and an April Amazon announcement promised $25 billion in Mississippi investment and 2,000 projected jobs. The AI Competition Center launched in 2023, and in 2025 House testimony Pickering called for competition across the AI economy from fiber, wireless, energy and AI models. "AI should not be a bicoastal story. It must be a national one," he said.
