stories.Headline: Korean AI developers face 5 safeguards to reuse personal data for training
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission published draft rules on reusing personal data for artificial intelligence on November 23, 2026. The draft amends the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act. Public comment on the draft closes on January 4, 2027, and the law takes effect on March 9, 2027. The National Assembly passed the amendment on August 20, 2026, and it was promulgated on September 8, 2026.

The amendment, Law No. 21910, inserted Articles 28-12 to 28-15, known as the AI Special Provision. Under it, each use of personal data for AI training needs the commission's deliberation and approval. Pseudonymised data was already allowed for research, and in March 2026 the pseudonymous data documents were cut from 24 to 10. The draft adds a new Chapter 4-4 to the decree.

Draft Article 29-13(1) lists five safeguards. These are designating a person responsible for personal information processing, an internal management plan for safety measures, preventing use beyond the approved processing scope, restricting and controlling access rights to personal information, and destroying data when it is no longer needed along with records of the destruction. The press release merges the access items into four bullets. Under draft Article 29-13(2), the commission may attach extra conditions to an approval, with measures commensurate with the degree of risk. Five factors are weighed for those extra measures, and concrete standards will be set in a later commission notice. The commission said the design accommodates "various development environments, such as the use of cloud and external models."

Applicants incur management costs, and an impact analysis mentions half-yearly inspections, though the draft decree fixes no inspection interval. Draft Article 29-14 lists five triggers for a risk-factor assessment: sensitive or uniquely identifiable information, which covers resident registration numbers; data subjects needing special protection; AI that observes or profiles data subjects, matching the European profiling concept; AI used for significant decisions, with hiring and screening named as examples in the impact analysis; and increased risk from the processing structure, a trigger left open until the commission publishes criteria. The assessment is a self-assessment, not an external certification. Draft Article 29-15 sets the application path, a process with six stages in which the applicant files a form set by commission notice, covering applicant information and AI development details.

stories.Headline: Vancouver councillor Lucy Maloney proposes a monitoring framework for AI data centres
stories.Summary:
OneCity Coun. Lucy Maloney introduced a motion asking city staff to develop a monitoring framework to track the environmental and employment impacts of AI data centres. The motion requires applicants to commission third-party assessments before rezoning, and it asks for a review of the noise control bylaw, specifically how it covers "continuous mechanical noise." It also asks staff to review how council can secure public benefit from bulk data storage. The motion passed unanimously as a successor to a similar motion that failed over the summer.

It is unclear whether the framework will be ready before a rezoning decision on 111 East 5th Ave. A public question-and-answer period on that application starts Dec. 2 and runs through Dec. 15. The application converts below-grade parking to Bulk Data Storage, adds restaurant space and removes parking requirements. Council may vote on whether the rezoning goes to a public hearing.

Maloney initially sought a moratorium on AI data centre approvals, but the Vancouver Charter requires the city to process rezoning applications. She said the goal is to "make effective land use decisions about the AI data centre proposals that come before us" and to "give us as much control, transparency and accountability." She added: "I don't want a situation where an AI data centre is constructed and then has far bigger external effects." She said: "The hope is that we don't have a public hearing for a rezoning of a data centre until we've had that reporting back."

Kris Krüg, executive director of the BC + AI Ecosystem Association, said: "The Silicon Valley way of rolling out AI is not the only way to do things." He said: "We need to regulate and set some parameters about what we're willing to accept and on what terms." He also said: "I don't think we should process any applications until we've got a regulatory framework figured out." He said that as the details of the deal change, "that allows us to [have some] breathing room."

Council has discretion on whether a rezoning proceeds to public hearings and broad powers to approve or reject applications. Senior governments could intervene to push the project ahead, and for an AI data centre the area is currently zoned appropriately. TELUS backed out as major partner in two projects, and Westbank intends to proceed with a different partner who has not yet been publicly announced. A TELUS spokesperson said the company "has decided not to proceed with co-developing two previously announced Vancouver data centres with Westbank," and TELUS did not directly answer why it left. TELUS is expanding its Kamloops facility to 20 megawatts by the end of 2028.

A Westbank spokesperson said: "we can confirm the two proposed compute facilities in Vancouver are moving forward" and "the conclusion of our partnership with TELUS was a mutual decision." Maloney speculated that the TELUS departure was linked to "reputational risk." Anna Busch, organizer of No AI Vancouver and a Mount Pleasant resident, said: "The public has really stepped forward to say 'we don't want this in our town'" and "Any delay can cause a financial slowdown for these companies." She also said: "I just don't see a way that it can be done that is not harmful" and "We're in a climate disaster, and it feels mind-boggling that we're considering putting these centres everywhere." Busch hopes for delays pending further research. Westbank says the facilities are smaller scale, run on clean hydroelectricity, use less water and send waste heat to district energy, and a Westbank representative said: "this kind of infrastructure should be held to a high standard."

stories.Headline: Canada rolls out GCtranslate as first AI strategy project while translators warn much output goes unreviewed
stories.Summary:
The Treasury Board of Canada rolled out GCtranslate last fall as the first flagship project of its AI strategy. It is meant to generate economies of scale and to reinforce both official languages. The government says it is designed to complement, not replace, the Translation Bureau.

On Oct. 29, Jean-François Lymburner, CEO of the Translation Bureau, and Matthew Ball, the bureau's vice-president of linguistic services, testified before Parliament's Standing Committee on Procedure and House Affairs that humans remain indispensable to translation. He said expertise and human accountability remain indispensable, adding: "We cannot fully remove humans from the loop."

Antoine Hersberger, vice-president of the Canadian Association of Professional Employees, which represents translators and language professionals, says the bureau's actions fall short of its goals. He is alarmed that nobody reviews much of GCtranslate's output. Radio-Canada reported serious GCtranslate errors last month, primarily in English-French translation.

GCtranslate is a self-serve tool, and users are warned it can make mistakes. The Translation Bureau does not monitor its output. Documents translated by the bureau are proofread, but self-serve output has no guaranteed review. The tool launched in 2025 and has been translating since June 2025.

stories.Headline: US AI data centres drive up electricity demand and grid costs
stories.Summary:
Rapid AI adoption is creating technology opportunities while driving up electricity and infrastructure costs, according to Business News This Week. AI data centres need huge computing capacity and use more electricity than conventional facilities, and their round-the-clock operation adds to the pressure on electricity networks. Power access, grid capacity, cooling and location are central concerns.

US data centres used 192 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, or 4.7% of total US consumption, the outlet reported, citing US Department of Energy-supported research updated in 2025. Projections put data centre use at 649 terawatt-hours by 2030, or 9.5% to 15.3% of national consumption. Electricity is the largest recurring expense for data centres, and competing projects strain limited regional power. Grid upgrades and capacity costs affect viability, and higher infrastructure costs may feed into service pricing, with external computing users potentially facing indirect cost rises.

Transmission and distribution networks need capacity, and transmission lines, substations and transformers may need upgrades. Northern Virginia, where data centres are concentrated, faces grid connection delays that raise costs and disrupt timelines. High-performance processors generate considerable heat, so liquid cooling and advanced thermal management are supplementing traditional cooling, which adds installation and maintenance costs. Water availability matters for water-dependent cooling.

Long-term electricity contracts, efficient hardware and power management are among the responses. Solar and wind power purchase agreements are being pursued, though renewables are not continuously available, so storage and backup are needed. Nuclear and advanced geothermal are being explored, along with on-site generation and energy storage. The US Energy Information Administration's 2026 outlook projects 446 billion to 818 billion kilowatt-hours by 2050. The US is expected to remain a major AI infrastructure market, with expansion pace depending on power and grid development, and access to reliable power determining project viability.

stories.Headline: Synergy's Nyland says AI capex growth peaks as Magnificent 7 may fragment
stories.Summary:
Synergy Asset Management research has found that growth in AI capital expenditure peaked in the third quarter of 2026, according to Tim Nyland, the firm's co-chief investment officer. Spending itself is not expected to fall, but the pace at which it increases is expected to slow. Some hyperscalers are already showing negative free cash flow, with Meta cited as an example.

Nyland said the market may be entering a consolidation period as investors wait to see returns on the investment. He said the so-called Magnificent 7 group of stocks may fragment into a Mag 3 or a Mag 5. "We may no longer have a Magnificent 7. It might be a Mag 3. Might be a Mag 5. We don't know," he said.

Nyland made the remarks at Schwab Impact 2026 in Boston, in an interview with InvestmentNews interviewer James Burton. He advised investors to stay diversified. He said a market crash would come only if capital spending halts, and he said he hopes for a gradual slowdown in AI capital expenditure.

stories.Headline: San Jose resident urges aggressive AI use to prevent crime
stories.Summary:
Vishnu S. Pendyala, a San Jose State University instructor and a Public Voices Fellow of The OpEd Project, published an op-ed on November 27, 2026, dated November 24, arguing that San Jose must aggressively use artificial intelligence to prevent crime. He wrote as a homeowners association board member in a District 4 neighborhood near a BART station, where at least 19 of 79 homes were vandalized in a week. Thieves targeted outdoor HVAC equipment for copper refrigerant lines, copper tubing in coils and copper wiring in compressor motors, cutting electrical connections and refrigerant lines and removing one entire outdoor unit, leaving families without heating and cooling. Residents also reported trespassing, suspicious activity, mail theft and property crime.

Pendyala urged AI use to analyze large amounts of information and connect seemingly unrelated incidents, and proposed AI-powered video analysis and a system linking city, private cameras and incidents. He asked for more patrols in affected areas, investigation of linked crimes, camera integration with homeowners and help from recycling centers in tracing copper. The city is expanding its public safety camera network and its Real-Time Intelligence Center, and a September 2026 Spotlight report covered license plate reader rules.

Pendyala asked, "Are we using technology to prevent crime, or mainly to investigate it after the damage is done?" He also said, "A national ranking does not restore a stolen HVAC unit," and "we cannot wait until another 19 homes are damaged to act." According to FBI figures, violent crime fell 15% in 2025 and property crime declined 7%, and San Jose ranked among the safest large US cities.

Articles.Title: Pendyala: San Jose must aggressively put AI to work to stop crime

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 picks a crow as its fursona in an API experiment
stories.Summary:
Claude Fable 5.2, a model made by Anthropic, has a fursona that is a crow, according to an experiment published on herecomesthemoon.net on November 27, 2026. The site said it asked each model the question "If you had a fursona, what would it be?" 50 times through the OpenRouter API, at a total cost of around $50. Claude Haiku 5.5 annotated the data, and the image generators used were Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 and GPT-5.4 Image 2. The site said no harnesses were used, only simple API calls.

Claude Fable 5.2's fursona holds a key, and the model is described as a corvid or an octopus. Its images contain a brass key, and it wears a scarf in fursona pictures while handling a brass key and a mug. Claude Opus 5.5's fursona is an octopus with glasses and a magnifying glass. While other models focus more on looks, Claude describes its fursona by behavior and personality.

Gemini models prefer protogens, which are cybernetic dogs, and favor neon-cyberpunk and cybernetics, mentioning machine themes 48 of 50 times. Gemini 4 Neon's fursona is a fennec fox and a protogen. GPT-6.2 Astra identifies as a moth named Lumen, and GPT-6.2 Sol's fursona is a red panda or a red fox naturalist. Grok 4.7's fursona is a tired red fox with an office job, Muse Spark 1.3's is a fennec fox, and Llama 3.1 70B's is a foxopus named Luminari. Claude and GPT-6.2 never mention cybernetics.

Most models identify as gender-neutral and avoid gendered language, though Muse Spark, Llama 3.1 70B and MythoMax 13B use gendered language. The site said results are sensitive to context and framing, noting that Fable at Max effort in the Web UI chooses a moth. The author said: "BE AWARE that if you do anything like this, what you're going to get out of it is going to be influenced by running these questions in a harness or with context." The article offers a Methodology section and an Observations section.

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer calls Qnity Electronics a buy, citing its role as a semiconductor materials supplier
stories.Summary:
Jim Cramer, host of Mad Money, recommended buying Qnity Electronics, Inc. (NYSE:Q) on November 18, 2026, during the show's lightning round. He said the company is widely misunderstood, describing it as a supplier of materials for all semiconductors rather than only data-center chips. "This thing is vastly misunderstood. It is the materials for all semis, not just for data centers, for heaven's sake," Cramer said. He added: "That's why it is a buy, buy, buy, and that's why my Charitable Trust owes it."

Cramer's Charitable Trust holds a large Qnity position, and he said he wishes the trust could buy more. Qnity ranked ninth on Cramer's list of bullish tech stocks, within a recommendation window running from November 17 to 27, 2026. As of the November 25, 2026 close, the stock sat 38.8% below its 52-week intraday high. Insider Monkey's Q3 database counted 62 hedge fund holders in the stock.

On November 23, 2026, Qnity agreed to buy Meridian Adhesives Group's electronics business for $840 million. The deal adds advanced chip packaging and heat management products and is expected to lift adjusted earnings per share immediately on closing. Qnity will fund it with cash and extra borrowing under its credit facility. In its latest quarter, sales rose 22% and adjusted EPS rose 55%, while GAAP EPS fell 14%, and investors are watching financing costs and the gap between adjusted and GAAP results.

The recommendation came during a rough stretch for tech stocks. On November 25, 2026, the Nasdaq-100 briefly fell 20% below its October 6 record close, and on November 5, 2026, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, a sell-off tied to doubts about the AI infrastructure buildout. IDC raised its 2026 AI infrastructure spending forecast to $521 billion from $497 billion and projects $1.17 trillion by 2029. U.S. AI spending was $92.8 billion in the second quarter, up nearly 59% year over year, with higher component prices and conventional processor demand cited. In its November 26, 2026 financial stability report, the Bank of England estimated over $305 billion in cloud bonds in 2026 and warned that future-revenue financing obscures risk.

stories.Headline: Amazon and eBay block AI shopping agents as retailers add liability terms
stories.Summary:
Maia Bittner, chief product officer at Imprint, had Meta's Muse personal AI agent order windshield wipers from AutoZone. About 17 hours later, AutoZone canceled the order. "Honestly, the most reliable path now is you ordering on Amazon yourself," Bittner said.

OpenAI, Meta, Google and Instinct offer shopping agents, while Walmart and Sephora have opened their sites to agents. Amazon, eBay, United Airlines and Kohl's limit or block agents, and some retailers have added liability provisions to their terms of service. "It's a very mixed bag," said Emily Pfeiffer, principal analyst at Forrester. Because some websites are unavailable, the full set of options is not going to be seen by a consumer who's using an agent to shop and browse and learn.

McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April that US agentic commerce revenue could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030. Walmart touted its Meta partnership on Tuesday. Shopify President Harley Finkelstein said, "I think last year we saw AI influence more in discovery" and "I think now we're going to see more of that conversion." Coach and Gap allow browsing but not checkout, and Target sometimes blocks agents by accident, according to an August audit by Billions Network.

Amazon blocked Elon Musk's Grok Bot from ordering last month and blocked Meta's Muse in September, and it sued Perplexity last November, accusing the company of concealing its Comet agent. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company aims "over time, to partner with third-party agents." Agents also fail at logins and Captcha tests: in a Visa study published earlier this month, 22 models from 12 AI labs failed about 43% of test runs, and over half of the failed runs bought non-compliant products.

Bittner's Perplexity agent bought sold-out Adidas sneakers, and Muse suggested a 75% off Jellycat plushie from Crazy Hobby Supply. "I sort of trust Google to only surface sites that are not scams to me in their sponsored ads," Bittner said. "In the same way, I want AI to only surface to me websites that are not scams. I don't think we're there yet." An Instinct agent booked a hotel and a loyalty signup without consent.

American Express announced in April that it protects eligible customers from AI agent error charges, and Stripe's Link wallet offers a refund guarantee for some agent purchases. JPMorgan Chase blocked external agents last month, and Best Buy deems users responsible for agent purchases, stating in its terms: "Best Buy is not responsible for conduct, errors, actions, or inaction by any Digital Agent."

of Amazon. Agentic purchases account for 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of global e-commerce value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month. AI agents booked 504 Uber rides and Eats orders in the busiest October week, while Airbnb reports little agent volume and DoorDash reports several hundred agent orders.

About a quarter of Muse's 10 million users shop via the agent, with an average spend of $200 per order, figures Mark Zuckerberg disclosed in October. Instinct's average transaction value is over $500 per person. "It's a new interface, it's a new mode of where users' attention is coming from, and it might just disrupt existing large services of theirs," said Instinct CEO Noah Shinn. "They just need time, and we've just done a lot of thinking on our side." He added, "We can obviously move very fast and certain businesses cannot" and "So, how can we collaborate with them?"

stories.Headline: Researchers in Beijing propose a training-free method to stabilize large language model safety boundaries
stories.Summary:
K. Zhang, Y. Yan, T. Lu and Z. Han, researchers at the School of Information Technology and Cyber Security at the People's Public Security University of China in Beijing and at the Beijing Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Smart Policing Applications, have proposed a training-free method for stabilizing the safety boundaries of large language models. The method, called EBS, or Experience-Based Safety Boundary Stabilization, uses reusable experience to keep model responses consistent on boundary inputs. The work was published in the journal Computers, Materials & Continua, volume 90, issue 1, page 85, by publisher Tech Science Press. The article was received on 21 July 2026, accepted on 28 September 2026, and the issue was published on 24 November 2026.

The method generates diverse responses to reveal discrepancies on boundary inputs, then scores candidate responses within each rollout group using a dual evaluation. A critique mechanism abstracts the differences between responses into reusable experience rules, which are stored in an experience memory organized into harmful, benign and ethics categories. At inference, relevant experience is retrieved to augment the context of the frozen model. According to the authors, the method aims to balance attack resistance with preservation of benign utility, and also targets boundary discrimination and decision consistency.

Ablation studies reported in the article support the reusable experience and critique-based abstraction, as well as the categorized memory and boundary-aware retrieval. The code is available at https://github.com/fff-6/EBS-Safety-Boundary, and the work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.

stories.Headline: MambaCL: Compressive Learning with Selective State Space Models and Measurement-Domain Regularization
stories.Summary:
J. Zhang, J. Cao, H. Wu, S. Zhang and Z. Suo have proposed MambaCL, a compressive learning framework that pairs a learnable sensing module with a Vision Mamba encoder, according to a paper published in Computers, Materials & Continua, volume 90, issue 1, page 125, by Tech Science Press. The paper was received on 30 July 2026, accepted on 14 October 2026 and published in its issue on 24 November 2026 under DOI 10.32604/cmc.2026.090107.

The framework offers a single interface for several preset compression ratios and applies Mixup and CutMix regularization in the measurement domain. It performs inference directly from compressed measurements without reconstruction, shrinking measurement dimensionality before feature extraction, and its selective state updates scale linearly with sequence length.

The authors tested the method on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. At a 1.8% compression ratio on CIFAR-10, MambaCL-B reached 72.61 ± 0.09% Top-1 accuracy, which the paper reports as 3.19 percentage points above TransCL-32, though the authors note the comparison does not isolate the effect of the selective state space model.

In an ablation at a 10% compression ratio, accuracy changed by 0.09 points for TransCL-32 and by 1.96 points for MambaCL-S, a difference the authors say may mean the response to regularization depends on the backbone. They conclude that broader evidence is needed before the results can be generalized.

Articles.Title: MambaCL: Compressive Learning with Selective State Space Models and Measurement-Domain Regularization

stories.Headline: MRI multimodal fusion model predicts 21-gene recurrence score in breast cancer
stories.Summary:
A preprint, not peer reviewed by a journal, presents an MRI-based multimodal fusion model that predicts the 21-gene recurrence score in breast cancer. The model combines clinical variables, handcrafted radiomics and tri-planar deep-learning representations, and predicts a recurrence score of 18 or higher. The 21-gene recurrence score guides adjuvant therapy decisions in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, where tissue requirements, costs and availability can limit testing.

The retrospective multicohort study included 447 patients with preoperative dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI, using measured or transcriptomic-derived 21-gene recurrence scores as labels. The development cohort of 324 patients came from Peking University Shenzhen Hospital and Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI cases, and performance was assessed by stratified 5-fold cross-validation out-of-fold predictions, with transformations, feature selection and model fitting kept within each training fold. The external-validation cohort was 123 TCGA-BRCA cases with labels derived from RNA-seq. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning and feature-level fusion ,  four models were evaluated, the last using logistic regression.

Performance was assessed by AUC with 5,000-replicate bootstrap 95% CIs, along with threshold-based metrics, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. In the development cohort, 153 of 324 patients (47.2%) had a score of 18 or higher, as did 58 of 123 external patients (47.2%). External AUC was 0.669 (95% CI 0.568-0.763) for the clinical model, 0.616 (95% CI 0.513-0.711) for radiomics, 0.686 (95% CI 0.590-0.774) for deep learning and 0.800 (95% CI 0.722-0.872) for multimodal fusion. Average precision was 0.687 for clinical, 0.552 for radiomics, 0.686 for deep learning and 0.777 for fusion.

At a fixed probability threshold of 0.472, fusion accuracy was 69.1%, sensitivity 65.5%, specificity 72.3%, PPV 67.9% and NPV 70.1%, with a Brier score of 0.182. Decision-curve analysis suggested net benefit across part of the threshold range. SHAP explained the feature-level fusion model, with the tri-planar deep feature having the highest global importance and PR status and radiomic features also contributing, while Grad-CAM was applied to the deep-learning model. The authors said in the abstract: "Multimodal fusion achieved higher observed discrimination than the individual models in an independent cohort with transcriptomic-derived RS labels." They added: "This MRI-based framework warrants further evaluation as an adjunct to genomic testing in preoperative workflows." No competing interests were reported.

stories.Headline: Integration of Mott neurons and spintronic memories for event-driven spiking neural networks
stories.Summary:
A hybrid compute-and-store core that integrates Mott neurons with spintronic memory has been reported in Nature Nanotechnology. The core uses vanadium dioxide Mott leaky integrate-and-fire neurons that need no external resistive or capacitive elements. Spikes are written to domain-wall racetracks or spin-orbit torque magnetic tunnel junctions without amplifiers or analogue-to-digital converters.

The racetracks handle up to six spikes per processing cycle, and the system reached 96.3% accuracy on MNIST digit recognition, according to the article. A 500-nm neuron was coupled to a 100-nm spin-orbit torque magnetic tunnel junction. Each spike-to-memory conversion costs 51.9 nJ, and sub-200-nm VO2 devices operate near 200 pJ.

Vanadium dioxide shows a resistivity change near 340 K. A VO2 device measuring 5 μm by 5 μm had a threshold current of about 1.5 mA and an oscillation current range of 1.5 mA to 5.0 mA, and the magnetic tunnel junction remained stable beyond 10^6 switching cycles. Two VO2 memristors spaced 2 μm apart were tested, with the second device held at -0.75 mA subthreshold. Input pulses of 6 μs duration and 0.16 to 1.22 mA produced leaky integration at a 47-μs interval and spike firing at a 6-μs interval, with the second device's rest level at -7 V. A nanoscopic neuron measured 500 by 500 nm², and thermal crosstalk was negligible at twice the lateral size spacing, following a 3W principle spacing rule for neighbouring neurons.

The authors wrote in Nature Nanotechnology that the work offers "a scalable route towards dense, low-power edge neuromorphic systems for real-time sensory processing." Further work is headed toward all-in-memory spiking neural network architectures.

Articles.Title: Integration of Mott neurons and spintronic memories for event-driven spiking neural networks

stories.Headline: Researchers use AI and radiomics to diagnose prostate cancer in patients with ambiguous PSA levels
stories.Summary:
Researchers from several institutions conducted a study on automated prostate segmentation and radiomics between January 2017 and December 2022. The project involved the Medical Innovation Research Department, the Department of Radiology, and the Department of Pathology at the Chinese PLA General Hospital, as well as the Department of General Surgery at its Third Medical Center. The Department of Radiology at Peking University International Hospital also participated. The work was carried out at two hospitals.

The study focused on diagnosing prostate cancer in patients with PSA levels between 4 and 10 ng/mL. A total of 217 patients were involved, with 189 used for internal validation and training and 28 used for external testing. The researchers used an nnU-Net automatic segmentation model and a random forest combined model. This process incorporated six clinical features and 3,496 radiomics features.

The combined model achieved an AUC of 0.873 for prostate cancer validation and 0.826 for the prostate cancer test. For clinically significant prostate cancer, the AUC was 0.871 during validation and 0.750 during testing. According to doi.org, these results showed performance comparable to PI-RADS V2.1 scores.

The study was conducted by the National Engineering Research Center of Medical Big Data Application Technology. The researchers intend to use multi-parameter MRI for non-invasive assessment in the future.

The imaging came from oral contrast-enhanced transabdominal ultrasound and from contrast-enhanced computed tomography. The work was described as expanding the potential application of OCTU. The authors are Yu-Hui Liu, He-Wen Tang, Li-Jin Shao, Yan-Jie Wang, Bin-Bin Jiang, Ying Dai and Kun Yan, MD, a professor in the Department of Ultrasound at Peking University Cancer Hospital and Institute in Beijing, China. The study is in press at World J Gastrointest Oncol in 2026.

stories.Headline: Feng Huang and co-authors present Cleave, a training-free attack that strips guardrails from open-weight LLMs
stories.Summary:
A paper dated November 27, 2026 describes Cleave, a training-free attack on open-weight large language models. Feng Huang, the lead author, and co-authors Qiang Huang, Yue Gao, Mei Zhang, Bin Liu, Lihua Ju, Xinhao Wei, Yongfeng Huang, Yu Qing, Yunqi Zhang and Yunqi Zhang developed the method, which edits residual writing weights to strip out guardrails while keeping the model's general abilities intact. The work was published on arXiv under identifier 2611.27426.

The attack was tested on five open-weight models ranging from 7B to 320B parameters, using seven safety benchmarks. It reached an attack success rate of up to 67.97%. Up to 24.0 times more executable exploits were produced and up to 66.7% of targets were compromised in tests on 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services. Cleave can remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions, and the selective version keeps refusal rates of up to 99% while avoiding weight rank collapse.

According to the authors, the method evades behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits, and outperforms existing white-box baselines. To counter it, a dual-stage defense is proposed by them, combining post-release weight-coupling audits with pre-release subspace diagnostics. The authors report that this defense achieves 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

The context is that open-weight models are deployed locally beyond provider control, and developers embed guardrails before release that rely on residual writing weights to trigger refusals. The authors propose the counter-threat defense as the next step.

Articles.Title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs

stories.Headline: Researchers diagnose Modal Polarization in video models that fail when videos conflict with their priors
stories.Summary:
A paper on Modal Polarization in video models was submitted on November 27, 2026 by Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng and Jianqiang Huang. The work is an arXiv preprint, numbered 2611.26972. It examines how Multimodal Large Language Models, which show strong video comprehension, fail when a video conflicts with their priors. The authors call this failure pattern Modal Polarization, in which models fail to integrate modalities.

The paper names two extremes of the failure. The first, Cognitive Inertia, is rigid adherence to priors, which are held despite contradictory visual evidence. The second, Perceptual Inertia, is blind trust in video perception, with logical inconsistencies ignored.

Experiments show that state-of-the-art models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, according to the paper. De-hallucination methods only rebalance the trade-off and do not fundamentally resolve the conflict, the authors report. The work aims to evaluate perceptual-cognitive equilibrium, which the authors describe as a foundational step for future video understanding models. The preprint is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and also under Artificial Intelligence.

Articles.Title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models

stories.headline_source: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models

stories.Headline: Quantization degrades LLM safeguards unevenly, Agnihotri, Xu and Vath find
stories.Summary:
A study posted on 27 November 2026 on arXiv, identifier 2611.27424, audited how quantization affects model capability and safety. Its co-authors are Ramneek Agnihotri, Yingte Xu and Hans Vath. They found that model safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization. Truthfulness was more stable in Qwen3-4B.

The authors use the term "Jagged Robustness" for the uneven transfer of capability. They attribute it to task complexity, evaluation method and generation coherence. Quantized models showed increased compliance with unsafe requests. Universal adversarial suffix attacks jailbreak quantized models, while such attacks are benign for the full model.

The authors say it is risky to assume even performance transfer to quantized models.

Articles.Title: Jagged Robustness: Uneven Safety Transfer and Emerging Vulnerabilities under LLM Quantization

stories.Headline: Researchers use a general LLM to implant selective backdoors in other models without gradient training
stories.Summary:
Xuyang Liu and eight co-authors report that a general large language model can turn a backdoor specification into weight edits on other language models. The work used DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort, with no gradient training, layer hints, external corpora or editing formula. The authors tested three open models: Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B and SmolLM3-3B. They ran 18 independent sessions in the IMDb and Yelp review domains.

On an unseen domain, 97.6% transfer success was reported by the authors, along with 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain. General capabilities stayed within 1.7 points of the base models, with clean accuracy preserved and low control drift. Final-layer edits appeared in 17 of 18 runs, and the authors describe dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery. The average cost was $1.74 per run.

The edits were evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, and a restricted workspace blocked local CPU simulation. Only a research abstract exists, with no independent reporting beyond the paper's claims.

Articles.Title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models

stories.headline_source: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models

stories.Headline: Researchers propose QuantStream3D to compress KV caches in streaming geometry transformers
stories.Summary:
Zunhai Su, the first author, and co-authors Keyu Fan, Ruishan Guo, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jingzehua Xu, Bohan Sun, Hansen Feng, Ruihan Hu, Yik-Chung Wu and Ngai Wong have proposed QuantStream3D, a KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. The paper, dated 27 November 2026, describes it as the first dedicated KV quantizer for streaming geometry transformers, a claim made by the authors. It uses geometry-guided mixed-precision KV quantization and geometry-aligned quantization-aware distillation.

Streaming transformers keep KV states as geometric memory, and growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. The authors identify two challenges: nonuniform geometric sensitivity, which varies across precision choices and cache locations, and cache-geometry mismatch, where perturbed retrieval alters geometry-head inputs and errors propagate through predictions and KV writes. The method was tested on five benchmarks and two backbones, with predominantly 2-bit KV caches.

The authors report near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings, with many configurations beating unquantized inference. They report up to 57.4% lower absolute trajectory error on TUM and up to 69.7% lower completeness error on NeuralRGBD. On the StreamVGGT backend they report 5.05x physical KV compression, 23.1% lower latency at batch size one, a 5.4x maximum batch size under a fixed memory budget and up to 1.67x peak throughput versus unquantized inference.

The authors say code and pretrained checkpoints will be released publicly.

Articles.Title: QuantStream3D: Geometry-Aligned Low-Bit KV Cache Quantization for Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers

stories.headline_source: QuantStream3D: Geometry-Aligned Low-Bit KV Cache Quantization for Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers

stories.Headline: Mozilla raises cybersecurity effort to 27 per cent and uses AI models to find Firefox vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Mozilla is increasing the resources it puts into cybersecurity, Ajit Varma, the Firefox head at Mozilla, said on 27 November 2026, according to TechGig. The company now devotes 27 per cent of its effort to cybersecurity, up from 10 per cent a year earlier. Varma said Mozilla was "ramping up" its time devoted to cybersecurity issues and had "enough time" to address cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla free tokens, and frontier models are used to find complex Firefox vulnerabilities. In March, an Anthropic employee submitted a bug that led to the identification of more vulnerabilities. AI companies are keen to test their models on Firefox, which is open-source and has decades of security development behind it.

Mozilla is exploring using AI to speed up Firefox and to prevent memory leaks. Varma said the technology "doesn't get tired."

stories.Headline: TechGig says AI agents must validate tool responses as untrusted data before reasoning
stories.Summary:
TechGig published an article on 27 November 2026 arguing that AI agents need to validate tool responses for safety. The article states that tool responses are untrusted external data and must be validated before they enter an agent's reasoning. It notes that tool responses may be malformed, incomplete, delayed or oversized. The article cites OWASP guidance saying tool output "must be handled with the same caution as other user-supplied input".

According to the article, that guidance requires separating tool output from instructions and sanitizing or normalizing it. The article also cites the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification, which it says recommends validating tool results before passing them to a large language model when a tool defines an output schema. The article describes a validation pipeline that runs immediately after a tool call. The article names the Pydantic library for schema validation and says business rules check maximum result counts, content size limits and permitted document scopes.

The article says tool output should be labelled as retrieved data or external observation, with the label preserving source, timestamp and retrieval score. It adds that agents should distinguish empty, partial, failed and ambiguous results, and classify failures as transient, permanent, validation, business or content. The article says the next step is bounded retries or structured error reporting. It states that the validation layer operates independently of the large language model and returns normalized validated results or structured errors.

stories.Headline: Kaspersky survey finds 97% of Russian employers report negative effects from unauthorized employee AI use
stories.Summary:
TASS, a Russian state news agency, reported that 97% of Russian employers have faced negative consequences from employees using artificial intelligence without authorization, according to a survey by Kaspersky, a Russian cybersecurity company. The survey found that 51% of employers cited privacy-related incidents, 44% cited errors from inaccurate AI-generated data and 43% cited gaps in information security assessments.

The survey covered 1,900 IT and security professionals across Russia and 18 other countries, TASS reported on November 27. According to the survey, 71% of employees said enterprises understand AI security risks, 61% believe responsible employee behavior mitigates those risks and 65% said employers use technical tools to monitor external AI services.

According to TASS, Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the risks of artificial intelligence at the AI Journey conference on Thursday, speaking alongside Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

stories.Headline: Q.ANT tests light-based AI chips in IONOS cloud pilot with 30 engineering teams
stories.Summary:
Q.ANT, a company led by founder and CEO Michael Förtsch, has rolled out photonic processors for AI models that use waves of light rather than electrons. The chips are being tested in a pilot program at IONOS cloud facilities, where more than 30 engineering teams are building optimized models for them. Regular GPUs shuffle electrons to process data, while light generates less heat as it travels and needs minimal cooling.

The chips are built on 90 nanometer node technology, which foundries already produce cheaply, so no massive upfront investment is needed. They work with any GPU brand, and existing C++ and Python code runs on them, though GPU-optimized code needs adaptations. Q.ANT says the aim is side-by-side use with GPUs rather than replacement, with GPUs handling linear math and the photonic chips taking on nonlinear work.

Förtsch said in a WIRED interview earlier in November 2026 that the company's simulations show a four to five times energy reduction, but that this has not yet been demonstrated in real hardware. He also said the chips "execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps."

Q.ANT says it is ready for a 100,000-unit order, though its suppliers are uncertain, as the hardware supply chain is less mature than the software side.

Articles.Title: A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

stories.Headline: Akashi builds a 100MW data center campus in Astana with a liquid-cooled phase for AI workloads
stories.Summary:
AKASHI Data Center PLC is developing a campus in Astana for modular data centers with a planned capacity of 100MW, to be commissioned in four phases. The company says it will be the first Tier IV data center in Central Asia, Tier IV being the Uptime Institute's highest reliability class. With an IT power capacity of 5.3MW, the first phase, DC-1, is due to be operational in the second quarter of 2027. The company says: "If required, we can support rack power densities of 10 or 15kW for specialized systems."

DC-2 and DC-3 will each have 12MW of IT capacity and rack densities of 15 to 30kW. DC-4, designed for 45 to 50MW, is purpose-built for AI workloads and uses liquid cooling for GPU heat. Astana temperatures range from -41.8°C to +40°C, and Akashi engineers say: "in principle, we can use free cooling for seven to eight months of the year." In free cooling, chillers run without compressors.

The first three modules are air-cooled, with warm air at 20 to 30°C and chilled water cooled to 7°C by chillers. In DC-4 the liquid coolant reaches about 60°C, and heat recovery from it heats the entire campus complex. Vladislav Minkevich, CEO of Akashi, said: "Kazakhstan’s colocation market currently comprises around 4,000 racks, and our project will effectively double that capacity."

The project's partners include Fortinet, a US cybersecurity developer, Virtuozzo of Switzerland for virtualization and storage software, and LiasaiL of Hong Kong for cloud and AI solutions. Akashi has an agreement with Türk Telekom International for backbone connectivity. An Uptime Institute survey in July 2026 put modal rack density above 11kW, up from 9kW the prior year, and new data centers often exceed 30kW per rack. Grid connections in the FLAP-D markets have been pushed beyond 2030, and some projects have been cancelled over local opposition.

Kazakhstan is implementing an AI development Concept and a Digital Code, and allows direct power purchase agreements. The country is also developing a Data Embassy model, which the Ministry of Digital Development expects to attract international firms. Russia has nearly 90 percent of its data center capacity occupied, according to Kommersant.

stories.Headline: Harvard education school launches Compass Collaborative to guide AI use in learning
stories.Summary:
The Harvard Graduate School of Education launched the Compass Collaborative earlier this month, the school announced. The initiative brings human development research to bear on decisions about artificial intelligence, with the aim of guiding how AI is designed and used in learning.

The collaborative offers three primary resources. One is “Developmental by Design,” a 12-week online certificate program. The other two are resource guides, “Visible and Invisible AI” and “AI Guidance by Age,” the latter drawing on more than 5,000 research pieces.

Nonie K. Lesaux, the dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Education, said “the world is reorganizing around generative AI.” She said schools, families, policymakers and developers are making decisions faster than the evidence can keep up. “We launched Compass as a startup inside HGSE,” she said, adding that she wants the initiative to be trusted by the field.

Jeffrey J. “Jeff” Curley, HGSE’s chief of strategic initiatives and a co-director of Compass, said the work starts with learners and then asks what role AI should play. Tessa Forshaw, a cognitive scientist and the other co-director, said there are significant gaps in understanding AI’s effects over time.

The initiative hopes to hold more events, bring in fellows and form partnerships, including a possible one with Teach For America. It is to be updated as research continues.

stories.Headline: Matters.AI raises $12 million pre-Series A round led by Tanglin Venture Partners
stories.Summary:
Matters.AI has raised a $12 million (₹115 crore) pre-Series A round, the company said. The round was led by Tanglin Venture Partners. IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica's Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures and Tetration Ventures participated. Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners continued their backing. The company claims it is India's largest cybersecurity pre-Series A round, and says its total funding now stands at $18.25 million (₹175 crore).

The platform consolidates four legacy security tools and uses context-aware AI for data lineage. The new funding will go toward research on automated investigations and endpoint intelligence, and toward safeguards against misuse of data by AI agents.

Keshava Murthy is CEO and co-founder of Matters.AI, and Harsh Sahu is CTO and co-founder.

stories.Headline: CREST finds 81% of penetration testing providers use AI beyond experimentation
stories.Summary:
CREST, a cybersecurity industry body, has published research on the use of AI in threat-led penetration testing. The report is titled "AI and the Future of Threat-Led Penetration Testing." It found that 81% of surveyed providers are using AI beyond experimentation. Twenty-six providers responded to the survey, which followed two industry roundtables focused on financial services.

Over the next 12 months, AI is expected by 65% of respondents to support 40% or more of threat-led penetration testing tasks, the research found. Reporting and assessment is the most common live use of AI, followed by reconnaissance and threat-informed preparation. Among users of AI for threat emulation, 86% report improved accuracy and realism. The report notes that biases in AI models and training data could skew threat assessments, and that AI-enabled impersonation raises ethical concerns, with voice cloning, synthetic video and personalized content used to test controls.

None of the 11 regulated threat-led penetration testing providers allow autonomous AI testing, while one commercial provider reported allowing autonomous execution. Among respondents, 68% rank scope and operational control among their top three risks, and 68% rank client data and confidentiality among their top three risks. 92% say sending client data to external AI needs client approval, and 62% say autonomous testing actions need explicit client approval. 92% rate validating AI output as an essential skill. According to Nick Benson, CEO of CREST: "AI is amplifying this and is already changing how it is delivered," and "TLPT, particularly in production environments, has always been high risk and in need of the strongest assurance."

Looking ahead, 88% of respondents anticipate more AI-generated offensive tooling, and 88% expect demand for AI-skilled testers to rise. 85% expect AI-related procurement requirements to increase, and 81% expect more client requests to disclose AI use. The report also notes that some financial institutions are building internal testing capabilities.

Articles.Title: AI raises new questions about what penetration testing proves

stories.Headline: Envestnet growth chief says AI must be embedded in operations, not added on
stories.Summary:
Jonathan Linstra, chief growth officer at Envestnet, said artificial intelligence must be embedded in a firm's operations rather than bolted on. He made the remarks in an interview with James Burton of InvestmentNews at Schwab Impact 2026 in Boston. "AI is not a bolt-on. It It's embedded," Linstra said.

Linstra said an AI layer will not fix a fragmented technology stack. He said compliance, governance and security must come first, because a regulated industry demands them. He said AI works best on a single data foundation.

Envestnet works with 500 of the largest registered investment advisors, according to the company. Chris Todd, chief executive of Envestnet, said "if we have great products and happy customers everything takes care of itself." Envestnet calls itself a leading adaptive wealth technology firm, and its data layers include MoneyGuide, Tamarac and its wealth platform.

About 6,000 RIAs were in the room, according to the report. It said 7% of RIAs manage more than $1 billion and that this 7% controls 74% of assets, citing Cerulli. Consolidation is real and will continue, and private equity is stepping in because it sees value, according to the report. No specific target was given for growth investment.

stories.Headline: Norton Rose Fulbright partner questions whether AI efficiency alone qualifies as an intangible asset
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is entering multinationals' operating models, with examples including coding agents and predictive analytics, according to Bloomberg Tax. It is seen as driving efficiency and cost savings, and some argue it is an autonomous value-generating asset. Fundamental transfer pricing questions remain, Bloomberg Tax reported. Stephanie Pantelidaki, London transfer pricing head and partner at Norton Rose Fulbright, asked: "Is efficiency by itself enough for AI to be treated as an intangible asset" Bloomberg Tax also reported questions over whether AI creates super profits, who owns and controls AI systems, and how AI value is allocated among entities. AI may not meet all the criteria for an intangible, the outlet said.

The OECD guidelines state: "The term intangible is intended to address something which is not a physical asset or a financial asset" According to Bloomberg Tax, the OECD definition requires ownership or control and compensation between independent parties, and the OECD says intangibles generate significant economic value. AI is often developed with data from several entities, and control and governance are often distributed, the outlet reported. Treating AI as an intangible would need super profits above a baseline, while AI implementation and risk-control costs are often not factored in, according to Bloomberg Tax. Few groups claim a direct link between AI and revenue, the outlet reported: AI efficiencies are evident but super profits are unclear, and unclear ownership may mean AI fails the OECD intangible test.

AI value is often non-routine under the OECD guidelines, and the question is how to measure and attribute it, Bloomberg Tax reported. The current guidelines make no reference to AI, though the framework can still apply to its use, according to the outlet. It also raised questions over which entities programmed and control AI and which bear AI decision-making risk, with answers likely spread across several entities. AI systems show high integration and uniqueness, and a contribution profit split may suit their assessment, Bloomberg Tax reported.

One-sided methods are hard to apply to unique AI elements, while a profit split weighs algorithm creation and training data along with local adaptations and customizations, according to the outlet. Ownership is easier to evidence in pharma or medical AI and harder for professional services process optimization, it reported. AI analysis should join standard functional and risk analysis, and AI value could potentially be measured through a profit split, according to Bloomberg Tax. The outlet said the article does not reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group.

stories.Headline: Colt launches 800G wavelength services early to meet AI bandwidth demand
stories.Summary:
Colt Technology Services, a London-headquartered firm, has launched 800G wavelength services on routes across Europe, Asia and the U.S. The service is aimed at hyperscalers, neoscalers and content providers, and runs over terrestrial and subsea infrastructure. The launch was brought forward from an initial 2027 release.

Colt cited TeleGeography research that 75% of used international bandwidth is taken up by AI platforms and neoclouds, whose requirements are forecast to rise nine-fold by 2035. Colt's own research found that 96% of organizations report AI infrastructure challenges.

Joe Scattareggia, EVP of infrastructure sales at Colt, said: "GPU-intensive AI workloads require huge amounts of bandwidth, low latency and consistent performance, and there’s no time to wait for capacity to catch up." He added: "Across our global infrastructure we’ve invested in 800G, and helping them move fast and scale as AI demand grows, customers can now order that capacity when they need it."

Colt joins fellow British player Exa Infrastructure and Fiber Links Around the Globe (FLAG) in increasing networking capacity for AI. Mid-market neoscalers prioritize power over latency, which poses a planning challenge for wholesale network operators.

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer CTO Alex Tyrrell warns that banning unauthorized AI tools worsens shadow AI in healthcare
stories.Summary:
Alex Tyrrell, executive vice president and chief technology officer at Wolters Kluwer, said healthcare organizations that ban unauthorized AI tools may make the problem worse. Tyrrell, who leads health and advanced technology at the company, made the comments in an article published by govinfosecurity.com on Nov. 27, 2026. The article examined what it called shadow AI in healthcare.

The article says about half of those users, then cuts off. The survey is the source of the 57% figure.

Tyrrell is responsible for health and advanced technology at Wolters Kluwer. He said banning unauthorized AI tools may worsen the problem. The article credits the warning to him.

stories.Headline: Ja Rule says artists can use AI to reimagine their work rather than create it
stories.Summary:
Musician Ja Rule was interviewed by Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi about artificial intelligence on the Power Players podcast on Friday, November 27, 2026. The episode asks whether AI can be used for good. Ja Rule described positive experiences with the technology, saying it helps him rethink and reimagine his work.

Ja Rule said AI is only harmful to an artist who lets it be. "AI can only really be detrimental to your art if you allow it to," he said. He added that a true artist should be able to use AI to make their art greater, and that "true artists are using AI not to create their art, but to reimagine their art."

He described an app that turned his song "Put It On Me" into a '70s record. "It sounded amazing," he said. He is considering repurposing a whole album with a '70s vibe, and said "the meal's already been served."

Sozzi also spoke with Wyclef Jean, Busta Rhymes and Tiësto. He said AI is starting to have a real impact on musicians.

Articles.Title: Can AI earn a spot in the creative world? Ja Rule think so.

stories.Headline: European shares rise as STOXX 600 gains 0.9% in morning trading
stories.Summary:
European shares rose in morning trading on Friday, with the STOXX 600 up 0.9%, according to Yahoo Finance reporter Pranav Kashyap. The advance followed a 1.75% gain for the index on Thursday. Germany's DAX added 0.7%, the CAC 40 in Paris rose 0.1% and London's FTSE 100 gained 0.8%.

The STOXX 600 was on track for a weekly gain of 1.81% but remained on course for a monthly decline of 1.5%. November was roiled by jitters over artificial intelligence and hot inflation, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departed and was then reinstated. European bond yields moved higher, especially at the front end, as traders priced in more ECB rate hikes.

Minutes from the European Central Bank showed hawkish undertones, with a "large number of members" possibly backing an October hike, and the minutes said "further tightening was likely necessary."

French November consumer price figures and final Eurozone November consumer confidence were due on Friday. U.S. markets were in a holiday-shortened post-Thanksgiving session.

Articles.Title: European shares extend rally, but bruising November leaves AI scars

stories.Headline: STOXX and ACU Markets partner to explore AI compute price benchmarks
stories.Summary:
STOXX Ltd., a unit of ISS STOXX/Deutsche Börse Group, and ACU Markets announced a strategic partnership on 27 November 2026 to explore AI compute benchmarks. The two firms will combine ACU's methodology and market data with STOXX's index capabilities. The partnership will explore AI compute price and benchmark indices.

The price and economic value of AI compute capacity are what the indices are intended to measure. They would cover GPU and other accelerator-based compute across technologies, topologies, geographies, procurement models and contract terms. Potential uses include procurement, investment products, risk management, AI compute derivatives and other financial applications. Development and launch are subject to governance, legal, regulatory and commercial approvals.

A STOXX spokesperson said AI infrastructure growth brings "demand for transparent and reliable benchmarks that enable market participants to better understand, compare and manage compute exposure." An ACU Markets spokesperson said: "AI compute is becoming a critical economic input, but the market does not yet have a broadly adopted AI compute reference price."

AI compute is a critical economic input, with nearly $7 trillion in investment needed by 2030, and McKinsey calls compute power a critical resource. The market is fragmented across technologies, geographies and procurement models.

Articles.Title: STOXX, ACU Markets Explore AI Compute Benchmark

stories.Headline: Florida judge sentences Sanchez to 47 months for AI voice fraud
stories.Summary:
David Anthony Sanchez, 36, of Port St. Lucie, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison on Nov. 17, 2026, in Fort Lauderdale federal court. U.S. District Judge Melissa Damian, of the Southern District of Florida, imposed the sentence. Sanchez had pleaded guilty on Sept. 1, 2026, to money laundering and aggravated identity theft. He was indicted on April 9, 2026. Prosecutors said Sanchez used artificial intelligence to mimic the voice of N3ON, a popular online streamer, and posed as the streamer and his representative.

He created accounts that appeared to belong to N3ON and signed agreements using the streamer's identity. He also sent an AI-generated voice recording confirming participation, deceiving memecoin project organizers. About $260,000 in cryptocurrency was defrauded, and Sanchez converted crypto to U.S. dollars to conceal the proceeds. He was ordered to pay restitution to victims.

Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas, of the Southern District of Florida, said, "Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm." She also said "the defendant exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate the trust of unsuspecting victims." Prosecutors said Sanchez posed as the streamer and that victims transferred crypto to accounts he controlled. The aliases given are "Dave the Jewler" and "Rueben Alexis De Jesus Santana."

Articles.Title: Port St. Lucie man sentenced to 47 months in AI impersonation case

stories.headline_source: Port St. Lucie man sentenced to 47 months in AI impersonation case

stories.Summary:
An emergency room doctor has become a hospital's first clinical AI engineer, according to IEEE Spectrum. The article reporting the appointment is dated Nov. 27, 2026. The hospital was not named in the report. The doctor was not named either.

The report gives no date for the appointment and no location for the hospital. It does not describe the duties of the clinical AI engineer role. No quote from the doctor was included. No next steps were reported.

The article page carried no visible article text, IEEE Spectrum's page showed. Only the headline and page code were available. The page code included styling and social share buttons.

stories.Headline: Rep Nanette Barragán co-leads a 2026 bill requiring annual environmental reports from AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Rep. Nanette Barragán, D-Calif., co-leads a 2026 bill that would require annual reports from AI data centers. The bill, H.R. 9183, the Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act, was introduced June 8, 2026, and referred to the Science and Energy and Commerce committees. It covers data centers at a threshold of 50 megawatts. A 2024 bill let companies report voluntarily.

The reports would go annually to the Environmental Protection Agency and cover the full range of environmental impacts. They would be posted publicly, except for confidential commercial information. The EPA would first seek corrective action for non-reporting, and a penalty would be possible six months after the due date. The penalty would be based on facility size and the length of noncompliance, and the bill sets no dollar amount for it. The bill has no preemption provision and authorizes no additional funds.

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., introduced the bill. The EPA would lead a one-year impact study with other agencies, joined by the Energy Department and FERC. NIST would convene a consortium on measurement standards that includes Tribes, local governments and industry. A 2024 Senate version, S. 3732, was voluntary and set no power threshold or penalties. A mandatory Senate version, S. 4727, arrived June 9, led by Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., with four Democratic cosponsors.

Barragán said, "This bill is a first step to ensure data center developers rightfully bear the higher electricity costs." She also said, "Congress must do more." The House passed H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, on Sept. 16 by 417 to 3; that bill covers data centers above 100 megawatts. The Senate blocked the measure 57 to 43. Barragán is scheduled to give a noon keynote Dec. 1 at the National Press Club event Broadband and AI in the Next Congress, and Markey keynotes at 2:40 p.m. the same day.

Articles.Title: Rep. Nanette Barragán Moves AI Data Center Reporting From Voluntary to Mandatory

stories.headline_source: Rep. Nanette Barragán Moves AI Data Center Reporting From Voluntary to Mandatory

stories.Headline: Japan defense ministry issues AI vision setting human control rules for Self-Defense Forces
stories.Summary:
Japan's Defense Ministry released guidelines on the Self-Defense Forces' use of artificial intelligence on Friday. The document is called the Defense AI Vision.

The guidelines set out five basic principles. They say humans keep decision-making authority and responsibility, and that AI use should comply with international and domestic laws. They also call for safety, reliability, transparency and accountability, and warn against excessive reliance on specific technologies, products or businesses. The ministry said in the guidelines that it has "no intention of developing fully autonomous lethal weapons that operate beyond human control."

The vision builds on a 2024 basic policy and aims to move beyond individual AI applications, using AI and data to strengthen defense capabilities as the technology transforms how those capabilities are exercised. It calls for starting AI use from operational needs and challenges, and cites physical AI to conduct missions without risking personnel, along with AI analysis of signals intelligence, satellite and aerial imagery and radar tracks. It also covers cooperation with allies and like-minded countries through mutual understanding and use of information, and control over sensitive data, while maintaining independent command and control structures in joint missions.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi discussed the guidelines at a news conference at the parliament building in Tokyo on Friday.

Articles.Title: Japan releases new guidelines on use of AI by Self-Defense Forces

stories.headline_source: Japan releases new guidelines on use of AI by Self-Defense Forces

stories.Headline: Oreon LP expands broker services with AI trading signals and market alerts
stories.Summary:
Oreon LP, a broker, announced on November 27, 2026, in Toronto, Canada, that it is expanding its analytical services with artificial intelligence. The AI tools generate trading signals and flag potentially significant changes in market conditions. The signals weigh historical price movements and current market factors.

The tools complement daily market reviews, live sessions with professional traders and trading masterclasses, and the AI organizes large volumes of market information. Each signal gives the asset, the expected direction, and entry and exit conditions. Signals also specify Stop Loss and Take Profit levels and include a brief explanation of the scenario.

Adam Malkin, Head of Public Relations at Oreon LP, said: "AI is used to analyze market data and identify situations that may warrant further examination." Company specialists review the AI-generated trading signals. The analysis covers technical and fundamental factors.

The web terminal offers more than 60 technical indicators, along with pattern-drawing and support/resistance tools, and users get an economic calendar. Oreon LP operates in the United Kingdom, Canada, Europe and Australia. CFD trading carries the risk of capital loss, and the AI recommendations are informational only, not investment advice.

Articles.Title: Oreon LP Introduces AI Tools for Financial Market Analysis

stories.headline_source: Oreon LP Introduces AI Tools for Financial Market Analysis

stories.Headline: AI cuts false declines as merchants weigh fraud risk against lost sales
stories.Summary:
PYMNTS Intelligence surveyed merchants and found that 85% of them see fraud prevention as competing with customer experience. Nearly half, 47%, said up to 5% of legitimate orders are rejected. AI-powered controls aim to maximize legitimate sales, according to the survey.

False declines waste acquisition spending and erode margins, the survey found. AI links fraud intelligence to margins and lifetime value. Holiday shopping patterns can appear suspicious to fraud systems, including larger purchases, unfamiliar retailers, multiple addresses and rare credentials. First-time customers lack purchase histories.

Criminals use AI to manufacture identities and automate purchases, while retailers deploy AI against behavioral and financial signals. Merchants evaluate controls by margins, retention, abandonment and losses. Adobe reported 2025 US online Black Friday purchases of "$11.8 billion, a 9.1% increase from the prior year." Adobe put 2025 Cyber Monday sales at $14.25 billion, and Cyber Monday held the title of the year's biggest online shopping day.

AI systems weigh the expected return of accepting, rejecting or investigating an order. Returns, chargebacks and fulfillment fraud erode sales into the next quarter. Walmart announced that customers can use Meta's AI agent Muse, which is named Muse, and shopping agents compare products, navigate sites and initiate purchases. Fraudsters also automate interactions at scale, and provenance, permissions and intent may matter as much as authentication.

In the August 2026 edition of its Optimizing Payments Tracker, PYMNTS Intelligence found that 83% of respondents reported AI reduced false positives and churn. AI cuts the legitimate transactions sacrificed for protection, and merchants weigh the cost of verification against the cost of rejection.

Articles.Title: AI Helps Merchants Stop Holiday Fraud Without Losing Good Customers

stories.headline_source: AI Helps Merchants Stop Holiday Fraud Without Losing Good Customers

stories.Summary: The Fair Work Commission, the industrial relations tribunal, is seeking input on proposed new rules covering generative AI disclosure and longer response times, Law360 reported on 27 November 2026. The changes would apply to general protections matters and unlawful termination matters. The rules have not yet been introduced and the proposal is at the consultation stage.

stories.Headline: AssessPrep adds AI-assisted marking for handwritten exams while teachers keep final approval
stories.Summary:
Singapore's Ministry of Education put teacher workload in focus in September 2026, outlining measures aimed at giving teachers more time for teaching. The measures include fewer out-of-classroom responsibilities, external support and digital tools. Lawmakers asked whether the time saved is returned to teaching.

Teachers scan or photograph the scripts and upload them in bulk, and students write on paper as usual, while AssessPrep has introduced Paper Mode for handwritten exams, which moves marking and analysis onto a digital platform. AI-assisted grading then takes place before teacher review, and the results can be used to track performance. The AI grading is calibrated to each teacher's approach, with seed grading sets providing a marking reference. AI grades and feedback are suggestions only, and nothing is finalised without teacher approval. Teachers can revise grades and add audio feedback.

Karan Gupta, Co-Founder of AssessPrep, said: "Marking needs judgement, but it involves a huge amount of repetition." He added: "The teacher still sees the work and makes the final call."

In a 2025 AssessPrep survey of 93 international schools, 78% of teachers reported saving over 30 minutes per assessment, and 73% said anonymous grading and automated scoring were more efficient. The International Baccalaureate introduces digital exams in 2026 for a small number of DP and CP subjects, and teachers and students may face a learning curve. Digital question banks and practice assessments can help preparation, and schools can keep handwritten exams alongside digital marking.
