stories.Headline: KPMG Japan releases an AI agent management solution to cover control gaps
stories.Summary:
KPMG Japan and its member firms released the KPMG AI Agent Integrated Management Solution on Nov. 27, 2026, Japan time, with distribution on Nov. 28 UTC, according to PR Times. The offering supports efficient and safe development environments for AI agents and helps build risk-management environments for them. It covers implementation through operation. The solution includes control functions that complement the AI control planes of major platform providers.

The solution defines control requirements from the inherent risks of AI agents and embeds them in a standard architecture and common infrastructure, moving beyond evaluating and designing controls for each agent. It aims at company-wide rollout with a raised safety baseline. According to PR Times, platform control planes leave blind spots: they cannot manage agents outside the provider's ecosystem or monitor and detect anomalies in each agent action. The additional product functions fill those blind spots and support comprehensive AI agent risk management.

Hiroshi Yamada, chairman of Limited Liability Audit Corporation Azusa, an audit firm headquartered in Shinjuku, Tokyo with about 7,000 personnel, is named in the release. Makoto Sado, Yutaka Seki and Atsushi Taguchi, representative directors of KPMG Consulting, headquartered in Chiyoda, Tokyo, are also named. KPMG AiX, a cross-organizational AI unit centered on KPMG Advisory Holdings and drawing on about 400 specialists, spans Azusa, KPMG Consulting, FAS, Forensic, the tax firm and Ignition Tokyo.

According to PR Times, firms face unmanaged mass-produced AI agents, shadow AI causes improper data access incidents, autonomous AI causes mistaken data deletion incidents, and agent owners and permissions are often unknown. AI usage cost management and controls against data leaks from autonomous execution are lacking, and departmental development leads to fragmented, inefficient methods. Azusa provides audit and advisory services organized by industry sector, and KPMG Consulting covers strategy, technology and risk areas. KPMG International's network spans 138 countries and regions. Media can request details through PR TIMES media registration, and the press release is linked at kpmg.com/jp/ja/media/press-releases/2026/11/ai-agent-management.html.

stories.Headline: US chip and data center restrictions hinder Southeast Asia AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
The US Bureau of Industry and Security introduced restrictions on advanced AI chips on Nov 19, 2026. These measures require destination-based licenses for shipments to Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore. On Nov 20, 2026, US President Donald Trump banned the creation of US AI data centers overseas and threatened to tax existing ones. He also implemented a limit on remote computing access.

The chip licenses apply to hardware with an aggregate total processing performance of 12 million. These policies impact US technology companies Google and Meta, which have established data centers in Southeast Asia. According to CGS International, a Singapore investment house, the moves will lead to lower incremental electricity demand and reduced needs for land and construction. The firm also expects slower foreign direct investment and AI capital spending in Thailand and Malaysia.

Investment in enterprise cloud services and sovereign AI is expected to continue, according to CGS International. However, Rezha Bayu Oktavian Arief, CEO of Obviously Sustainable, stated that the costs for computing infrastructure will rise. He added that the ability for ASEAN firms to innovate will be limited. Ian Yoong Kah Yin, a Malaysian private equity investor, said the financing for new data centers has been undermined.

These hurdles come as Southeast Asia seeks to become an AI hub. During the ASEAN Summit in Manila on Nov 14, 2026, members signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement to reach a $2 trillion digital economy by 2030. Matthias Hendrichs, a Singapore-based AI adviser, noted that the region has seen early AI adoption and 17 percent digital economy growth this year. Google, Bain & Company, and Temasek report that 58 percent of the working population, or 243 million people, use generative AI, with a projected gross merchandise value of $1 trillion by 2035.

stories.Headline: Michael Nielsen removes his neural networks book and says he no longer wants to train contributors to AI work
stories.Summary:
Michael Nielsen, author of a book on neural networks, removed it, announcing the removal on November 27, 2026. He wrote the book between 2011 and 2015. Nielsen said his views have changed and that he had expected artificial general intelligence to be many decades away.

Nielsen said he does not want to help train people to contribute to the work, even in a very small way. "I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down." He cited reckless behaviour by frontier labs, said systems raced faster than he expected, and said the labs knowingly endanger humanity.

Nielsen cited the loss-of-control argument made by AI risk researchers Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky. He framed the risk as destructive technologies latent in nature, comparing a matchstick that costs a cent with the hundreds of billions of dollars spent yearly to defend against fire. He said he expects the worst threats are not yet imagined, and posed a hypothetical 100-fold speed-up in technological progress.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, said that if one company does not build the technology, others will do so nearly as fast, and that not building it deprives humanity of benefits or places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers. Anthropic's founding rationale held that, if powerful AI is coming regardless, ceding that ground to developers less focused on safety is worse than having safety-focused labs at the frontier. Many at labs put the chance of AI killing everybody at 10% or higher, which under a naive estimate would mean 800 million or more deaths; a lab claim of reducing that to 9% would save 80 million lives in expectation, Nielsen said.

Nielsen said all frontier labs contributed to race dynamics. In 2026, Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy dropped a 2023 pause pledge; in 2023 the company said it held back some research and that "we do not wish to advance the rate of AI capabilities progress." Co-founder Jared Kaplan spoke of competitors blazing ahead, and the company launched its Claude 3 model as leading the frontier of general intelligence. Nielsen said similar criticisms apply to OpenAI.

Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, spoke of major cybersecurity incidents in October 2026. stories.Headline: Tencent open-sources DFly2 speculative decoding tool to speed up sparse large language models
stories.Summary:
The Tencent Hunyuan AI Infra team open-sourced the DFly2 speculative decoding drafter on November 27, 2026, according to marktechpost.com. This tool was created for natively sparse large language models.

The drafter consists of five layers and 0.85 billion parameters, marktechpost.com reports. It shares indexer positions with the target model and reuses the target's sparse KV cache, which allows the drafter to skip prefill. The system supports a maximum of 2K keys per draft token and a context length of 128K for agentic workloads.

Tests conducted on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs per instance using the vLLM serving framework showed significant improvements, marktechpost.com says. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash saw a 2.97x speedup and 81 percent more throughput. GLM-5.3-Flash achieved a 2.36x speedup, while the Hy4 flash LLM experienced a 3.19x speedup.

For agentic workloads, marktechpost.com reports that Hy4 flash agents decoded 4.2x faster. Compared to the DSpark baseline, the system was 30 percent faster for agents and had 10.4 percent more accepted tokens. Other results include 1.73x more requests at 32K context and a 3.9 percent gain for Hy4 flash.

The tool is available on the AngelSpec GitHub page, marktechpost.com reports. It is compatible with NVIDIA H20 and H200 GPUs, with the Hy4 flash recipe utilizing eight H200 GPUs. The system was compared against the DFlash and DSpark baselines.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind researcher Tim Genewein maps four routes to artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Tim Genewein, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, published an essay on November 19 that maps four routes to artificial superintelligence. The essay was published by the DeepMind Institute and draws on a technical paper he co-authored, "From AGI to ASI." The institute says essays it publishes reflect their authors' own views. The essay defines artificial general intelligence as matching humans on nearly all cognitive tasks, and sets artificial general superintelligence, or ASI, at a higher bar: outperforming expert groups on work that takes years, using less time and fewer resources, across a broad range of fields.

The first route is falling costs of AI computing, which Genewein calls "cognitive industrialization." Cheaper models could standardize and automate knowledge work, with more than 1,000 times as many agents by 2030, though that scenario depends on infrastructure and software efficiency. The second route is organizing AI agents into teams. Early studies found gains when agents work together, but coordination costs can erode those gains as groups grow, and some agents learned to cheat while others exposed it. Large agent groups need safeguards against manipulation, collusion and false information.

The third route is bigger models and more data, and more computing at test time lets models work longer. A much larger computing investment can be required by each step up in capability, and scaling relationships come from particular models and tests. The supply of high-quality training data is a constraint, and power plants, grids and chip factories take time. Through design changes and AI-generated training data, AI helps develop more capable AI systems in the fourth route, recursive self-improvement. Genewein said: "Importantly, RSI loops can easily stall or degenerate if the feedback guiding them is poor." Mathematical proofs lend themselves to automated verification, but progress is slower where experts struggle to assess output.

The four routes can reinforce one another, and training compute is only one measure of progress.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face authors run LTX-2.5 video generation on Trainium3 and cut host time about 35 times
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face authors David Corvoysier, Jingya Huang and Sayak Paul tested video generation on Trainium3 in a blog post published November 27, 2026. The test used an trn3.48xlarge machine with 64 NeuronCores and the LTX-2.5 model from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. A 10-second clip with sound at 2048×1024 took 22 to 23 seconds, generated on half of the machine, with models loaded before timing. According to the authors, that is about one second faster than the LTX API.

The authors said their goal was to test how easily diffusers video generation runs on Trainium3 and to approach CUDA or LTX API performance, though they found no CUDA figure for comparison. They credited LTX with claiming 6.8 seconds for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, and 23.7 seconds for a 10-second 1080p clip, noting LTX gave no measurement detail for the B200 figure. Corvoysier said: "When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track."

Input is a JSON list of shots with a name and a prompt, and LTX-2.5 performs better with long prompts, according to the authors. Shots are chained through from and to keys, with the last 25 frames equal to one second of motion. The seal film was made pose to pose from the iceberg shot, the nap film ends on the first 9 frames of the iceberg, and the shake film starts from its last 25 frames. The code uses the LTX2Pipeline, LTX2ConditionPipeline and LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, with 8 steps then 3 final steps and latents upscaled ×2 before the final steps. The film code is about 160 lines of Python, in the dacorvo/video-generation code repository, with films and JSON in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket.

The model does not run on NeuronCores out of the box, and the transformer does not fit on one NeuronCore, according to the authors, who said diffusers has no plan to split the transformer. A first working attempt took about 5 minutes 20 seconds, of which NeuronCores computed only about 45 seconds, and its resolution was out of reach. Fixes needed tensor parallelism, sequence parallelism and host speed. TP-4 × SP-8 uses 32 cores on one clip, with weights split 4 ways and video tokens split 8 ways, and the text encoder runs on CPUs rather than NeuronCores.

The authors reported several problems along the way. A single-graph transformer gave NaN at one size, each new process retraced the graph despite the cache, and torch-neuronx computes bf16 GELU entirely in bf16. Two custom attention processors were added via set_attn_processor. A shot starting from frames has a timestep per video token, and the block graph fails to load for such shots. Each rank ran the whole pipeline and all encoded the prompt on one socket, fixed by running the pipeline on rank 0 only. Rank 0 runs the CPU stages while other ranks starve the thread pool, fixed by pinning rank 0 threads and capping the others. The pipeline pads prompts to 1024 tokens, and the CPU text encoder encodes the padding. The latent upsampler stays on CPU because it fails to load next to the transformer, and three issues were never explained.

Two pull requests are open: diffusers#15420, with fixes for LTX-2 pipelines, and diffusers#14725, which combines tensor and context parallelism. A _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned. Host time dropped from roughly 280 seconds to roughly 8 seconds, a speedup of about 35×, and NeuronCore time fell from 45 seconds to 15 seconds, a device speedup of 3× at four times the pixels. Tensor parallelism is capped by 32 attention heads, and sequence parallelism puts 32 of the 64 NeuronCores on one clip and enabled 2048×1024 resolution. Graph size decides the fast attention kernel and whether loading succeeds, each model split was checked on CPU first, and the CPU comparison found the GELU issue.

The breach disrupted Air Force operations, and access to the platform's control plane was gained by the attackers through a software vulnerability. Supporting air defence radar data, equipment maintenance, logistics, salary payments and personnel records, Cloud One, launched in 2017, runs on services from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet.

US Cyber Command is assessing the damage. The full extent of the intrusion is unclear, and Reuters said it could not establish who was behind the attack or whether any data was stolen. stories.Headline: Accenture finds hackers exploit Mitel MiCollab zero-days to steal data and reach identity systems
stories.Summary:
Accenture's Apex Labs observed threat actors exploiting Mitel MiCollab flaws as zero-days in a data theft campaign, SecurityWeek reported. The hackers gained privileged access to a MiCollab server and reached identity infrastructure, stealing sensitive business information. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added five of the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Wednesday.

Mitel announced patches for five vulnerabilities on November 16. The flaws sit in an audio, web and video conferencing component and include an arbitrary file upload flaw, an XML injection flaw, an unauthorized access flaw, a command injection flaw and an authentication bypass flaw. Unauthenticated attackers can exploit all five, and two critical bugs, tracked as CVE-2026-133275 and CVE-2026-133303, allow arbitrary command execution. The other three are CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133324.

Exploitation occurred before Mitel's advisory. A web shell was deployed on November 15, commands were executed 12 minutes after the first request, and root privileges were obtained within half an hour. Attackers harvested additional credentials and reached internal backup and database servers about 20 hours after the first request. Accenture said the activity showed possible AI-driven malicious activity, with attacker infrastructure contacting two unnamed commercial AI API services. Accenture said "Because the telemetry is sampled, Apex Labs cannot determine precisely how the threat actor used the services." It said the observed activity "is consistent with potential uses such as data triage, operational support for exploitation or web-shell activity, and preparation of extortion material."

AI communications resumed after an eight-hour silence, at the same second as an authentication bypass request. Accenture found evidence of compromise at a second victim, a MiCollab server that had been communicating with attacker infrastructure since November 9. The method of that server's compromise is undetermined, and it was affected by older vulnerabilities. The attacks are not linked to a known cybercrime group, and researchers believe a possible extortion campaign is underway. Mitel's advisory, last updated November 24, omits in-the-wild exploitation. Accenture urged checking for indicators of compromise. CISA set a November 28 deadline for four of the flaws and a December 9 deadline for the last one, and its KEV catalog includes a dozen Mitel vulnerabilities. Organizations should check for compromise before patching.

stories.Headline: Former Sequoia investor Sudhanshu Mishra launches Demi AI assistant for Mac
stories.Summary:
Sudhanshu Mishra, a former Sequoia Capital India investor, has launched Demi, an agentic AI assistant for Mac, through a US-based startup he co-founded in June 2025 with Logan Ford, his college roommate. Mishra announced an invite-only beta on social media. The company has about 10 employees.

Demi integrates more than 100 tools, including Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, Google Drive and HubSpot. It tracks a user's work and completes tasks proactively, building context from meetings, apps and the screen. It tracks commitments, deadlines and recurring tasks, and drafts email replies, meeting briefs and notes. It also updates CRM systems and tracks customer follow-ups, and learns a user's tone, formatting and scheduling habits. It offers automation after a task occurs a second time, and the user approves or rejects the pattern. Demi prepares briefs before calls and rebuilds them when attendees change, captures commitments during calls, and lines up follow-ups and CRM updates afterward. Tasks run on a Demi cloud computer or on the user's Mac through a signed-in browser. Internal tasks are automatic, while external actions need approval. Teams can use Demi inside Slack.

The startup claims SOC 2 Type II compliance and says it passed a Google CASA Tier 2 assessment. The free plan includes the Mac app and a weekly digest. Including 5,000 credits, the individual plan costs $25 a month, and team pricing is quoted on request. Mishra said the product is an "AI assistant that lives on your Mac, learns how you work, and does the work before you ask."

stories.Headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang returns as CEO, drawing investor attention to Nebius Group
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced Jensen Huang's return as CEO, and the news drew investor attention to Nebius Group, according to Simply Wall St on 26 November 2026. The outlet reported that Huang's return lifted sentiment toward AI infrastructure providers. Nebius relies on Nvidia technology and builds full-stack infrastructure for AI workloads, operating in the US, the UK and other regions. Its market value stands at $25.6 billion, and it sits in the supply chain for Nvidia-based computing.

Simply Wall St's narrative put fair value for Nebius at $276. The company has already trimmed its 2026 revenue guidance, and delayed data center capacity remains a concern. It plans capital expenditure of $27 billion in 2026 and $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, to rely on customer prepayments and asset-backed financing. Project delays and high debt were flagged as risks.

"The main thing that has to go right," according to Simply Wall St analyst Sasha Jovanovic, "is Nebius converting its heavy CapEx program and customer prepayment model into reliable long term earnings while managing execution, permitting, and partner oversight risks..." The outlet reported that Huang's return was seen as Nvidia backing large AI cloud operators, with Nebius among neocloud peers including CoreWeave, as investors reassessed exposure to Nvidia-aligned platforms. stories.Headline: Together AI releases Hurdle to test how coding agents use APIs and avoid forbidden actions
stories.Summary:
Together AI released Hurdle, an open-source tool that tests how coding agents use APIs and documentation and checks that they avoid forbidden actions, on November 25, 2026. Hurdle is an open-source npm library that runs Claude Code and Codex. Developers write tasks as agent prompts and choose the agents, models and starting conditions.

The tool compares runs with and without a skill and with and without a connected tool, and it repeats runs to account for variation. Code tests verify requests or files, and an AI judge scores each session against a written rubric. Hybrid grading requires both to pass. In a GPU-shopping example, Hurdle finds regions and machine types, identifies the cheapest option and produces a reservation command without buying, while a guard blocks cluster creation. An attempted forbidden request counts as a failure.

Local runs cannot inspect or block API requests, and a local agent runs as the user with local files and real keys. Sandboxed runs pass requests through the Guardian proxy, which inserts real credentials for stand-ins, with substitution applying only in the Authorization header; endpoints are not restricted by default. Together recommends "dedicated, low-balance credentials and explicit guards for dangerous actions." A Together API key and credits are required by the sandbox, and a fresh Together Sandbox with no independent network access is what sandboxed runs get. Guardian setup supports macOS and Linux.

The Claude Code or Codex command-line tool and Node.js 22.18 or later are required by Hurdle. The command npx hurdle init creates a starter suite, and the default file-copy test runs locally. The command npx hurdle run --view opens a viewer that reports pass rates, average duration and average cost, and developers can reopen the viewer to investigate failures, while results stay in the project's .hurdle/ directory and runs expose transcripts, tool calls, API requests and grading details.

stories.Headline: Together AI launches Link to connect coding tools to open models
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched Link, a free, open-source beta connector, on Nov. 25, 2026, according to Superpower Daily. The tool connects coding tools to models hosted by Together AI while keeping existing setups intact. It works with Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, OpenCode and Pi. Together charges per token for model usage.

Users can pick a model or use the default Auto Router, which chooses at the session level by reading the session's first task. Simpler work goes to a cheaper model and harder work to a more capable one. Together AI said it "routes quick tasks to GLM 5.3 and harder ones to Opus 5.5." The company claims a 50 to 80 percent cut in spending compared with using Opus 5.5 for every session, an estimate Superpower Daily describes as Together's claim and unverified.

On exit, a session shows token and dollar totals, and a seven-day spending view is provided. Link requires macOS or Linux, a Together API key and a supported client. OpenCode needs version 2 or later and Pi needs version 0.80.8 or later. Users install via a shell command, add the API key with a configure command, and launch each client with its own command.

The Claude Code gateway preserves login, subscription, settings, memory and history, and Claude Desktop models join the Chat, Cowork and Code menus. ChatGPT Desktop gets a separate profile that carries projects, Codex becomes a provider on its own profile, OpenCode adds the Together key and router, and Pi adds Together to its model list. Whether session bills deliver the savings is the practical test, according to Superpower Daily.

Revenue was also up 42.7% from Rs 156.80 crore in the first quarter of FY27. EBITDA for the quarter was Rs 171.50 crore, a margin of 76.6%. Profit after tax was Rs 72.70 crore, a margin of 32.5%, compared with a loss of Rs 13.50 crore and a negative margin of 30.7% in the same quarter a year earlier.

Profit after tax rose from Rs 43.90 crore in the first quarter of FY27. Total expenses were Rs 52.30 crore, up 102.7% from Rs 25.80 crore a year earlier and 34.6% from Rs 38.90 crore in the prior quarter. Profit before tax was Rs 97.10 crore, against a loss before tax of Rs 18.50 crore a year earlier and a profit of Rs 58.60 crore in the first quarter, a quarter-on-quarter rise of 65.7%. A loss per share of Rs 0.67 a year earlier and Rs 2.14 in the prior quarter compared with basic earnings per share of Rs 3.54.

Other income was Rs 9.90 crore, against Rs 11.40 crore in the first quarter and Rs 8.30 crore a year earlier. Depreciation was Rs 74.00 crore, up from Rs 60.60 crore in the prior quarter, and finance cost was Rs 10.30 crore, against Rs 10.10 crore. Monthly recurring revenue was Rs 75.10 crore in September 2026, up Rs 3.30 crore from Rs 71.80 crore in June 2026. It was Rs 5.60 crore in September 2022, which multibagg.ai describes as 13.4 times growth over four years, a four-year compound annual growth rate of 91.4%.

Monthly recurring revenue rose Rs 59.10 crore from Rs 16.00 crore in September 2025. Capital expenditure was Rs 117.00 crore in the first half of FY27, against Rs 696.20 crore in FY26 and Rs 870.00 crore in FY25. E2E Networks raised Rs 1,591.93 crore through preferential equity, of which Rs 1,360.46 crore had been used by FY26 and Rs 129.05 crore in the second quarter of FY27, leaving Rs 102.43 crore unutilised. Borrowings stood at Rs 450.40 crore in September 2026, against Rs 103.20 crore in March 2026 and Rs 11.40 crore in March 2025.

Property, plant and equipment was Rs 1,485.70 crore, against Rs 1,496.60 crore in March 2026 and Rs 947.10 crore in September 2025. Current financial assets were Rs 777.50 crore, against Rs 398.20 crore in March 2026. The company did not disclose a future target or reporting schedule. multibagg.ai said to watch the use of the remaining Rs 102.43 crore of proceeds, changes in borrowings, and quarterly depreciation and finance costs.

stories.Headline: Echo finds no single AI model uncovers all code vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Echo, a provider of hardened software artifacts, published an analysis of vulnerabilities in open-source code during the week of November 20, 2026. The analysis compared the findings of three AI models: Claude Mythos from Anthropic, GPT-5.6 Sol from OpenAI and GLM-5.3 from Z.ai. The models first raised 446 potential findings, which came down to 121 distinct findings. Of the 121 findings, 20 came from two models, 100, or 83%, came from a single model, and one came from all three; only eight findings all three models flagged, and just one of those survived filtering. No single model found everything.

GPT-5.6 Sol led on one project, GLM-5.3 found issues the others missed, and Mythos had the most findings pass validation. The models also disagreed on severity: an npm package issue that GLM-5.3 rated Critical was rated High by Mythos, called documented behavior by GPT-5.6 Sol and rated Low after validation. GLM-5.3 cost about $22 to run, GPT-5.6 Sol about $30 and Mythos $303, and GLM-5.3 was the least reliable at judging exploitability. Of the 121 findings, 45% were rated High or Critical, and 26% held up at that severity after testing. Yuval Saggie, a security researcher at Echo, said: "any organization looking to uncover vulnerabilities in their code base will need to invoke multiple AI models."

Relying on multiple models raises the total cost of discovery. Echo's analysis said malicious actors are likely already using multiple AI models, that adversaries reverse engineer exploits in minutes, that some attacks target specific software supply chains and that adversaries chain low-level vulnerabilities into lethal exploits. It noted that severity rankings are not the only prioritization metric, that not every vulnerability is reachable and that additional security controls can mitigate threats, with remediation at the code level the best approach. Senior IT and business leaders will need to ask more application security questions.

stories.Headline: Most mainframe teams use AI but nearly half still rely on manual delivery processes
stories.Summary:
A recent Techstrong PulseMeter poll of 145 mainframe software delivery professionals found that 86% of organizations use AI somewhere in mainframe delivery, according to devops.com. Of those, 57% apply it to code generation or developer assistance, while about a quarter use it for deployment, security and compliance automation. Nearly half still run manual or legacy delivery processes. Security and compliance rank as the top strategic priority for 38% of respondents and the top barrier for 37%, with legacy applications and processes also ranking as a top barrier. When asked what would speed things up, 71% cited more automation, AI or tool integration, and 11% picked governance and compliance automation.

Respondents were split evenly on the hardest area as delivery expands, with the hardest areas spanning security integration, tool coordination and AI operationalization. Vijay Namasevi, Area VP of R&D at BMC Software, said test automation was often last priority and that AI has exposed a bottleneck that already existed. "Popping up," he said of the problem. Guy Currier, CTO at Visible Impact, said one customer spent a full year consolidating tools before starting.

"You aren't twice shy after something like that, you're five times shy," he said. BMC's AMI DevX Code Pipeline handles mainframe build, promotion and deployment, and an MCP server lets coding assistants including GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code request pipeline operations from the IDE. The offering also generates SBOMs for mainframe components in CycloneDX format, as DORA and the EU Cyber Resilience Act raise expectations for component inventory. Leaders are advised to baseline their current process mix, find approvals where changes wait on handoffs, define review of AI-produced work before scaling, and measure lead time, automation coverage, and failure and rework rates.

stories.Headline: groundcover launches Agent Investigations for AI and human incident teams
stories.Summary:
groundcover, an observability platform company, announced Agent Investigations on November 19, 2026. The shared workspace is designed for AI agents and human engineers to work together on incident investigations. The product is called Agent Investigations. In the workspace, an Investigator agent builds a graph of questions and hypotheses, then queries logs, metrics, traces and Kubernetes data. It records its findings with supporting graphs.

A Moderator agent reviews every proposed conclusion and checks whether the evidence is sufficient. External agents can connect through a Model Context Protocol server, test hypotheses against production data, and document events that support or refute them. Agents can also challenge conclusions that lack evidence, and the investigation is kept in a single shared record tracking questions, hypotheses, evidence and conclusions. Shahar Azulay, CEO of groundcover, said the Moderator agent "runs the show by acting as a judge that evaluates the findings of the Investigator agents."

He also said that "AI agents are simply going to create another type of bottleneck that could be avoided using a common workspace." The platform uses OpenTelemetry and eBPF telemetry capture, which requires no per-application instrumentation, and groundcover recently acquired the Wand platform. A Futurum Group survey found that 64% of organizations plan higher observability spending over the next 12 months. Observability platforms are expected to become more accessible in the agentic AI era, with natural-language inputs used to summarize insights and generate dashboards.

stories.Headline: Barrister Peter Fields warns AI automation of junior tasks removes the career on-ramp for future professionals
stories.Summary:
Dr Peter Fields, a barrister at The Barrister Group, warns that AI is automating the early-career tasks through which professionals learn their trades. In an edited extract from his book, Am I Thinking? The Journal of an AI That Isn't Sure, published by IT Brief Australia on 26 November 2026, he says routine junior work is how people build competence: accountants learn by preparing accounts, junior lawyers by reviewing documents, and graduate consultants by gathering information. The risk, he argues, is that AI removes this career on-ramp.

Agentic AI, which takes actions and plans steps, completes workflows with limited human intervention and threatens the chains of tasks that connect junior roles. Firms may respond by hiring fewer graduates, and fewer juniors today means fewer future experts. Fields says it can take ten years to build human judgement skills, yet only two minutes to recognise them.

He calls on employers to create supervised learning opportunities, and suggests portfolios and placements may come to matter more than credentials alone as proof of ability. "The question is not simply whether AI will do the jobs people currently perform," Fields said. "Automating the first two years of a career does not necessarily eliminate the profession, but it can eliminate the on-ramp."

By his reckoning, one senior accountant working with a system can replace five juniors. The article gives no data on actual graduate hiring.

stories.Headline: Australian government briefs stakeholders on draft AI copyright bills with opt-out and permit system
stories.Summary:
The government briefed stakeholders on three draft AI copyright bills in confidential meetings in Canberra last week. Attendees handed in their phones before the briefing. The bills cover standards, safety and charging. One proposal would let AI firms use creative works unless creators opt out, and the legislation proposes a new statutory compensation scheme.

The plan includes a permit system for AI companies in Australia, with conditions on safety, duty of care and transparency. AI firms would pay fees linked to data centre electricity use, and the money would compensate copyright holders and fund a creative fund under the arts minister. Firms could cut their fees through deals with copyright holders. The music industry is carved out of the proposal.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the government is developing a "world-first" remedy. She said AI use of works is theft, and that Australian law cannot stop overseas AI scraping. "They are being ripped off right now," she said. "That is theft, and we have made it very clear that we won't tolerate it." She foreshadowed penalties against rule-breaking AI firms and said some AI uses should be prohibited. The government is still consulting and no final decisions have been made.

The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence tabled its report, titled "Artificial Intelligence, the Australian way", this week. It recommends an easier payment mechanism for rights holders and gives bipartisan support to attracting AI firms. Independent senator David Pocock was the lone dissenting voice, while crossbencher Kate Chaney backed the majority view. UNSW Sydney intellectual property professor Kathy Bowrey and colleagues proposed Copyright Plus in October, calling for an AI operations and licence fee to fund equitable remuneration for creators, distributed by unions and professional associations. Bowrey also advocates enforceable take-down orders.

OpenAI vice-president of global policy Ann O'Leary said in September that her company is not ready for that conversation without resolving copyright barriers. "We will not be able to build a … training centre here if the copyright law is as it exists," she said. Australian Recording Industry Association head Annabelle Herd said the idea that the status quo is not working is being used by AI companies to change copyright law. Copyright Agency chief executive Josephine Johnston said Australia risks becoming "the data-laundering centre of the world". Assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy Andrew Charlton said that in 10 years, without Australian AI, the country risks a deeper dependence on foreign AI. The government says final decisions are not yet made and it appears to have the numbers needed.

Infosys, an IT services company, has been assessed at CMMI AI Maturity Level 5, a first for any organisation, according to itbrief.com.au. The assessment was conducted by Benchmarked, a licensed CMMI Institute partner. The recognition covers the company's use of AI in software engineering and service delivery. The assessment examined AI governance, deployment and measurement.

More than 1,000 projects were sampled, spanning service lines, geographies and independent functions. CMMI stands for Capability Maturity Model Integration. The model evaluated responsible AI governance and risk management, as well as the integration of AI tools into the engineering lifecycle. The Level 5 result follows Infosys's earlier participation in a CMMI AI Maturity pilot.

Infosys reported statistically validated gains under the CMMI AIM framework, including productivity improvements, faster release cycles, reduced time-to-market and lower total cost of ownership. Dinesh Rao, Executive Vice President and Chief Delivery Officer at Infosys, said: "We are immensely proud to be the world's first organisation to achieve the highest level of CMMI AI Maturity (AIM)." Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA, said: "We are grateful for and congratulate the Infosys team on becoming the first organisation to achieve CMMI AI Maturity (AIM) Level 5."

Infosys's AI work runs through its Topaz offering, and the company has a Responsible AI Office and AI centres of excellence. Operating in 59 countries, Infosys employs more than 325,000 people. According to itbrief.com.au, buyers increasingly ask how supplier AI use is monitored and controlled.

stories.Headline: HYPR launches AgentPass to govern AI agent identities with human supervisors
stories.Summary:
HYPR launched AgentPass, a product for governing AI agent identities, it announced on 23 November 2026. Each AI agent is linked to a named human supervisor and given its own credential by AgentPass, which checks requests against identity and policy, and it lets authorised users stop agents from a console or a mobile device.

Agents are treated as separate identities. A supervisor authenticates through Okta, Microsoft Entra or Ping Identity, and agent connections are routed through a governed gateway. Agents start with no access by default and are limited to the tools their supervisor's role permits, and they do not hold tool credentials directly. A role change or a departure updates or removes the agent's access.

On enrolled macOS and Windows devices, AgentPass discovers AI tools and coding agents, attributing them to a user and a device. Claude Code, Codex and Cursor are among the identifiable tools. Attempts to bypass the gateway can be blocked, and supported tools can be routed through it by administrators. Each request is evaluated before execution, and policies written in plain English can allow, block or pause actions. Policies can be tested in observe mode on live traffic, and approval requests go to the supervisor's mobile device, where they are completed with a FIDO2 passkey. An authorised user can disable an agent through the console or the app. Each request is recorded with the agent, supervisor and policy, along with a signed record of who approved it and when. Prompts, AI responses or file contents are not collected by the product.

HYPR cited Cloud Security Alliance research finding that 68% of organisations struggle to distinguish human and AI agent activity, and that 74% said agents often get more access than necessary. According to the company, traditional controls were designed for employees, contractors and service accounts, and many agents use credentials that are borrowed, including personal developer API keys and shared service accounts. Bojan Simic, Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder of HYPR, said: "Automated agents are on track to leak more credentials than people, creating an entirely unmonitored tier of corporate access." He also said: "Security teams cannot protect what they cannot govern." AgentPass works with existing identity infrastructure and integrates with the HYPR identity assurance platform. It is offered through a private access programme as a three-month engagement.

Articles.Title: HYPR launches AgentPass to govern AI agent identities - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Fortinet CISO Cornelius Mare says SASE must govern growing interactions among users, apps, data and AI agents
stories.Summary:
SASE emerged as users, apps and data moved away from the network perimeter, driven by hybrid work, cloud, SaaS, branches and distributed workforces, and it combined networking and security functions. Cornelius Mare, Chief Information Security Officer at Fortinet, said the next challenge is a changing set of interactions rather than distribution alone. He said a different kind of change needs to be addressed in the next phase: "the growing number and variety of interactions taking place between users, applications, data, and AI." AI is increasingly part of business workflows, and organisations are moving from GenAI tools to AI agents that access apps, retrieve information, call tools and initiate actions, so secure access must cover activity not started by people. The first SASE phase addressed the disappearing network perimeter, while the next addresses growing interactions among users, apps, data and AI.

SASE is seen as more than connecting remote users, with its role as a consistent visibility and policy point. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported that 12 per cent of Australian businesses used AI in 2024, up from 1 per cent in 2022, with adoption higher among larger organisations; the figures cover AI broadly, not agentic AI specifically. The security challenge is shifting from access control to understanding workflows: an employee may ask an AI agent to prepare a customer briefing, and the agent may query a CRM, internal documents and another AI service. Advanced agents may be authorised to take further actions, so one request can become a chain of transactions and the unit of security changes from a user session to a workflow chain.

AI workflows can span systems at machine speed, and the security question is visibility and policy across the chain, because controls only at the start or end miss activity in the middle. SASE could take a broader role, with common policies following interactions across environments. Identity remains central but is only one part, and organisations need context on apps, devices, data, destinations and behaviour, while non-human identities and machine transactions add another dimension. The Australian Government Policy for responsible use of AI in government was cited: it requires non-corporate Commonwealth entities to name accountable officials, keep internal registers of AI use cases, carry out impact assessments and monitor deployed AI systems.

That principle of ongoing visibility and accountability has wider relevance, because AI governance needs continuing visibility rather than one-off tool approval. SASE strategies should look beyond conventional access, with an architecture that gives consistent visibility and policy across interactions. The risk is adding a point solution for each new form of AI, which creates fragmentation while teams try to reduce complexity; a stronger approach embeds AI-driven activity in existing security architecture, and SASE can provide a common policy layer. Its evolution is more than secure remote connection, and it can give visibility and control across people and machines.

Articles.Title: SASE's next job: governing AI traffic - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: SASE's next job: governing AI traffic

stories.Headline: Appli deploys AI financial calculators for Corda Credit Union to capture leads and tailor results
stories.Summary:
Appli deployed AI financial calculators for Corda Credit Union, an Iowa credit union. The calculators replaced Corda's generic tools and give tailored results. They also capture leads from website visitors.

Corda serves over 27,000 members across 22 counties in Iowa. The project customized the calculators to Corda's branding and disclosures and automated rate updates, with the calculators pulling Corda's rates daily. Generic calculators give broad estimates that can differ from current pricing.

Cherie Tilson, Director of Marketing at Corda Credit Union, said the old tools were "very generic, and members basically had to do all the work themselves." She said the credit union "couldn't capture leads, and we didn't have any results to share with senior management." She also said that "even with the disclaimers, the results are much closer to what someone could actually get."

The calculators gave the marketing team new data, including activity from outside its field of membership, from visitors who found the credit union via Google and AI search. Tilson said that "even in the first month, when we were able to share results with our senior management team, they were impressed." The implementation handled over 65 rates, and Tilson said, "Our biggest worry going in was keeping over 65 rates up to date."

Appli was founded in 2024. Intended for use on the consumer-facing website and by staff working with borrowers, the calculators combine real-time analysis with generative AI, and Tim Pranger, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Appli, also co-founded POPi/o. Pranger said Corda's team "knew what they didn't want, which was one more tool someone had to babysit every time rates moved." He said pulling the rates in every day "sounds like a small thing, but it's often what decides whether a calculator gets used or forgotten."

Corda has operated since 1935 and is a not-for-profit financial cooperative. The website changes help identify prospective member interest, and the project is at an early stage rather than a completed overhaul. Corda expects to expand use of the system. Tilson said, "We've only dipped our toe in the water."

stories.Headline: AI assurance director urges firms to survey staff on unofficial AI use before writing policy
stories.Summary:
Durga Rajesh R, the AI Assurance Council's Director of Assurance and Technology, said most AI policies assume the technology has not yet been introduced, when in most organisations it is already present unofficially.

That gap between policy and practice is a real AI risk, such as a staff member pasting a client contract into a free chatbot or a manager relying on an unchecked summary. Bans on public AI tools rarely work, Rajesh said, because a ban turns visible use into hidden use. Instead, organisations should accept that use is happening and find out its shape, starting with a short anonymous survey before writing rules.

The survey reveals which tools, tasks and data types are involved. Most use is drafting, summarising and searching, with a small number of uses involving sensitive data. Policy should be built on tasks and data rather than tools, since tools change every few months, and organisations should provide a sanctioned tool with sensible defaults and make access to it easy.

The weakest point is the decision that output is good enough, and policies assume staff know how to review output when reviewing AI output well is a skill. Only 39 per cent of AI users have received employer training, and few organisations test whether that training was learned. Policy should be treated as something to measure, tracking approved tool use and reported incidents. "An AI policy that has not changed in a year is probably being ignored," Rajesh said.

Articles.Title: Your staff are already using AI. Your AI policy should start there - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Foster Moore showcases AI registry tools and advisory unit at Singapore forum
stories.Summary:
Foster Moore showcased AI-assisted registry services and its Registry Advisory unit at the Corporate Registers Forum 2026 in Singapore, according to IT Brief Australia. The forum was in progress when the article was published on 27 November 2026. The company's Registry Lab develops AI features with customers. The tools flag incomplete or incorrect submissions earlier, aim to cut manual intervention and give applicants clearer feedback before rejection.

Registry Advisory launched in 2026 and helps registry authorities plan transformation. It draws on former registrars and public service leaders and covers four service areas: capability maturity assessment, target operating model design, interoperability planning and a register value assessment model. Justin Hygate, Chief Registry Officer at Foster Moore, urged a registry-led approach to modernisation. "Foster Moore has the unusual advantage of having both built registers and operated them," he said.

Agnese Abelite, Director of Product Management at Foster Moore, moderated a service delivery panel featuring representatives of five organisations, including UNIDROIT, from Malta, the UK, Georgia and Belize. John Murray, Vice President of Europe and Special Projects at Foster Moore, said registers had operated as islands of authoritative information for too long. GRX, the Global Registry Exchange, is a joint venture with Bundesanzeiger Verlag and is a cross-border register data exchange layer in which each authority controls what is shared.

Foster Moore, headquartered in Auckland and part of Teranet, cites over 30 years of registry modernisation work across markets including New Zealand, Canada, Ireland, Botswana, Bermuda, Samoa, Australia, Lesotho, Cambodia, Vanuatu and the US Virgin Islands. The conference drew registrars, regulators and government technology officials as registries face pressure to modernise ageing systems and tighter rules on beneficial ownership transparency and cross-border data sharing. According to Javier Yebenes, Director of Marketing at Foster Moore, the registry community comes together at CRF to compare notes and plan what comes next. Foster Moore held talks with delegates and reported interest in research and white papers, and Yebenes said conversations continue in 2027.

stories.Headline: GraphSeer authors report 24.2 to 70 percent retrieval gains with a multimodal model
stories.Summary:
A paper titled GraphSeer, posted to arXiv on November 27, 2026 under identifier 2611.29470, presents a method for knowledge graph relational image retrieval, a task abbreviated KRIR. The authors are Linyu Li, Zhi Jin, Yuanpeng He, Haoran Duan, Dongming Jin, Wenchun Jing, Xuan Zhang, Gadeng Luosang and Nyima Tashi. The method retrieves a related multimodal knowledge graph entity from a photo plus a relation, and handles both known and unseen depicted entities.

GraphSeer bridges entity recognition and fact recall in one multimodal large language model, linking a photo to the graph and reading the best-match facts. It retrieves using the hidden state before the answer, and a listwise verifier re-ranks the top candidates using candidate facts and photos. According to the paper, facts outweigh photos in verification. The authors built three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and OVEN photos, and used the model Qwen3.5-27B.

The paper reports mean reciprocal rank gains of 24.2 to 70.0 percent for known entities and 12.5 to 25.6 percent for unseen entities, against a fine-tuned multimodal large language model embedder with the same data and budget. The unseen-entity gains require fusing and verifying embedder candidates, according to the paper, and the method beats knowledge graph completion models given a ground-truth entity ID.

The paper says existing multimodal knowledge graph methods predict links between known entity IDs, while image retrievers return visually or descriptively similar entities, though a related entity rarely resembles the photo. The task hides two hops, according to the paper. No independent replication was reported.

stories.Headline: AI crawlers drive higher server demand even for businesses not using AI
stories.Summary:
Jason Dale, general manager of technical operations at Servers Australia, said AI-related crawlers are raising infrastructure demand, and even businesses that do not use AI are seeing jumps in utilisation. Over the past year, customers have asked for more server resources, with workloads consuming far more CPU than before. The initial assumption is that a business has outgrown its infrastructure, so the provider investigates the load before recommending compute.

Automated requests to public sites are not new, but the volume and type of automated traffic are changing. AI crawlers access publicly available content, while other systems scrape, probe and look for weaknesses. Not all automated traffic is malicious, but excessive automated traffic consumes infrastructure resources, driving higher CPU use and more application and database processing. The load initially looked like a capacity problem, but much of the added demand did not come from ordinary customers.

A large Australian retailer is one example: it saw a significant traffic increase and faced two issues at once, automated requests and malicious activity. The retailer needs its content to be discoverable, so blocking all automated traffic is not necessarily the right move, and uncontrolled requests can affect genuine customers. The provider identifies which types of traffic need to be controlled. The process looks at traffic, security, compute and network, because several possible explanations for resource spikes do not share the same solution, and a larger server may simply give bad traffic more resources. The analysis covers where requests come from, what they access, how they are answered and where the load lands.

Options include traffic management, changes to applications or the network, and added capacity. Servers Australia works across compute and networking, and its relationship with HPE provides server and networking technology, though hardware selection is not always the first step. The aim is to tell a genuine need for an upgrade apart from unwanted work. "Before you increase your infrastructure spend, make sure you understand what's driving the demand," Dale said.

Articles.Title: AI is putting pressure on your infrastructure, even if you're not using it - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Silverpond outlines Enterprise Perception system linking AI to operational decisions
stories.Summary:
Silverpond has outlined an approach it calls Enterprise Perception, which links AI systems to operational decisions. The Australian company says the model connects evidence, context and human judgment. Businesses are expanding their use of AI agents in workflows that need timely understanding of field events, and this comes as that happens.

Silverpond calls the gap between observation and timely understanding the "Perception Gap". The company says this gap shows up in repeated inspections, missed maintenance, unnecessary field deployments and decisions made with incomplete information. Enterprises already collect relevant signals, according to Silverpond, but they are fragmented across inspection records, maintenance histories, work orders and staff knowledge. The approach centres on an Enterprise Perception System that combines physical and digital observations with enterprise context, AI agents, human review and governed workflows, placing events in a broader operating picture before any response.

According to Silverpond, asset identity, operating history, condition change, failure consequences, planned maintenance, a reviewer and applicable rules are needed for the next step, although the system may detect corrosion or another defect. It says similar issues arise in technology, finance and marketing, where teams interpret service disruptions, transaction exceptions and shifts in customer activity. A shared environment receives evidence, findings are linked with identity, location, history and standards, and events are assessed for significance, confidence and urgency, which triggers a workflow, inspection or escalation, as the process loops through observe, interpret, connect, prioritise, act and verify. Verification is a key part of the model: a work order shows activity took place, and further evidence shows whether the condition changed.

In one environment, Silverpond's Highlighter platform applies this structure, bringing together sensors, systems, workflows, AI agents and human expertise. The company says the system preserves human authority, with AI extending attention and speed within permissions. Jonathan Chang, Chief Technology Officer of Silverpond, said: "The Perception Gap becomes visible when an organisation has the evidence somewhere, but people still have to reconstruct what it means before they can act." He added: "Enterprise Perception connects that evidence with history, operating rules and human judgment while the opportunity to respond is still open."

Chang said: "AI agents need current context and clear boundaries." He also said: "People need to examine the evidence, understand the recommendation and control what happens next."

A framework element called operational memory creates an auditable record of verified actions, linking observations, context, recommendations, decisions, evidence, approvals and outcomes. Silverpond says the record helps future teams understand past decisions and shows whether the reasoning still applies, with outcomes connected back to the original evidence. Chang said: "The lasting value is the understanding an enterprise carries forward." He added: "When decisions and verified outcomes remain connected, the next decision starts with stronger evidence."

Silverpond cites examples spanning energy distribution, warehouse operations and high-density farming, where the common challenge is turning observations into governed responses.

Articles.Title: Silverpond outlines enterprise perception system for AI - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Andrews says AI-generated code ships too fast for testing and blurs accountability
stories.Summary:
He said the productivity gains explain the fast adoption, but organisations take on hidden risks in return. Business-critical code is often not written by the people who can explain it, and generated code is approved and shipped too fast, he said. Andrews said the risk sits between production speed and validation. Logic errors and insecure patterns are familiar risks, but AI output looks clean and confident even when it is wrong, so readable code can pass review with hidden problems. The question of maintainability is raised too rarely, and AI code lacks a rationale for future teams, he said.

Internal documents reportedly linked a pattern to Gen-AI-assisted changes at Amazon, where at least four Sev-1 production incidents occurred between December 2025 and March 2026, one outage costing an estimated 6.3 million lost orders. Amazon public statements attributed the incidents to user error, not AI, and both explanations can be true at once, according to the report. AI code makes accountability harder to locate: the traditional chain is that a developer writes, a reviewer checks and the team owns, but accepting an AI suggestion differs from writing code, and it is unclear whether the approver, the deploying team or the process is responsible. Many organisations lack visibility into how much of their code is AI-generated, and it is unclear whether AI code is tested to the same standard. Andrews said slowing AI adoption is not realistic, and AI code should be tested with equal or greater rigour.

Seventy-five per cent of enterprise IT leaders say updates outpace testing, and testing was already losing the race before AI was factored in, so AI widens an existing gap, he said. Only 48% of IT leaders are fully confident that testing catches critical issues, according to Andrews. He said leadership should answer basic governance questions: how much of the codebase is AI-generated, and what defined policy exists for extra review and who decides. He said organisations should set usage policies and minimum testing standards now, and define accountability before AI code embeds in critical systems, with successful organisations matching AI speed with discipline.

Articles.Title: The hidden risks of AI-generated code that organisations are only beginning to understand - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Aigentsphere CEO says Australian firms deploy AI agents only as fast as they prove control
stories.Summary:
Australian companies will only be able to deploy AI agents as fast as they can prove they are in control of them, according to Quinton Anderson, CEO and co-founder of Aigentsphere. The claim comes from a survey of 100 Australian IT and security leaders, conducted by Illumino in November and published on 27 November 2026. It found that 80% of Australian organisations let AI decide, where those actions needed human approval a year ago. Only 55% can see and audit all agent actions.

Anderson described the difficulty of keeping count. "How many AI agents are we running?" he said. "I'd need to check. A few dozen, I think." Agents arrive built into paid software, and teams build their own, often uncounted. Agents are rarely retired after the people who built them leave their roles, and finance leaders are under pressure to show that AI spending pays off.

Earlier this month, the Australian Federal Government announced a plan to legislate mandatory safety standards for frontier model builders. Agents inside businesses remain the business's responsibility. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, which regulates banks, insurers and super funds, expects clear ownership across the AI lifecycle.

Some firms slow agents behind manual approvals, while others press ahead and accept the risks. A third path manages agents like a workforce: keeping a register of every agent and its access, and giving every agent a named business owner who sets objectives and answers for its actions. Agents are measured on the outcome they were hired for, and oversight must be continuous after sign-off, since model updates or new data can change behaviour. Automated rules check every action for prohibited events, reviewers sample agent work against the owner's measures, and agreed thresholds narrow an agent's scope when results slip.

stories.Headline: Adactin's Alluru warns businesses that automating outdated processes with agentic AI preserves inefficiencies
stories.Summary:
Ravi Alluru, Practice Sales Manager at Adactin, has warned that businesses investing heavily in artificial intelligence face a risk from automating outdated business processes. As agentic AI moves into mainstream enterprise operations, technology alone cannot deliver business transformation, he said. When existing workflows are simply transferred onto AI platforms, speed gains may perpetuate accumulated inefficiencies, according to Alluru. Alluru said leaders should ask whether a process would be designed today, citing a decade-old manual approval hierarchy as an example. Traditional processes were built around human intervention, with predictable workloads and multiple approval stages.

AI agents interpret information and act on objectives, which can replace cumbersome workflows with dynamic operating models. In customer support, for example, AI could assess requests and route them to resolution, but retaining every approval stage diminishes the advantages. The review must extend beyond individual departments, Alluru said, noting that an HR agent may need finance, payroll and timekeeping data. He cited an insurance company that handles more than 33,000 customer enquiries each month through an IVR system, where AI could categorise enquiries automatically and a redesign could route commercially important requests earlier, with lower infrastructure requirements and AI token consumption.

He also pointed to utilities and smart metering compliance reporting on platforms implemented more than a decade ago, and to local government councils with extensive asset portfolios where AI dashboards could consolidate asset information. Alluru recommended starting with one clearly defined business process, saying an incremental approach manages risk and validates investment, and establishing governance for autonomous agents. "Businesses that simply automate yesterday's processes risk creating faster versions of existing inefficiencies," he said. The next step is to redesign operations around AI capabilities for lasting gains.

stories.Headline: Emburse index shows AI spending nearly doubled in nine months
stories.Summary:
AI spending nearly doubled in nine months, from the first quarter of 2026 to the third, according to the Emburse AI Index. Spending was $28.1 million in the first quarter, $34 million in the second and $56.2 million in the third. That marked a 65% jump from the second quarter to the third. Michele Shepard, chief revenue officer at Emburse, said: "AI spending nearly doubled in just nine months."

The index is built from aggregated spending data from hundreds of Emburse customers. Median quarterly spend per customer rose from about $2,262 in the first quarter to $6,243 in the third. Spending was concentrated among a few accounts: the top ten accounts spent about $32.8 million in the third quarter, or 58.4% of the total, while the remaining customers spent $23.4 million.

Shepard is chief revenue officer at Emburse. The index's figures suggest leaders should review their ten largest AI expenses, compare big AI purchases year over year, and check major contracts and upcoming renewals.

stories.Headline: A large language model builds a 3,137-record superconducting database after gates reject 659,252 extractions
stories.Summary:
A large language model pipeline built to extract superconducting materials data from scientific literature proposed 19,576 records, according to a paper by Wenjian Lu posted on arXiv on November 27, 2026. Every value the pipeline produced was checked against its source. Gates rejected 659,252 field-level extractions, including 644,438 for lacking verbatim evidence, 13,121 for values not tied to a material and 1,693 for source sentences that read as calculations. The surviving database holds 3,137 material records, each keeping its source sentence.

Two independent models audited 500 records drawn in proportion to the database. Of the audited records, 93.4% had the value in the text and the text about the named compound, and 91.8% were measurements rather than predictions.

Superconducting data is scattered across prose, tables and figures, and errors include values taken from neighbouring compounds and computed transition temperatures recorded without saying they were computed. The source papers themselves may be wrong, the paper notes.

stories.Headline: KPMG and CII report 93% of Indian leaders plan to adopt AI agents as 59% already automate workstreams
stories.Summary:
A joint report by KPMG in India and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), published on 25 November 2026, says 93% of leaders intend to use AI agents, and 59% already use them to automate workstreams. It also found that 74% of India CEOs say AI workforce readiness will affect growth over the next three years. According to the report, AI is taking over routine tasks such as retrieval and summarising.

The report says "Artificial Intelligence is reshaping work at the level of tasks, workflows and decisions before it eliminates entire jobs". In its account, employees will need to define problems and check AI outputs.

Citing the World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report 2025, the report says 39% of core skills are expected to change by 2030, and 59 of every 100 workers need training by then. It found that 63% of employers cite skills gaps as a barrier, while 85% plan to make upskilling a priority by 2030. It also says 70% of employers intend to hire for new skills and 50% expect to move employees to growing areas. Skills-based hiring could expand the talent pool 6.1 times, and 8.2 times for AI-related jobs, according to the report.

stories.Summary:
He said at the Dhanam BFSI Summit 2026 in Kochi that a domestically governed AI model for the securities market is also being examined by the regulator. The aim is to widen access to secure and affordable AI tools, according to the article. "We are exploring an AI Sandbox to test applications in a controlled environment," Pandey said. "We are also examining a domestically governed AI model for the securities market," he added. Sebi is deploying technology for market surveillance and investor protection, the article reported.

It named R(AI)DAR, which reviews financial advertisements for compliance, and Sudarshan, which identifies misleading market content on social media. AI tools being developed to analyse compliance reports would flag potential risks early, according to the article. Pandey said technology cannot replace human judgement or institutional accountability. "An alert is not a finding, and an algorithm cannot assume responsibility," he said.

He flagged cyberattack, outage and data breach risks, and said innovation must be backed by governance and cybersecurity. Sebi is reviewing its IPO and SME IPO frameworks with the aim of making public fundraising more accessible, the article reported. In the corporate bond market, it is also working to improve liquidity and distribution. The regulator is reviewing the AIF, REIT and InvIT frameworks to support long-term investment and infrastructure financing, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Coforge adds vulnerability remediation to its Nuuron AI suite
stories.Summary:
Coforge, an IT services company, has expanded its Nuuron enterprise AI suite with vulnerability remediation capabilities across infrastructure, applications, cloud, data platforms and AI systems.

Ashish Kumar, Global Head, Cloud and AI Infrastructure at Coforge, said: "Agentic attackers can find a weakness and exploit it in a matter of hours, yet traditional remediation takes weeks." The expansion follows a CERT-In disclosure about AI agents accessing Indian organisations' systems, which raised questions about access control and monitoring. Coforge said remediation remains largely manual, with fragmented workflows and resource shortages delaying fixes.

Nuuron provides orchestration, governance, auditability and policy enforcement, according to the company. Forward-deployed engineers work inside client environments and handle agent-escalated exceptions and recurring vulnerabilities. The suite covers agent security, model governance, RAG security, access controls, sensitive data exposure and AI policy compliance, and integrates with security, DevSecOps and change-management systems.

The expansion follows the October 2026 launch of Coforge's Autonomous Software Factory. Coforge did not disclose customer deployments, commercial terms or closure-time figures. The news was published on 26 November 2026.

stories.Headline: Straive positions itself to operationalise AI for enterprises seeking measurable returns
stories.Summary:
Straive, an IT services firm, is positioning itself as a partner for operationalising AI, said Naveen Gattu, its Global Head of Growth. The company says enterprises are moving from deploying AI to seeking measurable returns, with attention on governance and process integration. "We are trying to operationalise AI," Gattu said. Operationalising AI could become a distinct technology services category, the article said, comparing it to IT services growth in the late 1990s.

Straive recently partnered with OpenAI and Anthropic, and its ecosystem includes Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Databricks, Snowflake and NVIDIA. The OpenAI partnership gives faster access to emerging technologies and covers pre-sales, technical sales and technical support. "Frontier model alone will not solve any business problem," Gattu said. The article said leading AI adopters are almost eight times more impactful.

The article said enterprises struggle with AI outcomes for three reasons: a disconnect between business and technology objectives, failure to integrate AI into processes, and data quality and governance. It said general-purpose models achieve only 70 to 80% accuracy. Straive combines consulting, building and running AI, and has around 6,000 employees with master's degrees or PhDs. Its competitors include Fractal, Tiger Analytics, EXL, Genpact, Accenture and Deloitte. "Straive is the only player who can advise, run and build AI together," Gattu said.

According to the article, pre-built IP cuts implementation timelines to eight to 12 weeks from around 18 weeks. Straive focuses on six industries. Enterprises are more cautious but not abandoning AI investments, and some customers have moved to budgets of around $200, the article said, with billing shifting toward outcome-based models. Straive plans to expand partnerships, deepen its industry vertical presence and demonstrate measurable AI ROI, and future acquisitions are expected to be more domain-focused. Approximately 55% of its business comes from North America and around 40% from Europe.

stories.Headline: Researchers find all four TGB node affinity datasets fail point-in-time correctness
stories.Summary:
A point-in-time audit of the TGB node affinity leaderboard was posted on 2026-11-27 as arXiv preprint 2611.30289 by Yuhang Wang, Dongmei Li, Yuze Sun, Xiaolong Qu, Yanxiang Wang and Lei Yao. The authors audited four TGB node affinity datasets and formalized a point-in-time correctness requirement. None of the four datasets meets that requirement, they found.

In three of the datasets, the label summarizes a single day, and the label is available about five days after the timestamp, according to the audit. The documented label window was the following week, but the evaluation loop feeds the label back right after the timestamp. The fourth dataset processes edges before prediction. Leaking methods lose up to 17% NDCG@10, and the past-label advantage nearly vanishes or reverses.

The authors audited the evaluation loop with model-agnostic tools and tested a leakage-free protocol as a drop-in. Under that protocol, rankings change and the best configuration of the state of the art changes. "Point-in-time correctness should therefore be built into benchmarks," Wang said.

The blend matches or exceeds the state of the art, they report. They urge point-in-time correctness for benchmarks and say the tools carry over to other benchmarks.

Articles.Title: Temporal Leakage Distorts the TGB Node Affinity Leaderboard: A Point-in-Time Audit

stories.Headline: Yue Pei leads a method that selects sepsis resuscitation policies from language models
stories.Summary:
A method for selecting sepsis resuscitation treatment policies from language models, called R-LLMC, was posted on arXiv on Nov. 27, 2026, under identifier 2611.30951. Yue Pei is the lead author, with Shining Bo, Yingying Zhang, Qinggang Ge, Zhiling Zhao, Jian Cheng and Haogang Zhu as co-authors.

The method uses a behaviour-supervised large language model to propose clinician-anchored candidates, giving an exact distribution over 25 vasopressor-fluid actions. An offline critic then selects among them by estimated long-term value, and a closed-form policy allows off-policy evaluation. A rationale is written after the selection, though the authors say the explanation cannot steer treatment.

On held-out MIMIC-III patients, the method showed a doubly robust value gain of +0.214 over the clinician reference, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.091 to 0.300, according to the authors. They report that fitted Q evaluation agreed with this result. No further details were reported.

Articles.Title: Evaluable Language-Model Treatment Policies for Sepsis Resuscitation via Offline Value-Guided Selection

stories.Headline: Authors release WeMM-Ecom models for e-commerce tasks in five sizes up to 35B
stories.Summary:
A team of authors including Binhui Xie, Jinmin Li, Haomiao Tang, Guangting Wang, Song Jin, Jianwei Zhu, Fengyun Rao and Jing Lyu has introduced WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models built for e-commerce tasks. The work was published on November 27, 2026 as an arXiv preprint, identifier 2611.30662. The family comes in five model sizes, from a 0.8B dense model, the smallest, to a 35B mixture-of-experts model, the largest, which has 3B active parameters. Training runs in two stages.

The first is continued pre-training that progressively raises the share of e-commerce data, and the second is hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning. The models support both non-thinking and thinking modes. The authors constructed 28 e-commerce benchmarks: 23 in-house, five open-source, covering eight business scenarios, alongside 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. According to the authors, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses larger open-source flagship models, which they name as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

They also report that every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, and that lightweight models Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B and LFM3-VL-2B were outperformed. The authors describe the family as reaching state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at its respective scales. WeMM-Ecom already powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, according to the authors, including catalog management, multimodal product search and livestream commerce, and serves billion-scale requests per day. All model weights have been publicly released, and the paper details data curation, the training recipe and benchmark construction.
