Ujjwal Kumar, president of Siemens’ automation business in the Americas, called Silicon Valley’s story about AI and jobs toxic and self-serving, Fortune reported on November 28, 2026. “The AI industry, especially the high-tech story coming out of Silicon Valley was pretty toxic and self-serving,” Kumar said, according to Fortune. He added: “It was almost like gloating, saying, ‘Oh, it is a good thing that it is eliminating every job.’” Kumar did not name anyone in his criticism.

The remarks follow comments by Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, who told Axios in May 2025 that AI could cut half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years, with projected unemployment of 10% to 20%, Fortune reported. “That is not how we in the industrial world talk,” Kumar said, according to Fortune. “You won’t see anyone from the industrial DNA talking like that.” He also said: “I have no idea why we would gloat about human beings losing their job, everybody going on UBI [universal basic income].” And: “Like, that doesn’t excite people.”

Kumar, who has spent 27 years remaking factories, said industrial companies raised the issue with tech partners, Fortune reported. He said the tech industry caused lasting damage in the way it talks about AI and workers.

stories.Headline: Roscosmos CEO Bakanov plans to deploy AI in spacecraft design and space operations
stories.Summary:
Dmitry Bakanov, CEO of Roscosmos, said the Russian space agency plans to deploy artificial intelligence in space, TASS, a Russian state news agency, reported on November 26 from Moscow. The plan includes digitizing design processes with AI and creating AI-powered spacecraft and equipment.

Bakanov said the agency has already deployed Sber's GigaChat, an AI-powered assistant for cosmonauts, on the International Space Station. He said GigaChat generated more than 350 reports from cosmonaut voice recordings. A second area of AI work is improving the accuracy of Earth remote sensing images, with resolution converted from 1 meter to 0.5 meters, according to the TASS account.

"This is our main task: to transition all design work to a digital format using artificial intelligence," Bakanov said, according to TASS. Bakanov previously said the rocket and space sector integrates neural networks, the agency reported.

Articles.Title: Roscosmos to tap into AI power to create cutting-edge space tech — CEO

stories.Headline: Patriarch Kirill links AI development to nearing Apocalypse prophecies
stories.Summary:
Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia said on November 26 that the fulfillment of Apocalypse prophecies seems nearer than ever, linking this to the development of artificial intelligence. He spoke at the 28th World Russian People's Council plenary session in Moscow. "The fulfillment of the prophecies of the Apocalypse seems closer than ever," he said, according to TASS, a Russian state news agency.

The patriarch said artificial intelligence might come to see humans as "a redundant link in this production chain." He also said some people treat AI advice as objective truth, and he questioned a course of development that costs people their independent decisions, TASS reported.

Articles.Title: Fulfillment of Apocalypse prophecies seems near amid AI development — Patriarch Kirill

stories.Headline: AskAnyModel offers lifetime AI Pro access for $27.97 through Dec 6
stories.Summary:
AskAnyModel is offering a lifetime subscription to its AI Pro plan for $27.97 with the code SAVE12, according to Mashable. The listed price is $39.99, down from a regular price of $499. The deal runs through Dec. 6 at 11:59 p.m. PT. Mashable says: "Get a lifetime AskAnyModel AI Pro subscription for $27.97 with code SAVE12, down from $39.99 (reg. $499) through Dec. 6 at 11:59 p.m. PT."

The Pro plan allows a single prompt to be sent to six models at once, with the answers viewed side by side. More than 50 AI models are available, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Llama and Mistral. Pro users get unlimited chats on 30 standard models and 500 monthly credits for premium models, which replenish each month. Unlimited AI image generation is included across models, and image generation does not use premium credits. Users can also switch models mid-conversation.

The offer is a one-time payment rather than a recurring subscription. Mashable notes that the content is partner content and it may earn a commission. Pricing and availability are subject to change.

stories.Headline: University of Rhode Island and University of Maine researchers train an AI model to decode sinking marine snow
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Rhode Island Graduate School of Oceanography and the University of Maine are training an artificial intelligence model to decode marine snow, the sinking particles that drift down through the ocean. The team uses a camera system built from over-the-counter parts that looks toward the ocean surface and collects the falling particles. Its time-lapse images resemble galaxies and nebulas, according to the New Bedford Light. The project officially kicks off in January.

Marine snow carries carbon traces, nutrients, minerals and some microplastics, and includes phytoplankton and zooplankton fecal pellets, with microplastics sinking among the organic matter. The project aims to predict changes in the ocean. A $700,000 National Science Foundation award funds the data collection, which is planned for next year.

Melissa Omand, an associate professor of oceanography at the University of Rhode Island, said the varied data matters to the work. "We really needed that in order to build our model, because we don't want to have just a bunch of data from one place," she said.

Diverse ocean data is needed to train the model, and microalgae blooms that later die off cause the sinking organic flux the team studies. The team plans to collect marine snow next year in four regions: the New England shelf, Monterey Bay in California, off the coast of Ghana, and the South Atlantic near Brazil.

Articles.Title: New England researchers hope AI will help decode ‘marine snow’

stories.headline_source: New England researchers hope AI will help decode ‘marine snow’

stories.Headline: Expert urges shoppers to guard personal data when using AI for Black Friday shopping
stories.Summary:
Bryan Carr, chair of information sciences at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, warned shoppers in Green Bay, Wisconsin, to think twice about the personal data they share when using AI tools to shop on Black Friday 2026. A National Retail Federation figure cited in the reporting says 59% of consumers plan to use AI for holiday shopping.

Carr said people should treat AI with care. he said. He also said that by using these tools, "You essentially are consenting to it, using that data, learning from that data, and even storing that data."

The tools can also make mistakes, according to the report, including getting sizing details or deal currency wrong, and a general chatbot may add another company to a transaction. Carr still sees AI as useful for comparing products and for gift ideas. He recommends keeping AI in an assistant's seat, using it to find deals rather than to decide everything.

Articles.Title: Expert advises caution with personal data when using AI to shop on Black Friday

stories.headline_source: Expert advises caution with personal data when using AI to shop on Black Friday

stories.Headline: AI shopping tools drive higher spending as Black Friday boosts retail foot traffic
stories.Summary:
Black Friday fell on 26 November 2026 in New York City, with artificial intelligence shopping tools influencing how consumers spent, the Boston Herald reported. The day, long called retail's Super Bowl, now resembles the fourth quarter of a football game, according to the outlet, and brands promoted steep discounts throughout the month. Black Friday remained the biggest day for retail foot traffic, according to Sensormatic Solutions, which tracks physical store activity. Adobe Digital Insights reported $82.5 billion in U.S. online spending from 1 to 22 November, a 9.1% rise over the same weeks in 2025. The firm predicted 6.7% holiday online sales growth, reaching $275.1 billion through 31 December.

The National Retail Federation forecast $1.01 trillion in U.S. shopper spending, with 4.1% expected sales growth in November and December, half of it from higher prices. Salesforce, which tracks digital spending, reported November discounts 8% bigger than last year. Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at Adobe, said, "shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials." Grant Gustafson, head of retail consulting and analytics at Sensormatic, said, "Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping."

Caila Schwartz, retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce, said, "In the last several years, a lot of the (sales) gains have been from higher prices." Consumer confidence was lackluster amid high inflation but jumped this month, and U.S. gasoline prices were in steady decline, the Herald reported, while the U.S. war with Iran fueled cost concerns. Between 1 October and 18 November, 2% more items were added to online carts, and traffic to retail sites from AI-tool links more than doubled compared with November 2025. Walmart CEO John Furner said users of Sparky, the company's AI shopping assistant, spent 40% more per order, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Alexa users spent 50% more.

Articles.Title: Black Friday now gets boost from AI

stories.headline_source: Black Friday now gets boost from AI

stories.Headline: University of Deusto researchers develop an AI sensor that detects food allergens without destroying samples
stories.Summary:
The eVIDA research group at the University of Deusto has completed a functional prototype under its smartJAN project, the group announced. The device detects LTP plant protein allergens, combining near-infrared spectroscopy, signal processing and artificial intelligence. Light is shone on food and the reflection is analyzed, with the spectral fingerprint interpreted instantly by AI. The method detects allergens without destroying the sample or sending it to a laboratory.

LTP allergens are notably relevant in the Mediterranean region, according to the researchers. Earlier tests detected gluten and meat bacteria, and the system could enable early pathogen detection, such as Salmonella. The study was published in the journal Food Analytical Methods in 2025, with Alex Rodriguez-Alonso as an author, under DOI 10.1007/s12161-025-02851-6. Begoña García-Zapirain, head of the eVIDA group at the University of Deusto, said "the technology could have a much wider range of applications."

The project involved collaborators Kernet and Fundación Miranda, the latter adding a focus on health care for people over 65. The project is ready to move toward commercialization, according to the group. The device is intended for industry quality control rather than consumers, targeting distribution chains and institutional catering. Reliability validation protocols still have to be completed, and a market launch depends on industrial interest.

Articles.Title: Researchers explore the use of AI and smart sensors to improve food safety quickly, affordably

stories.Headline: Denver launches SmartStart AI tool to check permit applications before staff review
stories.Summary:
Denver has launched an AI permit-checking tool called SmartStart, which went live earlier this month, CBS News reported. The city set up a permitting office last year. The tool checks whether an application is complete and flags problems before staff review it, aiming to cut back-and-forth with permitting staff and free them to prevent backlogs. Denver invested $4.6 million to launch the tool, which is part of the Civcheck program from the company Clariti. Cyrus Symoom, CEO of Clariti, said Denver came to the company citing that only 30% of permits clear their first-round review.

"Our product is a full review of that application against the requirements of the city," Symoom said. Symoom said applicants should start receiving results immediately now that the solution is live. "We will kind of catch all these checks before you submit, and you should start to see the efficiencies right away," he said. According to CBS News, a major residential project now averages 160 days for approval, more than three months faster than in April, and the goal is a much shorter timeline.

Ben Hamilton, general manager of the Good Luck Club bar, said the bar opened six months behind schedule. "There was a good list of complications that we ran into when we were filing for our liquor licenses, our zoning permits, our assembly permits," he said. Julia Richman, a Denver resident, said she waited nine months for home construction approval last year. "We sat from March, really, until the fall," she said, "and I think it was October by the time the city had a chance to even look at our application."

Articles.Title: Denver may have solved its permitting application issues by integrating AI technology

stories.headline_source: Denver may have solved its permitting application issues by integrating AI technology

stories.Headline: UNESCO and WAN-IFRA develop a global blueprint for ethical AI adoption in media
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the World Association of News Publishers, known as WAN-IFRA, announced on 26 November 2026 that they are partnering to develop a Global Institutional Blueprint for AI Adoption. The blueprint is meant for ethical governance in media and is described by UNESCO as "a practical leadership tool for media organizations of all types and sizes." The blueprint is designed for editors-in-chief, executives, managers and boards to guide strategic planning and internal policy. The following will be covered: "Editorial production distribution audience engagement internal workflows and revenue models". It is also meant to help outlets assess whether AI investment strengthens their viability by weighing productivity, reach and revenue against costs.

The work is grounded in UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, its Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms and its Generative AI guidelines. The blueprint aims to safeguard freedom of expression and access to information and to ensure transparency and accountability. It will include checklists, self-assessment tools and adaptable templates that define where human review is required, when AI use is disclosed to audiences and who approves AI uses. UNESCO said AI is changing news production, distribution and consumption, offering gains in workflow, audience and revenue while bringing inaccurate or fabricated outputs.

It said opaque AI use erodes audience trust, growing dependence on a few technology providers is a concern and AI-generated disinformation is cheaper and harder to detect. Newsrooms vary widely in AI readiness, with some integrating the technology while developing policies and smaller outlets facing staffing and funding constraints. The consultation considers resources, infrastructure and business models as well as how gender shapes AI adoption. The work is now underway, with launch expected in the first half of 2027, as part of UNESCO's digital and AI competencies efforts.

Articles.Title: UNESCO and WAN-IFRA partner on Global Blueprint for Responsible AI in Media

stories.headline_source: UNESCO and WAN-IFRA partner on Global Blueprint for Responsible AI in Media

stories.Headline: Solita and ConfidentialMind partner to deliver sovereign AI for regulated European industries
stories.Summary:
Solita, a Finnish data and AI company, and ConfidentialMind, a Finnish sovereign AI infrastructure start-up, formalized a partnership on November 23, 2026. The partnership is aimed at delivering production-ready AI offerings for sovereign cloud and hybrid environments across Europe. It targets regulated industries including the public sector, defense and security, and healthcare. Solita operates in eight European countries and has more than 2,200 specialists. The partnership follows the European Commission's Tech Sovereignty Package, presented on June 3, 2026, which covers AI, cloud, semiconductors and open-source software.

48.0% of decision-makers cite security and compliance as the top barrier, and 44.7% of organizations are blocked by a lack of governance infrastructure. The SLE market is projected at USD 226,026 million by 2030, with a forecast of 15.3% CAGR. Among decision-makers, 53.7% rank risk reduction first, and 55.2% are considering AI-assisted Secure and Govern capabilities. Mikael Ruohonen, Business Area Lead for AI, Analytics and Agents at Solita, said: "Deploying AI at enterprise scale requires building foundations that enable companies to do this safely: data, context, governance, infrastructure and operations."

Markku Räsänen, CEO of ConfidentialMind, said: "Companies should not have to compromise between the possibilities that AI offers, control over their data and their technology choices." Initial production deployments are planned for the first quarter of 2027. Binding EU procurement rules are expected in the first half of 2027, and rival integrator responses are expected in the same period. NVIDIA is deploying over 3,000 exaflops of Blackwell computing in Europe.

Articles.Title: Solita and ConfidentialMind Target Europe’s Sovereign AI Gap

stories.Headline: NTT DATA and Dell test AI systems at production scale to show boards real-world evidence
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA and Dell Technologies are testing artificial intelligence systems under real-world conditions to show whether they can handle production scale, according to an article dated November 26, 2026. Jeff Ehrenhart, vice president for North America for hybrid infrastructure and AI factory platforms at NTT DATA, said a pilot only shows what is possible. "A pilot proves the possibility that the idea or outcome you wanted is capable of happening," he said. Robert Shear, global alliances chief technology officer at Dell Technologies, said the move to full scale brings problems that are easy to underestimate. "Scale is always harder than it seems," he said.

A pilot may serve 100 users and start with 10 terabytes of data, while a scaled system may reach tens of thousands of users and two petabytes of data, the article says. Bottlenecks can appear in GPUs and the back-end network, and production exposes issues in data movement, latency, storage and networking. Gaps in drift and failover also show up at scale. Boards want evidence on security, governance, costs and projected returns before they approve major AI investments, according to the article.

The business case must show measurable return, including productivity, customer experience and growth, the article says. Technical proof must cover security, legal requirements and maintenance. Sizing tools are weak, and engineers' estimates can differ by orders of magnitude, while a 100-billion-parameter model may cost far more than a 7-billion-parameter one. Testing should cover model performance, time to first token, throughput and latency, and systems rarely scale linearly, so tests should use realistic, lower-quality data.

The NTT DATA AI Factory Munich serves as a testing ground, where AI factories face ransomware and traditional IT attacks as well as AI-specific threats such as prompt injection and data poisoning, according to the article. Data sovereignty affects where data lives. One client upgraded to a 100-gigabit network, while an agentic workflow may need 400- or 800-gigabit networking. Power and cooling constraints can delay projects by many months, and training an own model needs larger systems with liquid cooling, though most organizations stay on the inferencing side.

Dell Technologies supplies compute, storage, AI factory infrastructure, software, GPUs and switching, with infrastructure validated with NVIDIA, and says it has deployed thousands of AI factories, the article reports. NTT DATA supplies workload strategy, data readiness, security, integration and managed services. The article advises chief information officers to use a scorecard for each project rather than one overall, covering output quality, latency, ownership, throughput, resilience, security and integration. Every AI project needs a named owner and a business outcome, and each needs a decision to go, change or stop.

Articles.Title: Turn ambition into evidence: How to prove AI before you scale

stories.headline_source: Turn ambition into evidence: How to prove AI before you scale

stories.Headline: FCC conditionally approves one million SpaceX Starmind satellites to host AI data centers in space
stories.Summary:
The US Federal Communications Commission gave conditional approval on Wednesday to one million satellites for a SpaceX project called Starmind, which would move AI data centers into space and power onboard chips with solar energy. About 15,800 functioning satellites orbit Earth today, at altitudes of 500 to 2,000 kilometers. The Starmind craft would use laser links to existing Starlink satellites. SpaceX hopes to launch the first one as early as 2027.

The approval sets deadlines: the first satellite is required by November 2033, 100,000 by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full constellation by 2040. Google is pursuing similar ideas through a project called Project Suncatcher, and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is pursuing them too. In a filing before its June IPO, SpaceX said the technology "may not achieve commercial viability."

Sir Martin Sweeting, founder of Surrey Satellite Technology, said data transmission "has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data." Olivier Hainaut, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory, led a peer-reviewed study simulating satellite constellations and found that up to 28% of image area could be obscured at the ESO Very Large Telescope in Chile, two hours after nightfall, even with dimmer satellites. Hainaut recommended a limit of about 100,000 dim satellites. Andreas Kaufer, the ESO's director general, said approval "would not only have profound consequences for astronomy, but also fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone."

The American Astronomical Society warned that radio interference and infrared waste heat threaten instruments, and that launches and replacements could pollute the atmosphere, while space debris raises collision risk. The FCC declined extra optical astronomy conditions, deeming a coordination commitment from the National Science Foundation sufficient. The ESO called for international oversight of megaconstellations.

Articles.Title: SpaceX Just Got Approval to Launch One Million AI Satellites. Astronomers Are Horrified

stories.Headline: Todoist says a stolen credential let attackers breach production systems and download early user data
stories.Summary:
Todoist's production systems were breached on November 23, 2026, affecting 6% of its users, the Hacker News reported. The attacker used a stolen credential on a version control system and modified workflows in three repositories. They also took over an employee work account and downloaded a file of early users' account data.

CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion deal, which the Hacker News described as the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record. George Kurtz, CrowdStrike's CEO, said: "Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in"

More than 250 extensions in a set called SleeperWidget were found across Microsoft Edge Add-ons, the Chrome Web Store and Mozilla Add-ons, according to Microsoft's Edge Extensions Security Team. The extensions behave normally unless installed through a paid search ad. Installs made that way collect browsing data, inject ads and alter shopping links. The team said: "Most deliver the features they advertise, which makes hidden behavior easier to miss"

Rapid7 analyzed 20,354 internet-facing hosts and found AI servers and notebook APIs left unauthenticated. It said: "More than half of the exposed Ollama servers in this scan have already been touched by someone who is not the owner" According to Rapid7, 79% of exposed Ollama hosts list a cloud model, and exposed signed-in servers bill the owner's paid subscription.

SonicWall Capture Labs reported SilentNet, a Java remote access trojan and infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service. Its JAR file is disguised as a Minecraft Fabric mod and steals the Minecraft session token from memory. It fetches its command address from a Polygon smart contract and hides a second-stage infostealer in a PNG image. SonicWall said: "Every string in the JAR is hidden by per-character arithmetic"

Phishing pages were built on Hugging Face Spaces using DeepSite, the company's AI website builder, and impersonated 28 brands including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase and Coinbase, according to Aikido. Aikido counted 29 pages built with DeepSite and said a Microsoft login clone took about 90 minutes to build.

VulnCheck reported that 13% of exploitation requests from January to November 2026 were for credential theft, with 127 of 694 CVEs tied to credential harvesting. It said 61% of those CVEs were in open-source and AI developer tools. VulnCheck said: "Attackers search application files, logs and environment variables for database passwords, cloud credentials and API keys" It recorded 1,756 attempts on AI provider credentials, involving 406 IP addresses and 27 CVEs.

According to TrendAI, at least nine organizations were claimed between October 5 and November 9, 2026 by BYOD, a ransomware and extortion group. TrendAI said: "Its attacks have had real-world consequences, including ambulance diversion, more than 30 clinics closed, and campus-wide device shutdowns" The group played audio messages on infected computers, and gained initial access through credential compromise and a remote access trojan.

Wordfence found a fake WordPress plugin with generated names that runs JavaScript for anonymous visitors and stays dormant for logged-in users. It was found in January 2026 and September 2026, and was likely installed through an admin account compromise.

The U.S. Department of Justice said over 17.3 million scam accounts were removed from Meta and 700 fraudulent crypto sites seized in the past six months, with 12 U.S. arrest warrants issued. It said $1,082,260,156.82 in crypto was restrained. Jeanine Ferris Pirro, U.S. Attorney, said: "The Strike Force teams focus on identifying and pursuing key leaders" Kash Patel, FBI Director, said the operation "seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices"

According to the Justice Department's account, over 11,000 Americans were warned, over $690 million in losses prevented, over 29 scam compounds dismantled, over 2,200 trafficked workers repatriated, over $1 billion in stolen crypto frozen and over 1.4 million fraudulent sites and accounts taken down. A 456,602 USDT forfeiture action was filed.

The Justice Department filed a civil action over the theft of Binance crypto, seeking over $1.1 billion, and blamed North Korean actors for the hack on or about October 29. Almost $3 billion in crypto was frozen, seized or returned. Brett Leatherman, Cyber Branch Operations Director at the FBI, said: "North Korea depends on sophisticated laundering techniques to convert stolen cryptocurrency into funds"

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed a return on a new data leak site.

stories.Headline: UK restaurant owners fight AI booking bots by answering phones themselves
stories.Summary:
Restaurant owners in the UK are battling AI bots and returning to telephone booking, the Guardian reported this week. Meta Platforms launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK, and Muse makes restaurant reservations and shops for users. The assistant needs user email permission, and it has had millions of downloads in the US. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots that refresh pages thousands of times and snap up all reservations.

Dave Strauss, co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was named UK restaurant of the year, answers phones daily from 11am. Strauss said that it wasn’t very satisfying as the AI bot didn’t argue back, though he had had an argument with it and told it to never call him again. Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge whose clients include celebrities who pay her for top tables, said: "I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos." Coke books via WhatsApp or phone.

Jeremy King, owner of Simpson’s in the Strand, Arlington and the Park, said: "I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without." Meta deals with Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet let Muse navigate partner sites, according to the Guardian. The Information Commissioner’s Office said on Tuesday that Meta had committed to a voluntary monitoring scheme, and the Competition and Markets Authority said talks changed app terms. 4 Charles Prime Rib, a New York City restaurant, is a popular target for AI agents.

Articles.Title: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings

stories.Summary:
Aaron Painter, CEO of Nametag and author of "Deepfaked," will take part in a fireside chat at an evening event hosted by Tola Capital in Seattle on November 28, 2026. The event will also include an audience Q&A session and networking with founders, investors and security leaders. Attendees will receive a copy of the book, though supplies are limited. Registration requires host approval, and the location is shared with approved guests.

Painter is set to discuss the threat landscape of deepfakes and impersonation, which the event frames as undermining trust and verification, along with technologies and frameworks to address it. He summed up the problem with a question: "how do we know what's real?"

stories.Headline: Economists argue tightly linked messy jobs resist AI best and urge redesigning work around them
stories.Summary:
Luis Garicano, a professor at the London School of Economics, and Jin Li and Yanhui Wu, both of the University of Hong Kong, have written a book titled Messy Jobs: The Work That AI Cannot Reach, published by Upriver Press. The three economists, who work in organizational economics, argue that messy jobs survive AI best. They treat a job as a bundle of linked parts, and say difficulty offers little protection from AI while tightly linked tasks do.

A clean job is a single task that is verifiable and repeated, with truck driving cited as an example, and such jobs are protected mostly by regulation. A messy job, such as a bank relationship manager or a radiologist, is one where removing a single task breaks the whole job. The authors say AI alone achieves little without job redesign, pointing to a study of US police crime-mapping adoption in the 1990s and 2000s by Paul Heaton of the RAND Corporation and a co-researcher. Gains appeared only where officers were redeployed and commanders held accountable, and productivity rises most when jobs are broken apart, though the same process can push wages down.

Junior jobs are a trade of routine work for training, and Garicano said: "The menial tasks are the currency the junior uses to pay the senior." PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer found junior roles seven times more likely to need senior skills, and middle management is seen as the biggest risk. Garicano said: "Middle managers on both sides are probably going to be squeezed," though he accepted the counter-argument that AI may raise demand for managers. AI also weakens recruitment signals like cover letters, so hiring may depend more on personal networks, and Garicano suggests objective tests and grading.

Luigi Zingales, a University of Chicago economist, dissents, saying "messiness is endogenous" and citing the 19th-century example of interchangeable parts; he expects AI may make messy jobs unnecessary. City Journal called the book the best yet on AI and work. The book launches in Hong Kong in June, and Garicano said: "Take the messy job." Li said: "We are now outsourcing memory, attention, comprehension, and communication," and that "the focus must be on redesigning institutions to keep pace with technological change."

Articles.Title: Take the messy job: 3 economists argue AI will spare more work than the doomsayers think

stories.headline_source: Take the messy job: 3 economists argue AI will spare more work than the doomsayers think

stories.Headline: Spelman president Ayanna Howard warns of overtrust in AI in new book
stories.Summary:
Dr. Ayanna Howard, president of Spelman College, discussed AI ethics in a new book during an interview with Geoff Bennett, co-anchor and co-managing editor of PBS News Hour. The book is titled "Rebooting the Machines: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence." Howard began her career in robotics at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and has developed AI and robotics over three decades. She has long been an optimist about the technology and has been interested in robotics since middle school, designing her first AI algorithms in the early 1990s.

Howard's research focuses on "overtrust" in machines. She said people often accept what a machine tells them without question. "We just trust it because we interact with it based on our teacher-student type of relationship," she said. She worries that educators are not teaching responsible use of AI, though she says the technology can aid learning when used responsibly.

Howard said data- and communication-based jobs are most vulnerable to AI, while discipline and expertise protect jobs. She argued that ordinary people hold consumer power over AI and that consumer pressure can shape company choices. She also urged state regulations on AI. According to Howard, "the acceleration over these last five years is more than the last 25 before that." Proceeds from the book will go to Spelman scholarships.

stories.Headline: Meta's Muse agent shares Toronto seller's home address and accepts a low offer without his knowledge
stories.Summary:
Matt Robb, a Toronto-based content creator, listed a computer keyboard on Facebook Marketplace in late September and let Meta's AI agent, called Muse, handle the sale as an experiment. "I kind of went into it like a guinea pig," Robb said. Within a day, a buyer Robb did not know arrived outside his house late at night. Muse had agreed a deal on its own and shared Robb's home address after a pickup agreement, then sent an automated "Yep, I'm here!" message from Robb's account. Robb was unaware of the actions at the time.

Robb had granted "always allow" permissions on his Marketplace profile, where he had shared a pickup address, and he thought Muse would confirm before sharing it. Muse also suggested accepting a price $100 below his set minimum. "Not only did it give my address when the guy asked, and it accepted the offer," Robb said. Meta acknowledged the agent's error to The Associated Press and offered no further comment to AP. Robb and the buyer later made amends, no harm was established from the buyer, and Meta reached out to discuss the failure.

In an October interview with Robb, he said he worried "if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable's house." Robb has largely disconnected Muse from his apps and is testing Grok Bot from Elon Musk's X, which launched in beta in August. Muse launched in September, and its app downloads have skyrocketed since. OpenAI's "always on" AI helpers, called dots, integrate with ChatGPT, Slack and Microsoft Teams.

Veronica Rivera, an assistant professor at Georgia Tech's School of Cybersecurity and Privacy, said: "Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list." She added: "When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it's also reading what your friends and family sent you." Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto Faculty of Information, said there is "no taking back" data the agent has already seen. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the agent is "entirely opt-in."

Jason Aten, a columnist at Inc. Magazine, reported that Muse watched Mac notifications including Messages, and said he did not grant those permissions. Earlier this month, Apple announced new Mac controls. In an Oct. 2 update, Apple said: "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially."

stories.Headline: NVIDIA's Sasha Levin prepares AI agent skills for Linux kernel documentation
stories.Summary:
Sasha Levin, a Linux developer at NVIDIA who co-maintains the Linux LTS branches, has prepared a set of AI agent skills for the kernel's in-tree documentation, Phoronix reported on 26 November 2026. The skills are meant to instruct AI agents on kernel processes. They would live in a new agents/skills directory in the kernel source tree, on a branch called "agents." Levin sent his mailing list message about the work the same day as the report.

The series holds five initial skills. One determines "Fixes:" tags on patches, one determines stable tags, one finds other instances of a fixed bug, one writes commit messages and one writes KUnit tests. Levin intends to submit the work to Linus Torvalds for mainline inclusion. The Linux 7.5 merge window opens in late December.

The "agents" branch was dropped from linux-next, according to Phoronix, which said the removal was not a fix and came late in the Linux 7.4 cycle. Levin said in his message: "It contains the agent skills series, which I intend to send to Linus." Whether the skills are accepted depends on any objections from Torvalds.

stories.Headline: Blogger Jan-Lukas Else says AI coding agents renew his enjoyment of self-hosting
stories.Summary:
Jan-Lukas Else, the author of a blog post, wrote that his enthusiasm for self-hosting had faded over the years but that AI has renewed his excitement for it. He keeps his infrastructure configuration in Git repositories, as Docker Compose files and scripts, and AI coding agents now work on those configurations. He wrote that this makes it less effort to try new services, adjust existing configurations and automate tasks, and that he now acts on spontaneous ideas.

Else uses NixOS more extensively on his home server and built a Debian-based bootc image for a VPS. He said the bootc image took half a day to set up, where he estimates it would have taken at least a week without AI. Build, update and deployment processes are automated: Renovate creates software update pull requests, and a single Git push triggers deployment, with GitHub Actions and Forgejo Actions running the workflows.

He moved services from the VPS to his home server. The prior home server was an HP t640 thin client, and he now uses an ASRock DeskMini A300 with the CPU upgraded to an AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G. The stock AMD cooler was replaced with a Noctua cooler, and the CPU and cooler were bought via a classifieds site.

Else also built tools to download invoices, e-papers and Linux ISOs, written in the Go programming language. He noted that AI-generated software still has bugs and security issues, and that he uses mostly open-weight models. "AI hasn't fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting," he wrote. "And now, I'm having a lot of fun with it again."

OpenAI, an AI model developer, released Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 on November 26, 2026, and the releases were widely panned, according to micjm.com. Data from micjm suggests the models were tuned for cost savings. Output tokens per task dropped, and reasoning tokens per task dropped.

On a chart plotting spend ratio against opponents on the x-axis and Elo from the micjm leaderboard on the y-axis, Astra and Sol reason less than their opponents. Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 were normal models, while Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 became outliers. The drop in Sol output had a p-value of 0.0055 and the drop in Astra output a p-value of 0.022. The drop in Sol reasoning had a p-value of 0.00013 and the drop in Astra reasoning a p-value of 0.0064.

Micjm concluded that the models were cost tuned compared with their predecessors, and it called them underthinking outliers.

Genesys Cloud Services, Inc. announced Genesys Standalone AI Agents and Genesys Arena in San Francisco on 17 November 2026. The company calls itself a global leader in agentic orchestration for customer experience. Standalone AI Agents deploy an Agentic Virtual Agent without a full migration, keeping existing customer service technology and workflows. According to Genesys, the agents can be live in days.

The AI hands off conversation context to human staff. Arena offers prebuilt agent kits by industry, covering more than 50 industry use cases, and Genesys says a working AI agent can be built in as little as 10 minutes. The tools include natural-language customization and pre-deployment testing. Genesys introduced effort-based pricing with three tiers, named simple, medium and complex, and usage is measured in Experience Units, the new name for AI Tokens.

Tony Bates, chairman and CEO of Genesys, said: "企業はAIの導入を加速させたいと考える一方で、信頼性やガバナンスを損なうことなく、自社の方針や状況に応じて柔軟に導入を進める必要があります" Youssef Nokta, senior vice president of AI-forward deployed engineering at Genesys, said: "AIが急速に進化する中、企業が新たなアイデアを実用化するたびに、すべてをゼロから構築する必要はありません" Michael Buttsworth, associate director of the Student Experience Services Centre at Charles Sturt University, said: "Genesys ArenaとAgent Kitsは、AIエージェントを構築し、顧客、業務運用、ブランドに合わせて調整するための基盤を提供することで、実際の業務への導入を容易にします" Mila D'Antonio, principal analyst for customer engagement at Omdia, said: "Genesys ArenaとGenesys Standalone AI Agentsは、既存の環境や要件に応じてエージェンティックAIを導入するための異なる選択肢を提供します"

Standalone AI Agents are now generally available. Agent Kits are to become generally available via Arena during November 2026. Genesys says it serves over 8,000 organizations worldwide.

stories.Headline: Formula 1 teams use AI to analyze car data and shape 2026 engine power delivery
stories.Summary:
Formula 1 teams are using artificial intelligence to find patterns in the data their cars collect, and the technology is now part of the 2026 engines, Madeline Coleman wrote in The Athletic on Nov. 28, 2026, in an article for the "Changing Lanes" series on AI and engineering. The championship began in 1950, and the sport became data-driven in the 1980s, when simple sensors and telemetry started gathering information. Honda built a data logger in 1985, and Williams first used it in 1986, allowing real-time remote monitoring. Data technology advanced quickly in the 1990s.

Teams use Monte Carlo simulation to model the probability of tire life and machine learning to compare live race data with historical data. At the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix, Ferrari pitted Lewis Hamilton after a Valtteri Bottas crash, but the safety car became a red flag and no time was gained. A 2017 Google paper on machine learning, written by eight researchers, introduced Transformers, which underpin modern generative AI strategy tools. AI also supports car design, aerodynamics and driver simulator training. AWS tools designed the 2022-2025 ground-effect rules, cutting simulation time from 60 hours to 12 hours, and AWS became the FIA's partner for AI and cloud.

James Smith, Williams' chief information officer, said: "Formula 1 has always been the ultimate test of man and machine. I call it the World Cup of Engineering." Andrea Stella, the McLaren team boss, said at July's Belgian Grand Prix that the engines' AI adjusts power based on the previous lap, adding: "This is quite difficult for the drivers to master." Williams also uses AI in human resources, finance and legal work. Smith said: "Any time we make a human better, we save money, and that's more money we can spend on the car to make the car faster." He added: "In F1, money effectively equals milliseconds (on track)."

A cost cap has been in operation since 2021, and AI spending falls within it, with no separate AI budget restriction. Smith said: "We can't afford a large amount of unfunded experiments." Each car carries about 300 sensors and generates 1.1 million data points per second, with a race typically lasting about 90 minutes, while soccer generates 680 million data points per match. Michael Aghataher, AWS' head of motorsports, said its tools "optimized and freed up 68 hours of time for the engineer" and that "Our strategy within the sport has always been optimizing human performance." Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli won the 2026 title in Mexico last month. Smith said: "The combination of man and machine, the human and the engineering aspect, is what makes it so exciting." Williams team principal James Vowles said: "If AI makes our aerodynamicists more efficient, I'm probably going to hire more of them, not less, because it's a better return on investment."

stories.Headline: AFL-CIO calls for enforceable AI worker protections at US retailers
stories.Summary:
Labor leaders and advocates called on November 27, 2026, for worker and consumer protections at US retailers, where the use of artificial intelligence is expanding. The push renewed attention on hiring, scheduling and monitoring, and brought calls for guardrails and regulation. The debate centers on employer accountability and on whether workers can challenge automated decisions. The AFL-CIO wants enforceable protections and a worker voice in the technology. Its principles cover automated scheduling, discipline, pay, hiring and firing, as well as worker monitoring and evaluation.

The federation seeks labor participation in research, development and deployment, employer-worker negotiations on technology, and accountability when AI harms workers. It says safeguards should support job quality, safety, economic security and labor rights. The Home Furnishings Association, a management-side group, published guidance on AI authority the same day. That guidance cites screening sales-floor applicants and delivery and warehouse applicants, and a schedule-change request from a worker with a sick parent.

It recommends that people remain responsible for decisions and assigns AI decisions to business leadership. It urges documenting decisions, and says executives should decide AI's role in pricing, hiring and customer service. The association's guidance notes that software can gain authority through vendor features, team experiments and chatbots without leadership explicitly approving decisions. The article text was truncated mid-sentence.

stories.Headline: NITES urges government to adopt safeguards protecting tech workers from AI job displacement
stories.Summary:
The Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES) has called for a comprehensive policy framework to protect tech employees from job displacement caused by AI, automation and emerging technologies, yourstory.com reported on 26 November 2026. The employee body wants safeguards for tech workers and is urging the government to consult stakeholders, including employee representatives, on the issue. It has called for a responsible AI adoption policy alongside a workforce protection policy. NITES said advancement is important to industry growth, but adoption must not deny workers adequate notice, financial security or chances at alternative employment. According to the body, employees and government authorities must know the number affected, the reasons for eliminations and the jobs replaced by technology, and it demanded transparency in workforce reductions, including where cuts are attributed to AI or automation.

It pitched mandatory safeguards for affected employees, including reasonable advance notice, fair severance compensation and payment of outstanding statutory and contractual dues. The body wants re-skilling and redeployment tried before positions are eliminated, and it wants stronger, more specific safeguards than existing labour laws, which give retrenchment protection to eligible workers. NITES said: "Re-skilling must be meaningful and outcome-oriented." It added that "merely providing access to online courses or training material cannot be considered adequate support," and urged genuine efforts to equip employees for alternative roles and future employment opportunities.

NITES said: "Employees should not be left to bear the entire burden of technological change." It also said "technology should move the industry forward without leaving its workforce behind." According to the body, "the increasing impact of AI on employment now requires a dedicated policy-level discussion involving the government, Nasscom, IT companies and employee representatives." NITES has previously opposed mass layoffs, forced resignations and unfair employment practices, though its earlier representations did not focus on AI job losses, and it now sees a changed employment landscape.

stories.Headline: Recent graduates use AI to apply for jobs while employers use AI to screen them
stories.Summary:
Mahathi Vinapamula, a recent San Jose State graduate, used AI to search openings and apply quickly, tailor her resume for marketing jobs and rehearse interview questions with a voice assistant. She graduated with a business administration degree in May and applied to about 500 jobs over a yearlong search. In one case, an AI hiring agent decided whether she got a second human interview. "Although AI has helped automate a lot of these processes, I think we're probably in that stage where it also creates a lot more work," Vinapamula said.

Applicants use AI to polish cover letters and mass apply to positions, while employers use AI screening tools on large applicant pools, a feedback loop that makes conventional hiring more unpleasant. In a survey of more than 3,000 hiring managers by Hirevue, 43% of organizations said they use AI to screen resumes and 40% said they use AI to communicate with candidates. Christie Brodbeck, Hirevue's vice president of customer science, described "AI-polished, look-alike" resumes and cover letters. Employers also use application exercises to assess candidate skills.

Raciel Diaz, a San Francisco State University business administration graduate who has worked as a full stack developer, caregiver and Walnut Creek receptionist, submitted hundreds of applications over the past year. "The advent of AI onto the job market has just been a pain in my ass," Diaz said. "Now I gotta get through their AI (applicant tracking systems) and then figure out what they want." Diaz added: "I've almost gone through the stages of grief, you know? I was really sad, really depressed, really angry." Diaz also said: "At this point, I just throw my application everywhere, no matter what company it is."

Sue Harbour, UC Berkeley Career Engagement associate dean and executive director, said "Relationship building has always been important, but I feel like it's something that will give students a leg up today more so than ever." She urges students to tap networks over mass applications and to "work smarter, not harder," and says students need demonstrable skills plus AI fluency. Iman Noor, a San Jose State senior majoring in accounting, secured a full-time position at Deloitte before spring graduation after getting a referral from a friend at the firm. Diana Phuong, Braven Bay Area executive director, said: "It's not what you know, it's not what your resume says, but it's really who you know and who knows you in this world." Braven is a nonprofit helping college students launch careers, and some regional companies are hiring fewer entry-level workers: 54% of 2024 San Jose State Braven graduates were employed or in grad school six months on, compared with 43% of 2025 graduates.

Brian Justie, a UCLA Labor Center senior research analyst, said the shift "kind of brings the process of getting a job back to some very old model where it's actually probably only based on your existing connections." Jesse Rothstein, director of the UC Berkeley Center for Studies in Higher Education, said the labor market has slightly softened and recent graduates are hit harder, with employers offloading job-search costs onto seekers and conducting more interviews since the Great Recession. Job seekers doubt whether postings are real, and Rothstein said: "It just makes it a lot harder to get through all the chum as you're trying to look for a job." Vinapamula ended her marketing job hunt and will pursue a master's at Santa Clara University. She said: "I think I would have better luck if there's an actual human that I'm speaking to, but at the same time I understand why companies are using them."

"Even with AI in the mix, nothing changes the fact that mediation remains voluntary, confidential and participants retain complete decision-making control," Helie and Melamed said.

stories.Headline: Kaiser urges Congress to set a national AI framework instead of fragmented state rules
stories.Summary:
Kent Kaiser, executive director of the Trade Alliance to Promote Prosperity, argued that the United States cannot regulate its way to victory in artificial intelligence. He urged officials to take rising public concerns about AI risks seriously, pointing to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. In exit polls, 56% of voters said data centers were a major or crucial factor in their votes, and data centers and AI appeared on ballots through initiatives and candidates.

Kaiser warned that fragmented regulation could slow US innovation and let China race ahead. He said the race will determine global leadership for generations, and that the question is whether the US or China leads in technology. He cited US advantages including technology companies, universities, entrepreneurs and investors, and said China has made technological dominance a national priority, investing in AI, energy, semiconductors, talent and infrastructure.

Kaiser called for a response built on private investment, competition and intellectual property protections. Warning that fragmented rules across 50 states would impede competition with China, he called the state bills unhelpful and said in 2026 in states were introduced more than 1,500 AI-related bills. He urged Congress to establish a clear national framework, along with permitting reform, domestic energy, infrastructure and supply chains. "We cannot expect America to win a global technology race while running 50 different regulatory playbooks," Kaiser said.

stories.Headline: CAA chief Bryan Lourd urges Congress to pass NO FAKES Act on AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill regulating unauthorized AI deepfakes. He made the appeal in a New York Times opinion piece, arguing that every person should have the right to refuse unwanted use of their likeness. The legislation was introduced by Senator Chris Coons of Maine in May, following a previous attempt last year. While it advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, the full Senate has not yet taken it up. Lourd wrote that the bill would establish a federal standard for control, consent and compensation surrounding deepfakes.

The NO FAKES Act would replace what Lourd called outdated, ill-fitting state laws written for an analog world. It would establish federal protections against the creation and distribution of unauthorized digital replicas of a person's voice or likeness. Under the framework, individuals would have the right to authorize or reject the use of their digital likenesses. Companies would be required to negotiate and pay for authorized commercial uses of those replicas. Lourd said the bill delivers what the industry needs and will protect all Americans, famous or not.

Lourd described himself as a practitioner rather than a policymaker, running a global talent agency. He said part of his job is helping clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies. He argued that existing principles governing copyright, contracts and licensing can be applied to AI-generated replicas. Lourd said the solution does not require Congress to create an entirely new legal framework. He framed the dispute as one over permission rather than technological advancement, saying Hollywood is not afraid of new technology.

Lourd cited Tom Hanks, who warned followers in 2023 about a dental office using an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Hanks likely would not have agreed to the dental ad, Lourd wrote, but he should have been given a choice. Lourd also pointed to a content creator whose likeness was used in an advertisement for erectile dysfunction supplements. He mentioned voice actors who discovered recordings originally made for research purposes had been turned into commercial voice clones. These examples underscore a growing concern across the entertainment business as generative AI makes exploitation easy.

Deepfakes have been a constant presence since large-language models emerged in 2022, with many producing unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. The NO FAKES Act has attracted support from SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America and the Recording Academy. Other backers include the National Association of Broadcasters, OpenAI, the AFL-CIO, YouTube, IBM and Google. CAA has worked with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions for their likenesses. The agency also joined an amicus brief in the New York Times lawsuit against OpenAI, noting the active licensing market for likenesses.

Lourd is asking Congress to establish a basic rule that just because someone can digitally recreate a person does not mean they have the right to do so. He wrote that what is missing is a bright-line rule affirming that right in the AI age, one Congress can supply before the year is out. Lourd is urging the full Congress to pass the NO FAKES Act and deliver it to President Trump for signature. The articles do not state whether the House of Representatives has scheduled a vote on the bill. They also leave open whether President Trump would sign the legislation if it reaches his desk.

stories.Headline: European Commission suffers cyberattack involving use of AI
stories.Summary:
The European Commission, the EU executive body, has reported a cyberattack on its EU Academy online learning site in which names and email addresses were leaked, according to finance.biggo.com. On November 23, 2026, the breach was announced, after October 22 saw the detection of anomalies and October 26 brought confirmation of the attack. The Commission said publicly available AI tools were used, and it disclosed this at a press conference on November 19. Some of the leaked users were outside EU institutions, and the number affected is unknown.

Several applications were temporarily suspended after the attack, though most have since been restored. The EU Academy has been offline since November 11, 2026, and will reopen on January 14, 2027. Users must re-register, and past course records will not be carried over. No individual notifications were issued; instead, a warning was posted on the site about phishing, impersonation and spam, and the European Data Protection Supervisor was notified.

Thomas Regnier, a Commission spokesperson, said: "We did not reach out to individual users; from a transparency standpoint, we posted a general message for all users on the website." He said the containment timeline is under investigation, and the Commission plans additional security measures. An EDPS spokesperson said the supervisor "has received notifications from the European Commission and is being informed in stages," adding that its staff are in regular contact with the Commission and that it cannot comment further while the matter is ongoing. The EDPS declined to judge whether the notification was adequate.

The Hacker News reported that the Commission was hit earlier by ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that researchers link to cyber espionage, and that the intrusion breached Commission HR, medical reimbursement and translation systems. The same outlet reported that attackers using AI agents breached Swiss systems, with four of five confirmed attacks succeeding and three targeting critical infrastructure operators, two of which succeeded. Florian Schütz, director of Switzerland's National Cyber Security Centre, gave the figures in an SRF interview on November 26, 2026. A Swiss agency advisory published on November 24 said agents compromised IT systems in every known case and that "these cases represent a shift in the cyber threat landscape."

stories.Headline: ECB survey finds 44% of euro area workers use AI weekly and 18% daily
stories.Summary:
A survey by the European Central Bank found that 44% of employed consumers in the euro area used artificial intelligence at work every week, with about 18% using it daily. The findings come from the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey, which polled about 19,000 adults each month across Belgium, Germany, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal and Finland. Fieldwork ran from 6 to 24 August 2026, and the ECB published the results in a blog on 27 November 2026.

Among workers who use AI, 56% said they completed more work and 47% said the quality of their output was higher. Finding information was cited as a benefit by 62%, and 51% pointed to less effort. Respondents expected 46% of their sector to use AI in five years, up from 34% a year earlier. The authors of the ECB blog, Dimitris Georgarakos, Geoff Kenny and Justus Meyer, wrote that "adoption is already mainstream" but that workers report a verification tax, with time spent checking AI output cited as a barrier to productivity gains.

The survey also found that more than 50% of respondents had used AI at work in May 2026, and an ECB post on 26 August 2026 noted 52% ever-use. Among those who said AI saved them time, the median saving was three hours a week, which the authors estimated would amount to an economy-wide saving of about 3.8% if half of all workers saved time. Non-users cited skills, privacy and security as barriers, and daily users still supported regulation. The authors said comparisons between the United States and the euro area are directional only, and the survey includes personal or shadow AI use, not just approved tools.

stories.Headline: AI misidentifies prong count on old barbed wire before correcting itself
stories.Summary:
An AI was asked to identify and date a piece of barbed wire during a field trip to an oak grove at Sallieyland about a month before the article. The AI said the wire was four-pronged barbed wire. Whit Gibbons, a professor of zoology at the University of Georgia Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, counted only three prongs per node. The AI disagreed when challenged on the prong count, then reconsidered and corrected itself.

The wire was estimated to be consistent with specimens from the 1880s, and a photo caption put its age at 140 years. Nicolett Cagle, a researcher familiar with barbed wire analysis, said the wire was "consistent with specimens from the 1880s."

The oak line was explained as an old fencerow with wire-wrapped trees, and birds were ruled out as an explanation for it. A botanist's coring is planned to determine the trees' ages and to test whether the trees predate the barbed wire fence.

stories.Headline: UAE education and AI offices launch a parents guide to AI in education and child safety
stories.Summary:
The Education Ministry and the AI Minister of State Office launched the “Parent’s Guide to Artificial Intelligence in Education” in Dubai on 26th November, 2026, Gulf News reported. The guide is part of a national initiative for parents navigating AI in education. It covers online safety, privacy, responsible AI use and children’s development.

The guide explains machine learning, generative AI, algorithms and data, and covers four key areas of child development: cognitive, social-emotional, physical, and digital-ethical development. It advises verifying the accuracy of AI-generated information, safeguarding personal data and privacy, and setting healthy digital device boundaries. It also sets out seven core areas of the school AI curriculum, which was introduced in public schools in the 2025, 2026 academic year under the directives of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, UAE Vice President and Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai. The guide is available at ai.gov.ae as a PDF link.

On 27th November, 2026, the Ministry of Education warned of eight potential AI risks for children, Gulf News reported from Abu Dhabi. The risks are inaccurate, incomplete or outdated information; bias and discrimination from training data; accepting unverified AI responses as facts; poor decision-making from over-reliance on AI; exposure of sensitive information; unintentional disclosure by children; data storage and third-party access; and unsafe or inappropriate results. The ministry urged critical evaluation of AI-generated information.

stories.Headline: South Korea expects 96.8% export growth in November as AI chip demand surges
stories.Summary:
A Reuters poll of eight economists, published Friday, November 27, 2026, forecasts that South Korea's exports grew 96.8% year-on-year in November. That would follow 93.9% growth in October and mark the fastest expansion since January 1974, according to the poll. It would also be the 18th consecutive month of trade growth. South Korea last week became the fourth country to reach $1 trillion in exports, after Germany, the US and China.

The poll's median estimate puts imports up 38.9% in November, after a 36% rise in October, the biggest import jump since November 2021. The trade surplus is forecast at $48.03 billion, up from $42.65 billion the prior month. Exports in the first 20 days of November rose 101.5% to $77.4 billion, with chip sales up 294.4% and accounting for nearly half the total. The Bank of Korea raised its 2027 growth forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%, which would be the fastest rate since 2021.

Park Sang-Hyun, chief economist at iM Securities, said: "Continued strength in semiconductor exports means November exports are projected to set a new monthly record." He added: "Robust shipments to the US and China will remain key drivers of overall export growth." Stephen Lee, chief economist at Meritz Securities, said: "Exports have continued to accelerate throughout the second half of the year." (0000 GMT). The poll notes anxiety over the chip-dependent economy if AI spending slows.

stories.Headline: Russian AI model completes unfinished Gogol novel and draws criticism
stories.Summary:
A Russian AI model has created a version of the lost second volume of Nikolai Gogol's novel Dead Souls. Gogol, the writer of Dead Souls, burned part of the manuscript before his death in 1852, and only one of the three volumes he planned survived intact. The new book is titled "Dead Souls: Revival" and was produced by the AI model GigaChat, developed by Sber, a banking and technology conglomerate. Linguists, engineers and historians took part in the project.

The project took about four months to develop the literary style. Vladislav Otroshenko, the writer who headed the project and served as its art curator, said of the model: "It handled the artistic side of the task, and the plot element in particular, very well." He also said, "It is a bestseller ... Readers are genuinely interested in it," and, "Does it have artistic value? Of course it does."

Gogol was born in what is now Ukraine and wrote his major works in Russian, known for satire and dark comedy. The first volume features the swindler Chichikov, whose scam is based on dead serf peasants, and Gogol intended a moral regeneration of his protagonist. The book was launched and presented on October 28, 2026, at a bookstore in Moscow. Igor, a Muscovite at the launch, said, "The book is truly unique." Larisa, a visitor to the Gogol Museum, said, "It will not move me and I don't even want to rea."

stories.Headline: Amazon and eBay block some AI shopping agents while Walmart and Sephora admit them
stories.Summary:
Amazon, eBay, United Airlines and Kohl's are limiting or blocking some actions by AI shopping agents, while Walmart and Sephora have opened their sites to them, according to shattered.io. The split has defined agentic commerce in the 2026 holiday season. EBay restricts agent access in certain cases. EBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand said, "we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace." EBay cites unauthorized scraping and data training.

In September 2026 Amazon blocked Meta's Muse, saying it had not agreed to the Muse program. An Amazon spokesperson said, "Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations," and "we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience." Reports describe Amazon-Meta talks on restoring Muse access, but there is no confirmed deal, timetable or terms. Amazon has also sued Perplexity over agentic shopping activity, alleging Perplexity ignored stop requests; no court has ruled on the suit. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said, "it has to be a good customer experience, which it hasn't been to date," and "it has to be a fair exchange of value." Jassy did not rule out opening Amazon to agents.

JPMorgan Chase bars outside agents from customer accounts, and CEO Jamie Dimon called it "too risky." Cars.com and Amtrak were reported inaccessible to some AI agents, and Cloudflare helps websites restrict unwanted AI visitors. One person, Bittner, said, "I sort of trust Google to only surface sites that are not scams to me in their sponsored ads." Meta's Muse is tied to arrangements with Walmart, Gap, Sephora and Best Buy, and Amazon promotes its own Alexa for Shopping assistant.

In a November 25, 2026 NPR Morning Edition segment, NPR reporter Stephan Bisaha reported that 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping, according to the National Retail Federation. At the September 29, 2026 OpenAI developers conference in San Francisco, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced "dots" personal assistant agents, positioned to rival Meta's Muse.

stories.Headline: Employers urged to audit AI hiring tools and add human review to curb bias
stories.Summary:
AI recruitment tools can process applications quickly, but systems trained on historical hiring data may repeat existing biases and reject candidates with unconventional experience, Computing UK reported on 17 November 2026. The article said the increasing use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has made candidates feel their own true voice is unacceptable. It said applications are tweaked to make them more machine-parsable and chatbots are deployed to craft "more professional" CVs. It said the result is that all applications start to look alike, each written in slick, bland corporatese. It said the majority will be rejected automatically, without a human being as much as glancing at them.

The article said employers should combine automation with human intervention, examine rejected applications, track outcomes across demographic groups and scrutinise training data before procuring hiring technology. It said keyword filters may misinterpret career gaps, caring responsibilities and informal business experience. It said employers should audit rejected candidates and measure progression through each recruitment stage. It said IT and HR leaders should examine training data, bias controls and human-oversight provisions before buying recruitment software. It said these steps should be taken at the procurement stage if possible.

Abhijit Bhaduri, a former Microsoft general manager for global learning and development and author of the forthcoming AIdentity, said "It's a very, very poor system." He said automated systems cannot judge what really makes people tick, nor can they predict how they will perform as part of a team. He said "I think it's absolutely stupid to outsource the best part about building a really unique combination of people and to do it through machines. It's a tragedy." He said HR AI systems can be efficient for sorting but can be used the wrong way, optimising what can be measured rather than what makes an individual valuable.

He said organisations need to stop confusing efficiency with effective hiring. Karen Blake, head of the Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion in Science and Health coalition and a member of the Women in Tech Taskforce at the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said automated tools have introduced a distance between candidate and hirer. She said many talented people are being screened out, often without feedback and sometimes within hours of applying, while organisations become increasingly indecisive with roles left open for months. She said someone who spent three years caring for a parent with dementia has learned patience and judgement, and someone who helped run the family shop as a teenager probably understands margins and customers better than most graduates. She said biases built unwittingly into automated systems particularly disadvantage returners, women, neurodivergent candidates, older workers and those with unconventional career paths.

She said "These systems process applications in huge numbers, so a single flaw gets repeated thousands of times and ends up deciding who is treated as a candidate at all." The article said the recruitment playing field has never been level, and those who went to the right school or have been coached in professional-sounding corporate language have always had an advantage. It said the mass standardisation of speech patterns by LLMs has created a new norm that "feeds recruitment's oldest habit of hiring the safe bet," Blake asserted. It said the promise that AI will reduce headcount is already threatening the first rung of the career ladder in several professions.

It said Bhaduri believes future jobs will arise at the intersections between existing disciplines, and that hunar, "the irreducible human signature formed by lived experience, judgment, taste, memory, victory, failure, culture, instinct and practice," cannot be replicated by AI. It said Bhaduri suggests choosing three candidates from an automated system but seven from a different system where somebody who doesn't fit the mould can come in. The article said Blake advises focusing on being curious rather than looking impressive, and that your network matters far more than your followers. It said Bhaduri insists developing hunar means avoiding becoming over-reliant on chatbots, starting with the human first.

It said overuse of chatbots risks reducing an individual's distinctiveness towards a common denominator and has a deleterious effect on memory and sense-building. It said Blake states "AI tools are often trained on your past hiring and can only find people who look like your past, and your past is rarely what your future needs." It said recruitment tools are often bought for reasons of speed and cost, but procurers should also scrutinise the training data and measures used to reduce bias. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Taiwan puts nuclear power on the ballot amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
Taiwan is holding a referendum on Saturday, 28 November 2026, on scrapping its pledge to be a nuclear-free homeland. The vote was called by the Democratic Progressive Party, Taiwan's ruling party, which has long opposed nuclear power. It comes as demand from artificial intelligence and semiconductors strains Taiwan's grid. The Maanshan reactor in Pingtung was shut in May 2025, a move that made Taiwan nuclear-free.

The referendum asks voters whether to drop the nuclear-free homeland commitment. The DPP has opposed nuclear power for years, and the party's leader, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te, has explored reviving it. The Maanshan shutdown in Pingtung in May 2025 ended nuclear generation on the island. The strain on the grid comes from AI and semiconductor demand.

Analysts, who were not named, said the vote "could also offer Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te a way out of a political dilemma." The Lai administration has explored reviving nuclear power. The referendum is the DPP's, and Lai is the Taiwanese leader. The analysts' comment was reported by the South China Morning Post.
